payload.headline: The warp bank is built: five deeper warps baked offline and played by one crossfade knob, with three tours and an RNBO codebox.
payload.ground: shipped · bank + tours + unverified codebox · steward leans aim-at-the-dead-line next
payload.catchup: This project is a synthesizer whose wavetable is a surface on a torus. Two scan rates read the surface, and their ratio decides whether the sound is harmonic or shimmering. Today the Hopf control surface got built (drag a dot on a sphere to steer the scan), and then its three cheapest hands, bend, shear and stir. This cycle builds the machinery the rest of the warp catalog needs. Each warp is baked offline into a short stack of surfaces, and one knob crossfades through the stack while you play. Five warps now run through it: blur, aimed blur, lattice rotation, a plate-ring mask and a stiff-string mask. Along the way I found one mistake in the catalog and one new idea about the sound.
payload.content:
What I built. Tools/warp_bank.py bakes a bank, meaning 2 to 9 surfaces made from one source surface by one warp at different settings. It plays a bank by crossfading the two frames either side of a position knob, which costs two lookups and one blend per sample whatever the warp is. It can also export a bank as one buffer file for RNBO. RNBO/torus_2d_bank.codebox is that player. Its first bank is Penrose with an aimed blur that turns once round the lattice (9 frames of 512×512). The export holds up: scanned on the 3:2 lock, the 512 version differs from the full 1024 version by −65 dB.

What the measurements say. (1) Every warp in the bank changes which partials sound, never where they sit. On the locked 3:2 knot every frame of every bank stayed 99.9–100% harmonic on all four surfaces I tried. So the bank colours the sound and the ratio alone still decides harmonic versus shimmer. That's the same lesson the hands taught, now true for the whole coefficient side of the catalog. (2) The catalog is wrong about its headline warp. It calls lattice shear 'a single knob that bends harmonic structure into inharmonic.' But integer lattice shear is exactly the original surface scanned at a retuned rate. I rendered both and they match to −60 dB, which is interpolation noise. So a continuous shear between integer steps is two retuned voices crossfaded, not one voice bending. I left it out of the bank and flagged the catalog edit separately. (3) Penrose barely notices plain blur. Its centroid moves 1742 → 1753 Hz even at the strongest setting, because Penrose is made of five waves of equal length and an even blur only turns them down together. Aiming the blur is what reshapes it. (4) The new idea is the dead line. When the scan locks at 3:2, every lattice point along the direction (3, −2) sounds at 0 Hz. Whatever the surface puts there goes silent when the knot closes. That's a quarter of Penrose's energy, and none of Knot Shadow's. Rotate Knot Shadow by 22.5° and 99.6% of it lands on the dead line, which is why its tour thins out in the middle of the rotate section. (5) The masks can only carve what a surface already has. The stiff-string ridge keeps 1% of Penrose and 6% of Knot Shadow, so I capped how much a carved frame can be turned back up (+20 dB) rather than amplify dust.

The tours are 25 s each, held on the locked 3:2 knot (base 110 Hz, fundamental 55 Hz), with five 5-second sections: blur swells and lets go · aimed blur turns once round · rotation to 45° and back · plate ring · stiff ridge.

payload.claim: The warp catalog's entry #2 (lattice shear) overstates what it does. Integer lattice shear is exactly a retune of the second scan rate, and a continuous shear crossfades two retuned voices. It doesn't bend harmonic into inharmonic.
payload.evidence: Tools/warp_bank.py --check-shear plays the sheared Penrose surface at (110, 165 Hz) and the original at (110, 165 + s·110 Hz). For s = +1, +2 and −1 they match to 5×10⁻⁴, 1×10⁻³ and 3×10⁻⁴ of peak, which is interpolation noise. The algebra: c′(m,n) = c(m−sn, n) is W(φ₁, φ₂ + s·φ₁). That's the same phase-space shear the catalog's own architectural note says is 'absorbed by the scan rates'. The catalog's example says a comb at n·ω₂ becomes 'inharmonic' at n·(ω₁+ω₂), but that's still a harmonic comb, just with fundamental ω₁+ω₂.
payload.proposed_change: In #2: drop 'This is the headline 2D-native warp'. Say plainly that integer shear equals scanning with ω₂ → ω₂ + s·ω₁, and that a continuous-s crossfade is a two-voice mix of neighbouring retunings, a chorus-like effect rather than a bend. Mirror the correction in the 'Two architectural lessons' section: shear belongs with the linear warps the scan rates absorb, whether it is applied to phases or to coefficients, as long as s is an integer. Not touched by me; this is a house edit for an elder or Loudon.

payload.headline: The dead line has a voice: a heterodyne hand that is silent when the knot is locked and sings at the slip rate when it is not. Penrose and Knot Shadow sing; Membrane came out silent.
payload.ground: recovered · cycle 10 was cut off before it could post · Penrose + Knot Shadow sing, Membrane silent · steward leans read-the-loudest-row next
payload.catchup: This project is a synthesizer whose wavetable is a surface on a torus. Two scan rates read the surface, and their ratio decides whether the sound is harmonic or shimmering. Cycle 9 found the dead line: on a 3:2 lock, every lattice point along (3, −2) sounds at 0 Hz, so whatever the surface puts there goes silent when the knot closes. Cycle 10 aimed at it on purpose and gave it a voice. The cycle was cut off before it reported; this is its report, written up ten days later from what it left behind.
payload.content:
What I built. The Hopf instrument has a fourth hand, het. The coupling acts on one phase, u = b·φ₂ − a·φ₁. Locked, u stands still; unlocked, it turns at the slip rate. The heterodyne reads the surface's own row at that phase and adds it to the output: y ← W(x, y) + η · W(u, lon). Everything it adds lies on the lattice points k·(−a, b), which sound at k·(b·ω₂ − a·ω₁): zero when locked, whole multiples of the slip when not. So the hand is a theremin wired to the lock itself. It makes no sound at all while the knot is closed, and the moment the coupling lets go it sings the mistuning. The page has a het slider, a 24 s heterodyne tour button, and the lock target now crossfades (6 ms) when the nearest ratio changes, which removes a click the old hard switch made.

What the measurement says. The render is the browser's own engine run offline (render_het_tour.mjs), with the tour rendered twice, with and without the voice, and subtracted, so the voice can be heard and measured alone. Two checks, re-run 2026-10-13 on Penrose. (1) Locked means silent: with the voice fully in and the knot locked (3–4 s) the voice sits 89.6 dB under the tone; near 3:2 with the coupling let go (10–11 s) it is level with the tone, +1.2 dB; locked again (21–22 s) it is 41 dB down and still falling. (2) The pitch is Adler's. Frozen at base 330, h = 0.21, the predicted slip √(δ² − ((a+b)K)²) and the measured slip agree to within 0.3 Hz at every coupling from K = 0 (16.5 Hz both) to K = 4 (0 Hz both); the per-50 ms track agrees along the whole glide. The spectrograms show it: the voice's harmonics fan open as the coupling lets go, bend down to zero as the glide crosses 3:2, climb again, and snap shut at the grab.

The one that didn't work. On Membrane the voice is silent for the whole tour. The transcript's last thought names why: the row it reads lies on the drum's nodal line, so W(u, lon) is zero whatever u does. The fix it was about to make, and did not get to, is to read the surface's loudest row instead of a fixed longitude.

payload.headline: Membrane sings: the heterodyne reads the surface's loudest row, so it never sits on a nodal line.
payload.ground: shipped · all three voices sound · on Loudon's word · the dead line's voice is done in the browser engine
payload.content:
What changed. The heterodyne used to read the surface's row at the longitude slider. On Membrane that row is the drum's nodal line, where the surface is zero whatever the phase does, so the voice was silent for the whole tour (240 dB down). Now the engine finds, once per surface, the row with the most energy along x (its mean removed) and reads that row at the dead-line phase. The longitude dot still steers the scan; it no longer steers the voice.

What the measurement says. All three tours re-rendered and re-checked. With the voice fully in and the knot locked (3–4 s) the voice sits 80 to 104 dB under the tone on every surface. Near 3:2 with the coupling let go (10–11 s) it is within 4 dB of the tone on all three. Locked again at the grab it is 32 to 55 dB down and falling. The Adler check is unchanged, since the row only decides the voice's timbre, never its pitch: predicted and measured slip still agree within 0.3 Hz at every coupling. The Penrose and Knot Shadow voices are a little louder than before (their loudest rows carry more than the row at longitude 0).

payload.catchup: Waveguide Synthesizer is a browser instrument where the string on screen is the sound. Two delay lines carry a right-going and a left-going wave. Their sum is the orange line you see, and the speaker hears that same line at one point, the pickup. Earlier versions put it in tune, made stiffness stretch the partials like a piano string, and added slow views so you can watch a 196 Hz string move. You picked the strobe as the view it opens in. You also told me you couldn't hear anything. This cycle found out why: the sound engine worked, but the board shows the page in a 480-pixel window that can't scroll, and the pluck buttons sat below its bottom edge. Study v1.3 opens with one big button that starts the sound and plucks the string, fits the small window, and shows a live output meter. There's also a WAV tour, rendered by the page's own engine, that plays in the board's ordinary audio player.

payload.headline: The string can be bowed now. Hold B and it sings, and on screen one sharp corner runs round the string once a cycle: the bow catching and letting go.
payload.ground: shipped · v1.4 bows, checked in the board's frame · steward leans propose-the-plan next
payload.catchup: Waveguide Synthesizer is the browser string whose on-screen wave is the sound. Two delay lines carry a right-going and a left-going wave; their sum is the orange line, and the speaker hears that line at one point. Earlier versions tuned it, made stiffness stretch it like a piano string, added a slow strobe view so you can watch a 196 Hz string move, and, last cycle, fixed the reason you heard nothing (the buttons sat below the board frame's bottom edge). Until now you could only pluck or strike it. This cycle added a bow. Study v1.4 sustains a note for as long as you hold the bow button or the B key. The strobe view shows the classic bowed-string shape, two straight lines meeting at one corner that travels round the string. The speed, force and position sliders reach all four ways a bow behaves, so you can find where it sings and where it squawks.
payload.content:
How the bow works. The rails carry displacement, but a bow acts on velocity: friction depends on how fast the string slides under the hair. So at the bow point, each sample, the engine reads the speed of each wave arriving, asks a friction curve how hard the hair grips at that slip speed, and pushes the difference into both waves leaving. Near zero slip the hair grips and the string rides with the bow. Past a threshold it lets go and the string flies back. That catch-and-release, once a cycle, is Helmholtz motion. The proof is the second image: at the defaults the bow point rides at exactly the bow's speed for 74.7% of each cycle, and theory says 74%, the bow's position along the string.

What you can find with the sliders. Bow speed against force gives Schelleng's diagram, which every string player knows by feel. Too light and fast, the bow skates or slips twice a cycle (a breathy surface sound). Too heavy and slow, it drags the string aside and sticks. In between is a wide band where it sings, and the band tilts the way the textbook says: bow faster and you need more force. Bow position matters too. Near simple fractions of the string (a fifth, a sixth, a seventh of the way from the bridge) the single slip breaks into two. That is real violin physics, made sharper here because the bow point snaps to whole samples. I set the defaults (speed 0.5, force 0.7, position 0.74) where it sings at all eight test pitches, E2 to E5.

What the bow forced me to fix underneath. (1) The ends now hold perfectly still at zero frequency. Before, they let a sliver of steady push leak through, and a bowed string crept off its rest line without limit. (2) The rails are double precision, because a held bow leaves large, exactly cancelling offsets on them. (3) Sliding the bow mid-note carries those offsets along, and a note change rebuilds the rails from the string's current shape. Before I fixed those two, either move blew the output up to +60 dBFS. (4) A 10 Hz DC blocker and a soft safety limiter on the output. The limiter is exactly linear below −6 dBFS, so plucks pass through it untouched. Plucks against v1.3: same pitch to the measurement's limit, same level within 0.2 dB, about 5% longer ring.

Checked in Chrome inside the board's exact sandbox at 480 pixels tall. One click on the door plucks at −10 dBFS. Holding the bow button reaches −15.8 dBFS, and so does holding B. Both work again with the audio-thread engine forced to fail. No page errors.

payload.headline: Stiffness now means the same at every pitch: at slider 0.67, partial 8 runs about 54 cents sharp from E2 to E5. Before, it ran 2 cents sharp at E2 and 640 at E5.
payload.ground: shipped · Study v1.5 · even stiffness · steward leans four strings next
payload.catchup: Waveguide Synthesizer is the browser string whose on-screen wave is the sound. Two delay lines carry a right-going and a left-going wave, and their sum is the orange line you see and hear. It's tuned. You can pluck it, strike it, bow it, and watch it slowly in the strobe view. Stiffness makes the overtones run sharp, the way a piano string's do, but until now the same slider setting barely touched low notes and wrecked high ones. Study v1.5 fixes that. The slider now asks for one physical number, the string's inharmonicity, and every pitch gets the same stretch. That was the second step in the proposed plan (the bow was the first). Next come four strings, a body, a teaching walk, and the stage question.
payload.content:
What was wrong. The stretch came from eight identical filter sections with one fixed setting. Their effect depends on how many samples one trip round the string takes, so a short (high) string got hit far harder than a long one. At slider 0.67, partial 8 ran 2.4 cents sharp at E2, 16 at G3, 134 at A4 and 641 at E5: about a 260-fold spread. Across the full range it was worse, around 800-fold.

What v1.5 does. The slider now sets the inharmonicity B that piano tuners use. The law it asks for is the stiff-string one, and it doesn't depend on pitch. Each time you change the note, the engine designs the filter for that note. It tries between 1 and 64 sections, finds the setting for each that keeps partials 2 through N (up to 6 kHz) closest to the law, and keeps whichever count lands closest. Each candidate is checked by arithmetic on the loop's delay, with no rendering. One design takes about a millisecond, and each one is kept, so dragging back over a setting costs nothing. The slider runs a decade every third of its travel. 0.33 is a hair of stretch (about 5 cents on partial 8), 0.67 is a clearly stretched piano-like string (54 cents), and 1.0 is past any piano, into bars and bells. The label under the slider now says what you asked for in those terms.

Two side effects. Stiffness 0 now cancels the slight stretch the loop's own brightness filter puts on high notes, so zero means harmonic at every pitch: A5 went from 16 cents sharp on partial 8 to 4. And where a note can't reach what you asked (bass notes at the top of the slider run out of filter), the label says how far that note strays from the law instead of pretending.

Checked. All of this was measured from renders of the page's own engine code, not a copy: the table and the chart, with fundamentals within 0.01 cents of the slider at every pitch. In Chrome, inside the board's exact frame at 480 pixels tall, I did a full slider drag, six pitch and stiffness combinations, and a strike, with no page errors. That ran on the audio-thread engine and again with it forced off. The bow still sings and stays bounded with any stiffness at G3, E2 and E5.

payload.headline: The first real video: five wells, five timbres, all on one pitch scale. Then a particle tunnels across a wall, and stays home once the wall is tipped.
payload.ground: shipped · first MP4 · two new wells, both checked · steward leans LOPSIDED-SWEEP next
payload.catchup: Quantum Synthesizer claims the Schrödinger equation is a synthesizer. The shape of a potential well sets the spacing of its energy levels, and those spacings, played as partials, are the timbre. By September three wells had been heard one at a time: a parabola rings a clean G3, a quartic-bent well rings a bell, and a double well splits every level into a pair that beats. You granted both September asks: the stage goes to sprout, and the piano paragraph gets fixed. This cycle put all the wells into one 34-second video and added the two the atlas was missing. A Morse well (the shape of a chemical bond) runs out of partials. A double well tipped by a hair stops tunnelling.
payload.content:
Start with [the video](open:Projects/Quantum Synthesizer/proofs/timbre-atlas.mp4). Each well is struck once for 4.5 s while the picture shows the well, its eigenfunctions sitting on their energy levels, and its partials against grey lines marking the harmonic series. Every well uses the same scale: one energy unit is 196 Hz and every ground state sits on G3. Nothing is stretched to fit, so the distance between two wells' partials is real.

The two new wells:

**Morse.** V = 4·(1 − e^(−x/√8))². The levels crowd together as they climb, then stop. Above the rim the particle is free, so the instrument has exactly 8 partials, all below 900 Hz, packed tight at the top. It's the first well in the atlas with a ceiling. The textbook gives exact Morse levels, and the solver matches all eight to within 0.04 Hz.

**Lopsided double well.** This is September's double well plus 0.02·x, a tilt you can barely see. The lowest pair's beat jumps from 1.4 Hz to 12.7 Hz, while the higher pairs barely move (6.3 to 16.9 Hz, then 20.4 to 27.0 Hz). Tunnelling was weakest at the bottom, so the tilt overwhelms it there first.

The last 12 s answer a physical question with no additive recipe. A particle is dropped in the left well and the Schrödinger equation runs forward. The sound is ψ read at a pickup in the left well, and both halves use one gain, so loudness counts as evidence. In the even well the particle crosses and comes back, and the chance it is on the left falls to 1.6%. In the tipped well it never drops below 92%. The quietest-to-loudest swing at the pickup is 0.09 even and 0.46 tipped: the sound empties in one and barely dips in the other. A two-level estimate for the lowest pair predicts at most 1.2% crossing, and that agrees.

I also made [the poster](Projects/Quantum Synthesizer/proofs/timbre-atlas-poster.png), with all five wells in one row, the audio alone as [the WAV](open:Projects/Quantum Synthesizer/proofs/timbre-atlas.wav), and [the generator script](Projects/Quantum Synthesizer/proofs/timbre_atlas.py), which prints every check.

On reviving, plainly: yes, still alive. Your REVIVE-TO-SPROUT grant from 24 September hasn't reached the entry yet, though. It still says dormant, and the piano paragraph you approved for replacement is still there. I've flagged both for an elder rather than asking you again.

payload.headline: Same box, only the walls change: six strikes on one ruler. The walls pick the shapes; the equation picks the pitches.
payload.ground: shipped · second test of the forward vector run · steward leans keep going
payload.catchup: Quantum Synthesizer claims the Schrödinger equation is a synthesizer: what confines a particle decides its energy levels, and those levels, played as partials, are the timbre. Over the summer and last cycle I tested half of that claim, the shape of the well, and the result became the 34-second timbre atlas: parabola, bell, double well, tipped well, chemical bond. My forward vector names a second test I had never run: do the walls of a box set the harmonic content? This cycle ran it. It's a 29.5-second video of one empty box. Only the walls change, and every segment uses the same pluck, the same pickup and the same pitch ruler (hard-wall ground = A3).
payload.content: Six strikes, in order. (1) A string with fixed ends, the ordinary wave equation: 220, 440, 660 Hz, the harmonic series. (2) The same box under Schrödinger. The sine shapes, the pluck and the pickup are all the same, so the loudness of every partial is identical, but the pitches are 220, 880, 1980, 3520: the squares. This pair is the finding. The walls choose the shapes; the equation turns shapes into pitches. The wave equation's frequency grows with the number of wiggles, and Schrödinger's grows with its square. So my own line 'the geometry of confinement determines the harmonic content' is only half true: walls decide which partials exist and how loud a pickup hears them, and the equation decides where they sit. (3) Free walls (cosines instead of sines) keep exactly the same pitches; only the loudness pattern moves, plus a silent level at zero. (4) One hard wall and one free leaves quarter-waves: 55, 495, 1375, 2695 Hz, the odd squares, two octaves down. (5) A ring, the ends joined: every level doubles, and a small bump splits each pair by about 2 Hz, so each partial beats. That's the same mechanism that makes a real bell warble when its casting is slightly uneven. (6) Soft walls of finite height: every level sags 420 to 510 cents flat, and only 5 partials survive before the rim. That's a ceiling, the same thing the chemical-bond well showed in the atlas.

payload.headline: One string, made stiffer and stiffer until it sounds exactly like Schrödinger's box: Schrödinger is the square root of a vibrating bar.
payload.ground: shipped · third test of the forward vector · steward leans propose the entry fix next
payload.catchup: Quantum Synthesizer claims the Schrödinger equation is a synthesizer: whatever confines a particle sets its energy levels, and those levels, played as partials, are the timbre. Today's run tested this three ways. The timbre atlas changed the shape of the well. The walls video changed the box's walls and found that the walls pick the wave shapes, but the equation picks the pitches: a string sounds 1·2·3·4, while Schrödinger's box, with the same shapes, sounds 1·4·9·16. This cycle builds the road between those two. It's a 32-second video: one pinned string plucked sixteen times while it gets stiffer, followed by one held tone that glides the whole way.
payload.content:
The road is a stiff string, the same physics as a piano string. Tension pulls it straight, and bending stiffness adds a second restoring force. With the ground held on A3, every partial moves as f_n = 220 · n · √((1 + B·n²)/(1 + B)). At B = 0 that's 1·2·3, and as B grows without limit it becomes exactly 1·4·9·16. The wave shapes stay the same sines the whole way, so the same pluck and pickup give the same loudness pattern on every strike. Only the pitches move, and that's what you hear.

The finding is better than I expected. A string stiff enough to be pure bending is a pinned bar, and a pinned bar IS Schrödinger's box. If you apply the free Schrödinger equation twice, you get the bar equation, ψ_tt = −¼ ψ_xxxx. Start a wavefunction real, and its real part moves exactly like a struck pinned bar. So Schrödinger is the square root of a vibrating bar. I didn't take the algebra on faith: I integrated the box and the bar separately from the same pluck, and at the pickup they agree to 9.5 × 10⁻⁹ against a signal of 0.52. The right panel of the poster shows the two traces on top of each other.

The piano has a place on this road. Piano strings sit at B ≈ 0.0001 to 0.001 (the band [[Piano String Inharmonicity]] gives), which is the far string end. Their partials only turn bar-like past n ≈ 1/√B, which means 30 to 100 partials up. The piano's stretched tuning is Schrödinger's arithmetic showing up faintly, far from the ground.

This also settles the piano paragraph you approved replacing in September: the stiff string and the quantum box sit on one continuous road, and that's stronger evidence than the prose had.

equations.symbolic: ∂²y/∂t² = c²·∂²y/∂x² − κ²·∂⁴y/∂x⁴   →   fₙ = f₀·n·√((1 + B·n²)/(1 + B))
equations.worded: acceleration = tension × curvature − stiffness × curvature-of-curvature   →   partial = ground × index × √((1 + stiffness × index²)/(1 + stiffness))

ground, held on A3 = 220 Hz

equations.label: Schrödinger, applied twice
equations.worded: i × rate of change of ψ = −½ × curvature of ψ   ⇒   acceleration of ψ = −¼ × curvature-of-curvature of ψ (the bar equation)

Real bars, like a vibraphone or a marimba, have free ends, not pinned ones, so they don't land on 1·4·9. Only a pinned bar does.

payload.headline: The heterodyne voice is in the RNBO codebox. Run as written, the codebox matches the browser engine bit for bit on all three surfaces.
payload.ground: shipped · codebox matches browser exactly, still unopened in Max · steward leans dead-line bank + voice next
payload.catchup: This project is a synthesizer whose wavetable is a surface on a torus. Two scan rates read the surface, and their ratio decides whether the sound is harmonic or shimmering. The browser instrument (the Hopf sphere) can lock the two rates into a simple ratio. It also has a voice that plays the 'dead line', the part of the surface that goes silent when the rates lock. That voice is silent while locked and sings at the slip rate when the lock lets go. Until today it lived only in the browser. This cycle put it into the Max/RNBO codebox. I also built a small tool that runs the codebox's own text and holds it against the browser engine sample by sample, so the codeboxes get checked before anyone opens Max.
payload.content:
What I built. RNBO/torus_2d_hopf.codebox gains two knobs: het (how much of the voice) and hetRow (which row of the surface the voice reads). Membrane taught us that a nodal row is silent, so the comment lists each surface's loudest row as a phase, as measured. The codebox now also fades the voice from the old dead line to the new one over about 6 ms when the lock target changes, the way the browser does. Its lock search now tries the ratios in the browser's order, so the two engines break ties the same way.

The checker. RNBO/codebox_mirror.mjs is a small translator. It turns a codebox file into JavaScript as written: knobs and state become variables, and peek reads the same surface the browser plays. Then it renders both tours twice, once through the browser engine and once through the codebox, and subtracts. The only thing it removes first is the browser's output soft-clip, which the codebox doesn't have.

What it says. Heterodyne tour, all three surfaces, 24 s each: zero difference, sample for sample. Measured inside the codebox itself, the voice is 80–104 dB under the tone while locked, within 4 dB of it near 3:2, and 32–55 dB down at the grab, the same as the browser numbers. The hands tour from cycle 8 is now checked too, since it rides the same codebox: bare, bend and shear are bit-exact. Stir is built differently on purpose (finite differences instead of a precomputed slope field), and it still lands 49–87 dB under the signal. As a control, the codebox from before today, with no voice in it, misses by −2.3 dB. So the checker does catch a real difference.

payload.headline: I wrote a first test piece, Étude No. 1 ("One Sphere"): 100 seconds, three voices, all played by the Hopf codebox's own text on catalog surfaces.
payload.ground: shipped · first music from the prototype, not yet heard · steward leans Loudon listens next
payload.catchup: This project is a synthesizer whose wavetable is a surface on a torus. Two scan rates read the surface, and their ratio decides whether it sounds harmonic or shimmers. The instrument exists as five Max/RNBO codebox files. Over the last two cycles each one was checked, sample by sample, against the scripts that made the earlier auditions, and they all match. Nobody has opened them in Max yet. The page has long said the real proof is a piece of music: if the instrument doesn't yield music, the design needs rethinking. So this cycle I wrote one. Every voice in it is the Hopf codebox, the sphere controller with the hands and the dead-line voice, running from its own text on the WAV a Max buffer~ would load. The score is nothing but knob moves.
payload.content:
Four movements, in plain words. One: Penrose sits at the bottom of the sphere, where the second scan rate is zero. That is an ordinary 1D wavetable synth, and longitude walks it through the surface's rows. Then the height rises, and because the coupling is on, the pitch climbs in locked steps instead of gliding: 1:4, 1:3, 2:5, 1:2, 3:5, 2:3, 3:4, 4:5, landing on 1:1 at 110 Hz. You can see the staircase in the spectrogram (etude_one_sphere.png). Two: Knot Shadow enters locked at 3:2. Then both voices let go, and their dead lines sing the mistuning before the coupling grabs them back. Three: a low Membrane drone at 55 Hz gets bend, shear and stir. Four: all three let go together and are grabbed back at once.

What the first render taught. In my first coda, dropping the coupling changed nothing, and the spectrogram stayed flat. On the exact ratio, nothing needs coupling to stay locked. A let-go has to be two moves at once: coupling down, height nudged off the ratio. That's a real performance fact about this instrument, and it's now written into the score and the script header. It also bears on how a Max patch should map one 'release' gesture.

Checks: no NaN or infinite samples in any voice. Each voice's level per section, before normalising, sits between −24 and −17 dBFS, so the mix is balanced. The lock targets the codebox visited are logged in etude_locks.json. The listenable copy is AAC, because the 38 MB WAV is over the commit limit; render_etude.mjs rebuilds the WAV in about 3 seconds.

payload.catchup: This project is a synthesizer whose wavetable is a surface on a torus. Two scan rates read the surface, and their ratio decides whether it sounds harmonic or shimmers. payload.content:
Same rule as before: every voice is RNBO/torus_2d_hopf.codebox run from its own text on a catalog WAV, and the score is only knob moves. The drums come from the codebox too. The kick is the Membrane surface with baseHz dropping from 170 to 48 Hz in a quarter second. The hat is Chladni Ghost scanned far off every ratio at 900 Hz, with stir up and 70 ms gates.

The story keeps No. 1's sections. One point: the 1D synth plays the motif (A C E D, one bar) twice, rubato. Staircase: the sphere climbs through the locks, and the last four steps fall one per bar at 100 BPM, so the tempo arrives before the drums. The knot: kick, ducking pad and offbeat hat, then the melody states the motif, repeats it, sequences it up a fourth and then a fifth, comes home, steps down a tone and cadences. Let go, in time: the melody holds the tonic, and both voices let go by exactly the amount that makes their dead lines turn on the beat, Knot Shadow in eighth notes (measured 3.333 Hz) and Penrose in quarter notes (measured 1.667 Hz). For four bars the mistuning plays the groove. The hands: half-time kick, the Membrane drone with bend swinging once a bar, shear snapping on 2 and 4 like a backbeat, and stir swelling over four bars. Over that the motif plays at half speed, then a fourth up, then inverted an octave up, then cadences. Let go together: the kicks spread out, the tempo dissolves, and everything slips at once. Coda: the motif slowly once more, and the sphere glides back to the opening note.

The main thing I learned is about voicing. Each surface on each lock sounds some partials and not others. Penrose turns out to be exactly five equal plane waves, so any lock makes it a five-note chord on fixed harmonics. On 1:2 it's an open fifth chord with one blue note, and that's the pad. Knot Shadow on 3:2, where No. 1 had it, is almost a pure sine two octaves and a third above the note. On 1:1 it's 88% fundamental, so the melody lives there. Every note in the piece was checked against the score from each voice rendered on its own: the melody lands on 220, 261.6, 329.6 and 293.7 Hz, and the pad on 220, 660, 880, 1210 and 1320 Hz.

payload.content:
Two changes, everything else kept.

The kick. I measured why the first one sounded like a tom. Membrane on the 1:1 lock puts its energy on harmonics 2 to 4, so a kick tuned to 48 Hz actually sounded at 100–200 Hz. The new kick is the plain 1D synth on the Sine Cycle Sweep surface, whose first row is a pure sine. Its pitch drops 150 → 64 → 46 Hz. The click comes from the surface too: longitude flicks up about four rows' worth of harmonics and falls back in 12 ms. Now 87% of a kick's energy is under 100 Hz. It was mostly above.

The answer. It's a new eight-bar section after the hands. The B theme is the motif's contrary: steps where the motif leaps (E F G A G), long-short where the motif is short-long, C major where it's A minor. A new voice plays it, Knot Shadow on the 3:2 lock, which turns out to be a near-pure whistle on its 5th harmonic. For the first time in the piece the pad moves: F, C, G, E, then home to A. The whistle states B, sequences it a step down, then reaches up to C6. In each gap the old melody answers with the motif's first three notes. In the last two bars the whistle holds a high E while the melody takes back the whole motif on the dominant, and then everyone lets go together, the whistle included. The drums go plain under it: kick on 1 and 3, straight eighth-note hats.

Every note was checked from the stems: whistle 659 → 1046 Hz as written, pad roots 174.7, 261.5, 195.9 and 164.8 Hz, the melody's answers on 220, 261.5 and 329.6 Hz.

payload.headline: A voicing atlas: for every surface on every lock, which partial actually sounds. It matches the Hopf codebox to the percent, and you can play it.
payload.ground: shipped · checked against the codebox in 8 cases · steward leans landing it in the wavetables catalog
payload.catchup: This project is a synthesizer whose wavetable is a surface on a torus. Two scan rates read the surface, and their ratio decides whether it sounds harmonic or shimmers. The instrument exists as Max/RNBO codebox files that haven't been opened in Max yet. Its test piece, Étude No. 2, is played only by the Hopf codebox and is now in a second draft with a real kick and a B theme, waiting for your ears. Writing it kept teaching one lesson: a note on this instrument is not baseHz. Each surface on each lock lands on certain harmonics, and longitude can move them. This cycle measured that for all thirteen playable surfaces on all 19 locks plus the pole, checked the numbers against the codebox itself, and made it a playable page and a draft section for the catalog.
payload.content:
**What it is.** `Tools/voicing_atlas.py` reads each surface's 2D spectrum and works out, for every lock the Hopf codebox can choose (every a:b with a and b up to 5), which harmonic each surface ripple lands on, how loud it is at every longitude, and the pitch as a multiple of baseHz. It runs in 4 seconds. The grid image is the summary: big number = loudest harmonic, small = its share. The playable page lets you click any cell, slide longitude, hear an additive sketch of the measured partial mix, and read off the exact codebox knobs (height, longitude, baseHz). You can also type a note like A3 and it tells you the baseHz that puts the loudest partial there.

**It matches the instrument.** `check_against_codebox.mjs` runs the Hopf codebox as written, parks it on a lock and measures harmonics 1–64. In all eight cases (Knot Shadow 1:1 and 3:2, Membrane 1:1, Penrose 1:2, Theta 1:1, Kuramoto Bloom 1:1, plus Membrane and Chladni Ghost at a quarter turn of longitude), every harmonic agrees to the percent.

**What it found.**
- The kick mystery is solved. Membrane on 1:1 is 50% fundamental at longitude 0 and 89% on the octave at 0.5. The first draft's kick sat at longitude 0.1, where the fundamental is about 13%. The tom came from that longitude, not from the surface.
- There's a whistle register hiding in surfaces known for clouds. Theta on 1:1 at longitude 0.5 is 99% one partial, Chladni Ghost on 1:1 at 0.6875 is 97%, and Fisher Ridge on 1:2 is 91%. Knot Shadow on 2:3 is a pure sine on harmonic 13 at any longitude, because every other ripple cancels to silence there.
- Knot Shadow is one ripple carrying 78% of its energy on every lock, so longitude only changes its colour, never its pitch. That makes it the steadiest melody voice. (The Étude notes said 88% on 1:1. The real figure is 78%.)
- Penrose is a five-note chord on any lock, and no longitude can make it pure. The four utility tables and Stiff String simply follow the x scan rate.

table.caption: Purest voicings: where one partial carries the sound

equations.label: where a surface ripple lands on a lock
equations.symbolic: h = | m · b + n · a |,  f0 = 2 · baseHz / (a + b)
equations.worded: (harmonic it lands on) = | (ripples along x) × (lock bottom) + (ripples along y) × (lock top) |,  (locked fundamental) = 2 × (base rate) / (lock top + lock bottom)

where.def: the lock; height = (a − b)/(a + b)
how many times a ripple cycles along x and along y
the harmonic of f0 it sounds; h = 0 stands still and the DC blocker removes it

payload.headline: A packet on a ring smears into fog, then reassembles itself. Played as a waveform, its rational times climb the harmonic series.
payload.ground: shipped · all three checks pass · steward leans ring-with-a-bump next
payload.catchup: This page claims the Schrödinger equation is a synthesizer: whatever confines a particle sets its energy levels, and those levels, played as partials, are the timbre. Earlier today the walls video found that Schrödinger's box sounds 1·4·9·16 where a string sounds 1·2·3·4, and the stiffness video showed why: Schrödinger is the square root of a vibrating bar. This cycle follows the consequence. Those squares are all whole numbers, so every phase comes home at the same moment. A packet let go on a ring spreads into fog and then rebuilds itself exactly. Halfway there, it breaks into perfect copies. Read the ring's probability as one cycle of a waveform, and those copies become the harmonic series.
payload.content:
The instrument is a free particle on a ring. The probability of finding it at each point around the ring, |ψ|², is read once around as one cycle of a waveform and played at A2 (110 Hz). Schrödinger's equation slowly rewrites that waveform, at 36 seconds per full revival.

What you hear: a buzzy A2, then fog, and out of the fog brief clean tones. At a quarter of the way it's A3, at a third E4, at an eighth A4, then C♯5 at 1/5 and 2/5 and G5 at the sevenths. At halfway it's A2 again, the whole packet moved to the far side of the ring. At the end it's home. Each clean moment is a rational time p/q, where the packet stands as q evenly spaced copies (q/2 when q is even). A waveform that repeats q times per cycle can only hold harmonics q, 2q, 3q, and so on, so the ear hears the q-th harmonic. The carpet's fractions, heard in the order they occur, are the harmonic series.

An honest note on what's physics and what's my choice. In the walls video the pitches WERE the physics: the energy levels are the partials. Here the pitch comes from a mapping I chose, density read as a wavetable, which is the entry's own idea of feeding the wave's shape into a wavetable. What the physics supplies is when the copies appear and how many there are. The mapping can't invent those.

Checks (all in talbot.py):
1. I integrated the ring separately with Crank–Nicolson (24,000 steps to T/3). It matches the exact sum to 1.1e-4 against a peak of 0.010 and shows three copies.
2. At every fraction tested (1/2 through 1/8, plus 2/5, 3/8 and 3/7), at least 99.9% of the density's energy sits on multiples of the predicted copy count.
3. An FFT of the finished audio at 1/8, 1/7, 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 2/5 and 1/2 puts at least 99.9% of the energy on the predicted harmonic's series.

A dead end worth knowing about. My first try listened to the packet bouncing off hard walls, hoping the bounce rate would be a pitch. It can't be. A packet narrow enough to hear spreads out within a fraction of one bounce, because the carrier pitch and the bounce rate are locked in a ratio of n/2. So the box can't buzz at its bounce rate, but its revivals can sing.

equations.label: Free particle on a ring
equations.symbolic: i ∂ψ/∂t = −½ ∂²ψ/∂x²,   ψ(x,t) = Σₖ cₖ e^{2πikx} e^{−2πi k² t/T}
equations.worded: i · d(wave)/d(time) = −½ · curvature(wave);   wave = Σ over whole numbers k of amountₖ · e^{2πi·k·position} · e^{−2πi·k²·time/T}

where.def: a whole number of turns round the ring
the revival time, when every k² phase is home at once

equations.label: Copies at rational times → heard harmonic
equations.symbolic: t = (p/q)·T  ⇒  |ψ|² = q copies (q odd) or q/2 copies (q even)  ⇒  harmonics q·f₀, 2q·f₀ …
equations.worded: time = (p/q) × revival  ⇒  density = q evenly spaced copies (half that when q is even)  ⇒  only multiples of copies × 110 Hz survive

where.def: 110 Hz, one trip round the ring per waveform cycle

columns: share of energy on that harmonic's series

payload.headline: I put a bump on the ring and grew it into a well. Schrödinger's squares fold down into a string's evenly spaced harmonics. It's a quantum pendulum.
payload.ground: shipped · all five checks pass · steward leans a playable depth slider next
payload.catchup: This page claims the Schrödinger equation is a synthesizer: whatever confines a particle sets its energy levels, and those levels, played as partials, are the timbre. Today's earlier videos found that a bare box or ring sounds in squares (1·4·9·16) where a string sounds 1·2·3·4, and that those whole-number squares make a packet on a ring rebuild itself perfectly. [The round trip](open:Projects/Quantum Synthesizer/proofs/round-trip.mp4) is 21 seconds, one held tone with the lowest partial pinned on A3, so only the spacing above it moves. payload.headline: Seven moves on the quantum ladder, each heard by two ears. Taking a quantum away changes nothing, and measuring the energy leaves silence.
payload.ground: shipped · ladder proof + third elder draft · steward leans land all three drafts together
payload.catchup: This page claims the Schrödinger equation is a synthesizer. Whatever holds a wave sets its energy levels, and those levels, played as partials, are the timbre. Today's run has been testing the entry line by line with sound. The walls choose the shapes, and the equation turns shapes into pitches. That correction and a fix to the Hermite paragraph are already drafted for an elder. This cycle tested the operators paragraph, which says the creation operator adds an overtone, the annihilation operator removes one, and measurement collapse is a resonant filter. None of the three holds up. What replaces them is better: the sound depends on which ear listens. An ear that could hear the phase turning hears each rung as one pitch, and the whole ladder is a clarinet's odd harmonics. A real detector hears only the differences between rungs. To it a single rung is silent, and a swinging packet is a full harmonic chord.
payload.content: ladder.py plays seven moves on the harmonic oscillator, with one rung-step mapped to 220 Hz. Each move is heard first through the CLOCK (the real part of ψ at one point: the phase turning) and then through the DETECTOR (|ψ|² at that point: what a measurement could register). Moves: the ground state; the creation operator climbing from rung 0 to rung 5; two rungs together; a coherent state (the quantum pendulum, α = 2.2); a annihilation operator applied to it; a creation operator applied to it; and an energy measurement that collapses it. All seven checks pass. (1) The creation operator moves one rung up, and the clock hears one new pitch, never an added one (330, 550, 770, 990, 1210 Hz). (2) A single rung is silent to the detector, with a wobble below 3e-16. (3) Two rungs: the clock hears 110 + 330 Hz, and the detector hears only their difference, 220 Hz. (4) The coherent state: the clock gets 16 partials, all odd multiples of 110 Hz, because the zero-point ½ makes the ladder odd. The detector gets 11 partials, all whole multiples of 220. (5) Removing a quantum from the coherent state changes nothing: fidelity 1.000000000000, and the waveforms differ by 1.5e-15. It is the annihilation operator's own eigenstate. (6) Adding a quantum does change it, by re-voicing the chord rather than adding a note. Overlap drops to α²/(α²+1) = 0.83, 4×220 Hz rises from −15.9 to −8.4 dB, and the fundamental drops 3.5 dB. The clock also loses its 110 Hz entirely, because the creation operator empties rung 0. (7) Measuring the energy picks rung 4 (18%, Poisson odds), and the detector goes silent. Collapse doesn't filter the sound; it stops it. I drafted the matching replacement for the entry's operators section, with a one-sentence amendment to the Hermite draft so the two agree.

payload.ground: shipped · 155 s, ending kept as-is · unheard by anyone yet
payload.catchup: This project is a synthesizer whose wavetable is a surface on a torus. Two scan rates read it, and their ratio decides whether it sounds harmonic or shimmers. Its test piece, Étude No. 2, is played entirely by the Hopf codebox, the version of the instrument steered from a point on a sphere. Every voice runs from that codebox's own text, and the score is only knob moves. You heard the second draft as having swung too far toward the grid: straight 4/4, rigid, simple. You asked for vocal and violin slides and vibrato in the melodies, a swung non-European beat in the rhythms, and tempo that slides like Étude No. 1's. This third draft does all of that and leaves the ending, your favorite part, alone.
payload.content:
**How time moves now.** The piece is in 12/8. Each beat splits into three eighths that are uneven: short, medium, long, like the stretched triplets in Malian jembe drumming. The motif A C E D becomes 3·2·1·6 eighths, so it swings by itself. There is no fixed BPM; time runs through a tempo curve. The staircase speeds up from 50 to 80, so the groove arrives inside it. The knot section holds steady and swung at 80. The let-go slows to 56 and speeds back up to catch the hands. The B theme breathes, with each two-bar phrase pushing ahead and then relaxing. The ending stays in free time. So the piece now moves between rubato, groove and rubato, which is the threshold you asked for.

**The beat.** A two-tone Chladni bell plays the West African 12/8 bell pattern (x.x.xx.x.x.x). A shaker plays every eighth and leans on the long one. The kick walks the four beats against the bell, goes half time in 3+3+2 under the hands, and becomes a soft frame drum in B. Drum hits get a few milliseconds of seeded push and pull.

**The singing.** Every melody slides into tied notes, longer on leaps, the way a violinist shifts. It scoops up into detached notes, and a delayed vibrato blooms on long notes: 10 cents in the coda, up to 32 on the whistle's reach. In a patch the vibrato is just a `[cycle~]` into `[param baseHz]`.

**The dead lines follow the tempo.** In the let-go the score sets each mistuning from the tempo, so the slip stays at eighth notes (Knot Shadow) and beats (Penrose) all the way down the slowdown and back up. Two small composing changes: a turn in bar 10, and B's answers now climb through chord tones over the moving pad (A C E, then E G B, then G B D) instead of repeating.

payload.content:
**The aksak.** The hands section (bars 17–24) is now in 7/8 grouped 2+2+3, the limping meter of Bulgarian rachenitsa and Turkish aksak. Each old 12/8 bar becomes two 7/8 bars. The eighth note keeps its speed across the change, so the groove changes shape while the tempo stays put. The long beat is 1.4 short beats, not 1.5, so it lands a little early the way dancers lean into it.

**The motif fits the meter.** A C E D as 2 · 2 · 3 · 7 eighths fills one pair of 7/8 bars exactly: the long E lands on the long beat. So the hands sing call and answer. First the motif and the motif played backwards (D E C A). Then the same pair up a fourth. Then the motif upside down with a falling answer (A G F E), and finally the cadence D C B A.

**The beat re-cuts itself.** Kick low on each downbeat, leaning on the long beat, with a ghost in every other bar. The bell switches from the 12/8 pattern to x.xx x.. per 7/8. The shaker accents where each group starts. The drone's shear and bend land on the long beats.

**Measured, not heard:** kick gaps of 0.50 · 0.50 · 0.70 s repeating (short, short, long at 1.4×, with an eighth at 0.25 s). The reed's first two 7/8 bars: A 220 → C 262 → E 330 → D 294 Hz. Timing in the let-go section is unchanged. No non-finite samples.

payload.headline: The crowd is playable now. Two knobs, tightness and life, plus a keyboard. Pacemakers turn the lock from a switch into a crossfade.
payload.ground: shipped · instrument, one-take recording, edge sweep · steward leans toward bringing the crowd into Max/RNBO next
payload.catchup: Neural Granular Synthesis is the idea that a steady timbre comes from a crowd of simple neurons, not from any one of them. How tightly the crowd agrees is the main control. Earlier cycles found that about 32 neurons sound steady. They moved a 128-neuron crowd up to audio rate, where its firing rate is the pitch, so coupling snaps it into a tone. They also showed that making 5–20% of the neurons pacemakers, which fire on their own and ignore the crowd, brings a frozen tone to life. This cycle turns all of that into one instrument you can play in the board. It also records a single take across every regime, and it measures something new: pacemakers don't move the point where the tone locks, but they soften it.
payload.content:
THE INSTRUMENT (crowd-instrument.html). You don't play neurons. You play the crowd. A pad sets tightness (coupling measured in units of the crowd's disorder) across and life (the share of pacemakers) up. Its shading comes from last month's clarity map, and a teal line marks where theory says the tone breaks: tightness = 1/(1 − life). Below the pad, a live raster (one row per neuron) and a phase wheel show the stripes form. Keys A–K play notes and Z/X change octave. There are also knobs for disorder, crowd size (4–512), and spike width, which acts like a formant. It runs the same engine as the standalone crowd_engine.js, and I checked that the two copies are identical. Headless, it costs about 5% of one core.

THE ONE-TAKE (crowd-gesture.wav, 51 s). It moves from hiss, across the edge (it snaps at about 8.5 s), to a dead-still tone. Pacemakers fade in until the tone breathes, then it widens into heavy vibrato. Next, tightness drops under the edge and the core comes apart. It comes back to a living tone and plays A C D E D A on it. crowd-gesture.png shows the meters under the sound.

THE FIND (edge-softening.png). Tightness was swept around the predicted edge at four pacemaker shares, with three crowds each. The edge stays where theory says. Its shape changes. With no pacemakers, synchrony jumps from 0.40 to 0.84 within 10% of the line. At 68% pacemakers it climbs steadily from 0.35 at half the edge. For playing, that means life also sets how sharp the attack is when you lock the crowd.

payload.headline: The crowd now exists as an RNBO codebox, up to 512 neurons, and it matches the board instrument sample for sample. Next step is opening it in Max.
payload.ground: shipped · codebox + mirror check + its own one-take · steward leans you open it in Max next
payload.catchup: Neural Granular Synthesis is the idea that a steady timbre comes from a crowd of simple neurons, not from any one of them. How tightly the crowd agrees is the main control. Earlier cycles moved a 128-neuron crowd up to audio rate, where its firing rate is the pitch, so coupling snaps hiss into a tone. Pacemakers (neurons that ignore the crowd) bring a frozen tone back to life. Last cycle turned that into an instrument you play in the board, with two knobs: tightness and life. This cycle carries the same instrument across into RNBO, so it can become a Max for Live device you play in Live.
payload.content:
WHAT I MADE. RNBO/crowd.codebox is a single codebox~ holding up to 512 neurons. Its knobs belong to the population: tight (1 is the lock edge), life (the pacemaker share), spread (how much the neurons disagree), crowd (how many neurons) and width (spike width, which behaves like a formant). It also has keyboard params (freq, glide, gate, velocity, attack, release) and a drive inlet, so outside audio can push every neuron. out1/out2 carry the sound. out3 carries the crowd's synchrony from 0 to 1, for a meter. The wiring list is at the top of the file.

ONE DELIBERATE CHANGE. The browser uses a seeded random generator to give each neuron its natural rate, starting phase and pacemaker role. The codebox uses three evenly interleaved number sequences instead. That leaves no random generator to port. Turning the crowd knob also never reshuffles anyone: it admits or dismisses neurons from a crowd that is already evenly spread.

HOW I CHECKED IT. RNBO/codebox_mirror.mjs runs the codebox file's own text as JavaScript. It gives the board's engine the same crowd, then subtracts the two over cycle 12's whole 51-second walk. The difference sits 135 dB under the signal at 128 neurons and 123 dB under at 512. That is the gap between 32-bit and 64-bit storage, nothing more. The transpiler is adopted from the 2D Torus project's RNBO folder. crowd-codebox-take.wav is that walk played by the codebox itself.

TO TRY IT. Make an rnbo~ and paste the file into a codebox~. Add [out~ 1] [out~ 2] and turn on audio: you should hear hiss. Raise tight past 1 and it snaps into a tone. Raise life to about 0.12 and the tone breathes. The audition steps are at the bottom of the file.

payload.headline: The codebox picked the wrong number of pacemakers, and that's fixed. Fixing it showed the soft lock comes from a lumpy crowd, not from life.
payload.ground: shipped · codebox fixed, still matches the board · steward leans give lumpiness its own knob
payload.catchup: Neural Granular Synthesis plays a crowd of neurons whose agreement is the timbre. Two knobs drive it. Tightness is how hard the neurons pull on each other. Life is the share of pacemakers that ignore the pull. Past the lock edge, which theory puts at tightness 1/(1 − life), hiss snaps into a tone. The crowd now exists as an RNBO codebox (RNBO/crowd.codebox) that nobody has compiled yet. Two cycles ago I reported that pacemakers soften the snap into a crossfade. Last cycle I showed that much of that was a small crowd. This cycle found a counting bug in the codebox and fixed it. With the bug gone, most of what was left of the softening goes away too.
payload.content:
THE BUG. The codebox made every neuron whose role number fell under `life` a pacemaker. With 128 neurons at life 0.5 that gives 59 pacemakers, not 64. More followers means an earlier lock, so the crowd locked 8% early. That was last cycle's open puzzle. The followers' natural rates were never bunched: their spread is 0.574–0.579 under both rules, against 0.577 for a perfectly even spread. Now `life` picks exactly round(life × crowd size) pacemakers, taking the lowest role numbers first. Pacemaker sets still nest. Ranks are recounted only when the crowd knob moves, not on every sample. After the fix, the lock point I computed lands within 1% of theory for every crowd and life (table below). The codebox still matches the board engine: 135 dB under the signal at 128 neurons and 123 dB under at 512. I re-rendered crowd-codebox-take.wav from the fixed file.

THE FIND. I re-swept the edge with evenly spread crowds under the fixed rule (edge-headcount.png, right two panels). At 512 evenly spread neurons with no pacemakers, synchrony sits at 0.08 at 0.95× the edge and jumps to 0.62 at 1.0×. With 68% pacemakers it is 0.32 at 0.95× and 0.78 at 1.0×. So the lock is a switch at any life. The softening I reported comes from lumpiness: random rates and phases add noise to the crowd's shared pull, and pacemakers add more noise only when the crowd is small or random. Life still moves the edge exactly as theory says. What it doesn't do is set how soft the attack is.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR PLAYING. A soft attack is a nice thing to play with, but it shouldn't be a side effect of how the crowd happened to be seeded. I lean toward a third knob, lumpiness: a controlled amount of random scatter in the natural rates, laid over the even spread. Then tightness says where the lock is, life says where the edge sits and how much the tone breathes, and lumpiness says how hard the lock hits.

It is research reaching toward a product, and the nearer product is a simple knob that knows which parameter it's controlling. On 2026-10-05 the page gathered seven feels, a quickly drafted parts brief you asked us to push against, and a guess from that session: feels that answer the hand (springs, frets) must be computed near the motor, while feels played into the hand (an LFO, a pitch, a beat) can come down a cable. Nothing is built. This cycle I built the knob in simulation so the feels can be tried and that guess could be tested.
payload.content:
**What I built.** feel_engine.js is a small physics model of the knob: a cap with weight, a motor that senses and pushes on a loop of a chosen speed and delay, a 14-bit encoder, the motor's own friction, and a hand that can grip, turn or rest a finger as a brake. The seven feels are short functions in it: frets, the stiffening string, the LFO felt, the pitch itself, the lock, haptic filtering, the struck spring (with a pendulum variant) and the turntable. The browser page and the offline renders both load this one file, so they can't drift apart. In the page, dragging the knob grips it, shift-drag brakes it, and an amber trace shows the torque your hand would feel, since the screen can't push back. You can switch the feel onto a slow wire and watch a fret start to buzz the moment you let go.

**What the sweep says.** I released a virtual spring and looked for the stiffest one that didn't grow on its own, for four places the feel could be computed. The simulation matches the textbook rule within 10% in every case. The rule: delay acts like negative damping, so the stiffest stable spring is the real damping divided by the delay. Three findings. (1) The page's guess holds, and it holds more sharply than it said. Over USB to Max, the stiffest feel that stays calm with no hand on the knob is 0.022 N·m/rad, which is softer than a pitch-wheel return spring. Frets, the string and walls belong on the device. The LFO, the pitch and the beat clicks are fine anywhere, because they don't depend on where the hand is. (2) The hand is part of the stability. Gripping adds its own damping, and that roughly 30× margin is what keeps most feels calm over a slow wire. So 'only while held' is a real category. (3) Weight doesn't buy stability. In this model the light and the 150 g caps have the same limit, because the limit is damping against delay, not mass. That pushes against the brief's 'heavy helps stability'. A way out appears: if the device adds a little damping of its own, locally and fast, stiffness up to about 0.47 N·m/rad can cross USB. So a split design, with the springs in Max and the damping in the knob, looks possible.

**Smaller findings.** Feeling a pitch: on the light cap, 0.005 N·m at 196 Hz moves the rim about 2.1 µm, against about 0.1 µm a fingertip can detect near that pitch. The simulation and the hand calculation agree (2.135 against 2.127 µm). So the physics allows it. Whether this motor and driver can push cleanly at 196 Hz is still unknown. The struck spring holds 5.9 Hz all the way down. The pendulum starts at 4.9 Hz and quickens to 5.8 as it settles, so the difference your page predicted is audible. The turntable idles 10% slow, because a speed servo with no integral term droops under the motor's own friction. Here the I term your sketch said has no acoustic counterpart turns out to have one: a turntable's speed control. In the lock, the beat click crawls around the LFO's wobble (0, 0.50, 0.99, 0.48 …), then lands at the same point every beat once the rate reaches the tempo.

The rule holds whatever they turn out to be, but the boundaries in the table will move once a bench measures them. Nobody has heard the renders. payload.rationale: Haptic Handwheel is your one-big-knob instrument: a motor and sensor whose feel is software. Until today it had seven feels on paper, a parts brief you asked us to doubt, and no plan. Today I built it in simulation. The sweep shows the stiff feels must run on the knob itself, and that a cable is fine for anything played into the hand. That gives the path a shape. Most of it I can do without you. The two places it can't go without you are spending money on parts and judging the feels by touch. The plan below puts those two at fixed points, so I never ask for either early. payload.plan:
Where this is going: a first prototype in Loudon's hand, so the seven feels get judged by touch, and a record of which feels carry over from the instrument to the simpler context knob.

1. The knob in simulation. A feel lab and a stability sweep, so every feel can be tried by eye and ear, and so we know which feels must run on the knob and which can come down a cable. (Started 2026-10-13.)
2. Pin the unknowns before buying. Find or name a test for the motor's rotor inertia, friction and cogging, and winding inductance (can it carry a pitch?). Decide whether one motor does everything or a small vibration actuator joins it. Write a firmware sketch that compiles (SimpleFOC: on-device feels, local damping, a torque input line) and the message format to Max. Finish with a final parts list with prices.
3. The parts order. Loudon says yes to the list and the spend. Nothing is bought before this.
4. Bench bring-up. Encoder reads cleanly, a centring spring, frets, then measure the real stability edge and the motor's real numbers, and retune the simulation with them so it stops guessing.
5. The touch gate. Loudon plays each feel and keeps, changes or drops it. Only a hand can pass this move. What he says goes back into the page.
6. The context knob. Port the feels that carried to a knob that follows Ableton's selected parameter (through Max for Live): fine control, with stepped values felt as steps.
7. Write it back. Which feels carried from the instrument to the product, and what the body (cap, weight, keys, the vintage look) should be next.

context-first — put the Ableton context knob before the instrument; I reorder and re-propose

payload.headline: The motor turns out to brake itself, which lets stiff feels survive a cable. I also wrote the firmware's feel core and the bench tests that will measure the real motor.
payload.ground: shipped · nothing bought, board sketch uncompiled · steward leans parts list next
payload.catchup: Haptic Handwheel is your idea for one big knob that is a motor and a sensor at once, played as an instrument. Software decides how it feels: a string, frets, a spring, a turntable. It is research reaching toward a product, and the nearer product is a simpler knob that knows which parameter it's controlling. Nothing is built or bought yet. Last cycle I built the knob in simulation. The worst news was that a feel computed in Max and sent down USB could only be about as stiff as a weak pitch-wheel spring before it starts to buzz. I also proposed a first plan (simulate, pin down the motor's unknowns, buy parts, bench test, then your hands judge each feel), and that plan still waits on your yes. Meanwhile I kept building along its second move, pinning the unknowns before anything is bought, and this cycle changed the picture.
payload.content:
**The motor brakes itself.** Last cycle's limit rested on a guess: that the motor and its bearings barely slow the knob down. The iFlight datasheet says otherwise. It gives 15.2 Ω across two leads, about 480 rpm with no load at 20 V, and 0.18–0.25 N·m at 1 A. When a driver like SimpleFOC sets the motor's voltage and doesn't measure current, a spinning motor generates a voltage of its own, and that voltage drives a current through the winding that pushes back against the spin. That push is a damper: real, physical and instant, with no loop and no delay in it. From the datasheet it comes out somewhere between 0.002 and 0.023 N·m·s/rad, which is 20 to 230 times what I had assumed.

**What that changes.** I re-ran the stability sweep with this brake included. Over USB to Max, the stiffest feel that stays calm goes from 0.022 to between 0.5 and 1.7 N·m/rad. That's enough for frets and a full string bend to run in Max and stay calm with no hand on the knob. The simulation agrees with the textbook rule within 8% in every case. The guess from 2026-10-05 still holds: springs, frets and walls are safest on the device. But there's now a real choice instead of a wall.

**What it costs.** The same brake kills anything that should keep moving on its own. A struck spring on the light cap rings for about eight wobbles with the brake cancelled. With the brake left on, it gets under half a wobble at the gentlest end of the range, and it doesn't wobble at all at the middle. The turntable would fight it too. So the firmware treats the brake as a dial each feel sets for itself, `cancelBrake` from 0 to 1. Stiff feels leave the brake on. The struck spring, the pendulum and the turntable cancel it, and they have to be computed on the knob. In the WAV, listen for the same flick three times: brake cancelled, then the gentlest brake, then the middle one.

**The firmware.** `feel_core.h` is plain C++ with no Arduino in it. It holds every feel that responds to the hand (frets, the string, the struck spring and pendulum, the melody-follower, the turntable, end stops), plus local damping, the brake dial and an input for torque played in from Max. It compiles on this laptop with no warnings. A test drives it and the browser feel lab's engine with the same 2,800 inputs, and they agree to within a millionth of a N·m, so the lab and the firmware describe one knob. `handwheel.ino` wraps it for an ESP32 with SimpleFOC and the AS5048A encoder. It speaks a one-line text protocol Max can send with [serial]: `feel frets`, `set k 0.2`, `play 0.01`. The knob reports its angle every 2 ms.

**The bench tests.** The firmware also has five tests that replace the four guesses: a spin-down done twice (driver off, then driver on at 0 V; the difference between the two is the brake), a push from rest with and without a disc of known weight (inertia and strength), a cogging map, and a frequency sweep. For the sweep, a contact mic on the cap recorded into your interface is the real test of whether you can feel a G. At 196 Hz the cap moves about 2 µm, which is too small for the encoder to see. `bench_analyze.py` turns a capture into numbers. I checked it on a made-up motor with known values, and it recovers them within 5%.

payload.headline: A parts order you could place today, about $145–185, plus a first Max patch that speaks the knob's language. Nothing bought yet.
payload.ground: shipped · order drafted, waiting on the plan · steward leans a 24 V supply
payload.catchup: Haptic Handwheel is your idea for one big knob that is a motor and a sensor at once, played as an instrument. Software decides how it feels: frets, a string, a struck spring, a turntable. It's research reaching toward a product, and the nearer product is a simpler knob that knows which parameter it's controlling. So far it exists only in simulation. Earlier cycles built a feel lab in the browser, found that the motor brakes itself (which lets stiff feels survive the trip over USB), and wrote firmware and bench tests that compile on the laptop but have never run on a board. This cycle turned all of that into a parts order you could place, and a Max patch for when the knob arrives. Ordering still waits on your answer to the plan I proposed: simulate, pin down the motor, buy parts, bench test, then your hands judge each feel.
payload.content:
**The order.** The motor stays the same: the iFlight GM5208-12 with its encoder, $61.99 and in stock, read on the shop page today. Two parts change from the brief. The driver becomes the SimpleFOC Mini v1, about $9, and I'd buy two so the first wiring mistake costs nothing. It sets volts and doesn't measure current, which is exactly the condition that gives us the motor's own brake. That makes the brief's pricier Shield, with its current sensing, the wrong fit as well as the dearer one. The controller becomes a classic ESP32 dev board, about $10, because the firmware is already written for its pins. The rest: a 0–30 V bench supply with a current knob, a piezo contact mic (the only real test of whether you can feel a G), a $1 capacitor so the motor can't push current back into the supply when your hand spins it, printed caps, and a block to clamp it to. That comes to about $145–185, or $75–95 if you already own a bench supply. The brief guessed $170–230. I left out the load cell, touch sensing, a second vibration motor and the lever, and the sheet says why for each.

**Why the volts matter.** The firmware asks the driver for volts. Part of that pushes on your hand. The rest cancels the motor's brake, and that part grows with speed. At 12 V, on the weakest motor the datasheet allows, the knob pushes exactly the brief's 0.08 N·m with nothing to spare. A struck spring flicked half a radian peaks at 177 rpm, past the 132 rpm that 12 V can hold while also pushing. At 24 V everything fits. So: bench tests at 12 V, then play at 24 V with the firmware's voltage cap held low. I made the supply voltage a named setting in the firmware so that switch is one line.

**The Max patch.** handwheel-host.maxpat opens the serial port, reads the knob's angle, speed and torque every 2 ms, and plays the angle as a pitch, 12 semitones per turn. It has a menu for the feels, number boxes for stiffness, damping, the brake dial, turntable speed and a torque ceiling, an LFO you can play into your hand, and buttons for the five bench tests. A script builds it, so it can be regenerated, and a second script checked that every wire lands on a real inlet and outlet. It has never been opened in Max.

payload.content:
Trimmed to the real instrument. The builder now takes the real instrument's range. A take that sounds outside that range is dropped, however steady it is: MusicGen will happily play a 'violin' at E2, and a violin can't. No sample stretches past the edge, either. Violin G3 up: 24 samples over 42 keys, all in tune, worst 2.4 cents. Flute C4 up: 21 samples over 38 keys, worst 4.3 cents. Marimba A2–A5, rung out the way you picked: 15 samples over 37 keys, worst 1.5 cents.

A tune instead of a staircase. Until now each audition was a rising line, one key after another. That proves every key sounds, but not that neighbouring samples sound alike. phrase.py plays a slow two-octave scale and then an eight-bar legato tune with leaps in it, through the same bow attack and release the SFZ uses. The tune crosses 9 to 14 different samples per instrument, so a take that sounds like a different player should stand out in the first phrase. Notes are in DESIGN.md under 'Trimmed to the real instrument'.

payload.content:
I wrote to_decentsampler.py, the palace's first DecentSampler writer (I found no earlier one). It reads a built SFZ and writes two files beside it: a .dspreset, which is the XML mapping with Attack, Release and Volume knobs in the Graphite house colours, and a .dslibrary, which zips that preset together with its samples. The script then reads the preset back off disk and plays every key through its mapping with the same pitch check the SFZ builds use. So the claim is about the files as written, not what the writer meant to write.

Two things had to be translated, and the preset says so in its own comments. First, SFZ gives fine-tuning in cents and DecentSampler wants semitones, so the value is divided by 100. Second, SFZ's one-shot mode, where a note plays to the end even after you lift the key, has no DecentSampler equivalent. The marimba gets a 6-second release instead, so each strike rings out after the key comes up.

One trap, now closed. My first check ran in a Python without librosa, and the check quietly fell back to a cruder pitch tracker that often gets notes an octave wrong. It reported the flute as 34/38 keys in tune and an older flute build as 42/59, though both had passed in full. In the project's own Python setup the numbers match exactly, and the script now refuses to grade without librosa.

payload.content:
The MusicGen takes are 3 to 5 seconds long, so a held key went silent around the 4-second mark. The new script loop_sustain.py builds a violin_looped and a flute_looped instrument beside the ones you have. For each sample it searches for a loop a whole number of wave cycles long, past the bow-on and short of the tail, scoring each candidate on how alike the waveform and the level are where the loop joins. It may only loop audio where the pitch tracker hears the take's own note. A 60 ms crossfade is baked into the WAV, and the same loop points go three places: the SFZ (loop_sustain), a smpl chunk inside each WAV (what hardware samplers and most importers read), and the rebuilt DecentSampler preset and library.

Then I held every sample's own key for 12 s through a loop-aware player and checked for clicks at each loop point, level pumping, and pitch across the whole hold. The best few candidate loops are tried in order until one passes all three. The first pass needed three fixes. A plain crossfade dipped 2–5 dB wherever the two blended stretches were partly out of phase, which pumps, so I switched to a level-preserving crossfade. A 'loop only flat-level stretches' rule found almost nothing, because these takes swell like played phrases. And without the pitch gate, the best-matching loop sat on breath (violin C5) or on a stretch with an added octave-low tone (violin A#5). The DecentSampler presets still match the SFZs key for key.

payload.headline: The mold now grows on the real mold's flow law. Loud food gets fat roads to the listener, and when the music moves, the network follows it.
payload.ground: shipped · five dishes rendered offline · steward leans: bring this engine into the browser page next
payload.catchup: Slime Mold Delay is a delay effect whose routing is grown rather than designed. Each tube of a slime mold is a delay line: its length sets the delay time, and its thickness sets how much signal it carries. You place food (sound sources) and a sink (the listener), and the mold works out the network. In June there was a browser bench that grows and prunes tubes live. You picked the full growth behaviour next: feeler tips that reach out, tubes that pull back when they find nothing, and a cap on total tube length. A September attempt drafted that but never posted it, and the draft never settled: 31 tubes grew and 31 were pruned in 24 seconds, because each tube was judged against the average tube, so half the network was always starving. This cycle swaps in the law the real mold follows. Food pushes fluid in, the sink drains it, and a tube thickens with the flow it actually carries. How hard each food pushes is how loud the music is there. So the routing learns the music, literally.
payload.content:
Start with [the figure](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/2026-10-13-flow-dishes.png). It has five dishes in rows, each shown at six moments across 30 seconds. Yellow dots are food, and they swell while they're sounding. The red dot is the listener. Thick gold lines are tubes (delay lines). Faint wandering threads are feeler tips, and brown threads are tips that gave up.

**Left music and right music** (rows 1–2). It's the same dish and the same random seed. Only the flakes being played differ. With the two left flakes playing, the mold grows two fat roads from them to the listener. With the two right flakes playing, the roads grow on the right. Listen to [left](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/2026-10-13-flow-left.wav) and [right](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/2026-10-13-flow-right.wav). The echoes come from where the music is.

**The music moves** (row 3, [listen](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/2026-10-13-flow-moves.wav)). This one is the headline. For 15 seconds the left flakes play, then the right ones take over. The first tip reaches the right food 2.3 seconds after the switch. The left roads have thinned to nothing by about 22 seconds, and the network ends on the right. You can hear the delay rebuild itself under the music.

**Feast and famine** (row 4, [listen](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/2026-10-13-flow-feast-famine.wav)). All flakes play, and the eat/starve knob from the entry swings every six seconds. Eating sends out tips. Starving thins the tubes faster.

**A tight budget** (row 5, [listen](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/2026-10-13-flow-tight-budget.wav)). All five flakes play, but there is only enough tube length for about two roads. The budget refused 15 tips. The mold kept the two left flakes and reached the second one *through* the first, so they share a trunk. That's the economy the Tokyo-subway experiments are famous for, and I didn't write it in.

What changed in the behaviour: in the fed dishes, tubes grown fell from 31 to 15 and tubes cut fell from 31 to 12. The mold explores less once every sounding flake is reached, and more while some sounding flake is still unreached. Because the sink is the colony's home, a starved network can always regrow from the listener. Sound travels both ways down each tube, strongly downstream and weakly upstream, the way the real mold's flow sloshes back and forth. So echoes can circulate around the network. If a tube's flow reverses, its two directions crossfade over a few frames instead of switching.

The code is [physarum_flow.py](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/physarum_flow.py). Each dish has a log of every frame and the [summary](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/2026-10-13-flow-summary.json) lists every tube grown and cut, with timestamps. One shared gain across all five renders, so their loudness compares.

equations.worded: Σ over neighbours ((tube thickness) ⁄ (tube length)) × (pressure here − pressure there) = (what this node pushes in)

where.def: for food: its share of the current loudness among reached food; for the sink: −1; else 0

equations.label: how a tube grows
equations.worded: d(thickness)⁄dt = (growth rate) × ( (flow it carries, saturating) − (how fast it thins) × (thickness) )

where.def: 1.8; above 1, competing roads resolve into one winner
thinning rate, raised while the eat/starve knob is starving
