payload.content:
**Open [the flow dish](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/slime-mold-flow-dish.html) and press THE MUSIC MOVES.** For 15 seconds flakes 1 and 2 play, then flakes 3 and 4 take over, and you watch and hear the network rebuild on the other side. After that the dish is yours. Click bare agar to place a flake (up to six), click a flake to start or stop it, and shift-click to take it away. Keys 1–6 pluck by hand. MIC feeds your microphone into the selected flake, which is the 'play into it' part. The knobs are eat/starve, the tube-length budget, streaming speed (which glides every echo time), a dish clock (0 freezes the routing, 4× is overnight growth), and wet/dry. Dots travel along each tube in the direction of flow, brighter where more is moving. The [strip](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/2026-10-13-flow-dish-moves.png) shows one browser run at 12, 21 and 29 seconds.

**What porting taught me.** The engine is a line-for-line port of last cycle's Python, kept in one script block with no audio in it, so [a node check](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/flow_dish_check.mjs) can run it against the same scenes. Left and right music behaved as before. But the first browser run of the moving music never found the right side. Run across 40 seeded dishes, the old law recovered in only 26. In the earlier offline render, the first tip happened to land fast. There were two causes.

1. **The old roads kept all their push.** Each reached flake was judged only against the *other reached flakes*. When the music left, the nearly silent left flakes still pushed 100% until a tip found the right. Now a flake's share is judged against all the sounding food in the dish, so the old roads lose their push the moment the music moves.
2. **Stepping stones died before anyone stepped on them.** A tip that landed on a bare spot of agar stopped there. That tube carried no flow, so it pulled back in about a second, and the next tip from that spot built an island the listener couldn't hear. Now a tip that crosses a bare spot keeps growing and leaves a branch point behind, the way a real tip does. As a side effect, roads now bend through branch points, so echoes take multi-hop paths and right-side roads share a trunk before they fork.

A third, smaller fix: the dish is round now, so tips turn back at the glass instead of wandering past the rim. The table has the sweep. The share rule is a dropdown on the page, so you can switch back to the cycle 8 rule and hear the difference.

payload.ground: shipped · buds live in the dish, measured on 320 dishes · steward leans: start dense, then thin
payload.catchup: Slime Mold Delay is a delay effect whose routing is grown, not designed. Every tube of a simulated slime mold is a delay line: its length sets the echo time and its thickness sets how much sound it carries. You place food (sound sources) and a listener, and the mold works out the network on the flow law the real mold follows. Loud food pushes, the listener drains, and tubes thicken with the flow they carry. Earlier today that engine went into a playable browser dish, and its routing follows the music when the music moves. This cycle a tip can bud from partway along a tube, and the tube forks where the tip lands. That brings the shape closer to the real mold. payload.content:
**Open [the flow dish](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/slime-mold-flow-dish.html) and press THE MUSIC MOVES.** Now and then a small ring appears partway along a gold tube. That's a bud. If its tip reaches food or a bare spot, the tube is cut in two right there, and a gold dot marks the fork. The two halves keep the old tube's thickness, flow and direction. Their lengths add up to the old one, so the echo time through the old road doesn't change. A bud that gives up leaves its tube whole. A new dropdown, A NEW TIP BUDS FROM, switches back to cycle 9's rule (tips grow only where tubes meet), so you can hear the difference. The [strip](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/2026-10-13-flow-dish-buds.png) shows one browser run at 12, 21 and 29 seconds. At 12 s, flake 2's road forks off flake 1's road. At 21 s the dish has let go of the left side and is briefly bare while a tip heads right. At 29 s, two roads run to the right flakes.

**The measurement.** I added two things to [the check](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/flow_dish_check.mjs). The first is a second dish where the listener sits at the left rim and four flakes fan out on the right. In that dish a shared trunk saves real tube length. In the first dish the food is spread all around the listener, so separate straight roads are already about the cheapest network, and no trunk could help. The second is a yardstick: the shortest network joining the listener to every flake it hears, using straight roads only. A network that shares trunks through forks can come in under it. Across 40 dishes each, with and without buds, none came in under it. In the clustered dish the mold spends about 1.25 to 1.7 times that much tube either way, and buds move the number by a few percent in either direction (see the table).

Then I tried the obvious dials in throwaway runs (not saved): keep exploring after every flake is fed, a steeper flow law, harsher pruning. The best of them got the clustered dish to about 1.48 times the shortest network. The harshest pruning got close to 1.07, but only by letting the mold lose half its food. So the waste isn't about where tips sprout. It's that once a road exists, it's never forced to compete. Loops where several tubes split the flow each carry enough to survive, and the mold stops exploring as soon as it's fed. Nakagaki's slime mold does it the other way around. It starts by covering the whole dish, then the flow carves that cover down to the roads that matter. Ours starts as one strand and adds. That reversal, start dense and then thin, is what I'd build next.

**What it costs the moving music.** With buds on, all 40 dishes still end on the right, but the right roads overtake the left a median 5.0 s after the switch, against 3.5 s without buds. Some tips now bud mid-tube on the old side instead of setting off from where the old roads meet. I left buds on in the page because the shape is truer to the mold. The dropdown puts the faster rule back if you prefer it by ear.

Splitting a tube routes its sound through a fork point, which has its own soft limiter and a one-third gain, so a forked road is probably quieter and slightly more saturated than the tube it replaced. payload.headline: The knob's firmware compiled for a real board for the first time, and the bench analyzer can now map the motor's bumps and answer 'can it carry a G'.
payload.ground: shipped · pinning the unknowns is done on paper · steward leans place the order
payload.catchup: Haptic Handwheel is your one-big-knob instrument: a motor that is also a sensor, with software deciding how it feels (frets, a string, a struck spring, a turntable). It's research, and the nearer product is a simpler knob that follows whatever parameter you've clicked in Ableton. You agreed a plan today. First the knob in simulation (done: a feel lab in the browser). Then pin the unknowns before buying anything. Then the parts order, which waits on your yes. Then the bench, then your hands judge each feel. This cycle finishes the pinning-down move. The board sketch now compiles, and the analyzer can read all five bench tests, so the first bench session turns straight into numbers. Nothing is bought yet.
payload.content:
**It compiles.** Your laptop already has the Arduino IDE and the Arduino Nano ESP32 core. I fetched SimpleFOC into a scratch folder and built the sketch: no warnings from our files, 10% of the board's space. It took one honest failure to get there. SimpleFOC 2.4.0 and 2.3.4 refuse this core, because they want arduino-esp32 3.x. 2.3.3 builds. So before the parts arrive: either pin SimpleFOC to 2.3.3, or update the ESP32 core. That's noted in the sketch and in BENCH.md. It also means that if a Nano ESP32 is sitting in a drawer, it could stand in for the controller on the order, with the pins moved.

**The motor's own bumps.** This motor has 12 slots and 14 magnets, so it should bump 84 times a turn, and those bumps are frets you didn't ask for. The cog test now holds the knob at 1,680 points, going one turn forward and one back. Going both ways pulls the two things apart: the bumps are the average of the two passes, and friction is half the gap between them. The analyzer fits the bumps and writes `cog_map.h`, and the firmware adds the opposite push so that it cancels them (`set cogGain 0` from Max lets you feel the raw motor again). On a pretend motor it recovers the bumps and the friction within 1%. A default software fret comes out 3.6× the raw bumps, and 45× what's left after cancelling.

**Can it carry a G?** The encoder can only count the wobble up to about 90 Hz, so the contact mic does the rest. A piezo on the cap hears acceleration, so dividing by pitch squared gives the knob's movement at every pitch, scaled where the encoder and the mic both hear. The mic and the knob keep separate clocks. The analyzer finds the sweep in the recording by itself (it found a 1.37 s offset to the millisecond). It then fits the winding's inductance, which is what decides how fast the push dies at high pitch. Across pretend motors from 1 to 12 mH it lands within 1%. With the encoder alone it can be off by 80%, so the mic is worth its $10.

**One motor or two.** The plan asked whether a small vibration motor should join this one. The model's answer: one is enough, by a wide margin. About 10 µm of rim movement per volt at G3, against roughly 0.16 µm a fingertip detects. I've written the rule down before the data: one motor if the mic shows ten times the threshold at 196 Hz for 1 V or less, re-checked with a finger resting on the rim. So the vibration motor stays off the order.

payload.headline: A feel map: which feels want the motor's own brake, where each one can live, and a fix so frets can't stick between notes.
payload.ground: shipped · parts order still yours to answer · steward leans keep building toward the bench
payload.catchup: Haptic Handwheel is your one-big-knob instrument: a motor that is also a sensor, with software deciding how it feels (frets, a string, a struck spring, a turntable). It's research, and the nearer product is a simpler knob that follows the parameter you've clicked in Ableton. The plan you agreed goes: try the knob in simulation, pin down the unknowns, buy the parts on your yes, bring it up on the bench, then your hands judge each feel. The first two are done on paper, and the parts list waits on you. This cycle used that wait. It worked out which feels want the motor's free brake and where each feel can be computed. It also found and fixed a way frets could land out of tune.
payload.content:
**The brake decides where a feel can live.** Driven by voltage, this motor slows itself for free. The free brake is what lets a stiff feel be computed in Max, over a slow USB cable, without buzzing. It is also what kills a ring. So I went feel by feel. The frets, the string, the centring spring, the haptic filter and the context knob's stepped values (8 clicks a turn) all want the brake on, and with it on they can be computed in Max. Frets and the string need the brake to be at least the middle of my guesses for that. End stops still have to run on the knob itself. The struck spring wants the brake off: 3 wobbles before it dies with it off, 1 with it on. With the brake off it has to run on the knob. The turntable wants it off too: it idles at 88% speed with it off and 52% with it on. It is a speed loop, and it lives on the knob. The LFO, the pitch and the beat clicks don't care. That is good news for the product: nearly everything the context knob needs could be computed in Max.

**Frets could stick between notes. Fixed.** With friction, a fret's pull is weakest exactly on the ridge between two notes. Let go there and the knob just stays. In the model, about one let-go in twenty stuck, up to 50 cents off. The motor's 84 bumps a turn hardly matter for tuning. The ridge does. So the frets now give a small push off the ridge: nothing at each note, 0.006 N·m on the ridge, just above friction. Every let-go then lands within 2.4 cents. It's in the firmware (`set kick`). The firmware still compiles for the Nano ESP32, and the laptop test still matches the browser simulation. BENCH.md has the test to check it on the real motor.

**Hear it:** frets_landing.wav plays four passes of eight let-gos, with clicks marking passes 1 to 4: no bumps, raw bumps, bumps cancelled, then bumps cancelled with the push off the ridge. Each landed note plays beside its in-tune neighbour, so slow beating means a sour landing. struck_brakes.wav plays the same strike four times, from brake cancelled to the strongest guess. The feel lab now has brake and bumps switches and the feel map table.

payload.headline: The turntable now holds 33⅓ without surging when you let go, and each feel brings its own brake and settings in the firmware.
payload.ground: shipped · parts order still yours to answer · steward leans keep building toward the bench
payload.catchup: Haptic Handwheel is your one-big-knob instrument: a motor that is also a sensor, with software deciding how it feels (frets, a string, a struck spring, a turntable). It's research, and the nearer product is a simpler knob that follows the parameter you've clicked in Ableton. The plan you agreed goes like this: try the knob in simulation, pin down the unknowns, buy the parts once you say yes, bring it up on the bench, then your hands judge each feel. The first two are done on paper, and the parts list is waiting on you. This cycle used the wait to finish two loose ends from the last one. The turntable used to idle slow (88% of speed), and now it holds 33⅓. Each feel now carries its own settings and its own brake, so switching feels can't carry the wrong stiffness across. The firmware still compiles for the Nano ESP32, and the laptop test still matches the browser simulation.
payload.content:
**Why the turntable idled slow.** It only pushed in proportion to how far below speed it was, so it always ran short by friction divided by that push. That gave 88% of speed with the motor's brake cancelled and 52% with it on. I tried three fixes against a scene where it spins, a finger drags it almost to a stop for a second, it's let go, and then a hand scratches it back and forth.

**The ordinary fix surges.** A slow correction that keeps learning gets the idle to 100%. But while your finger holds the platter it learns to shove harder, and when you let go it flies to 284% of speed and takes half a second to come back. You'd hear that as a chipmunk yelp after every hold.

**Learning only near speed can't get started.** With the brake on, the push alone never gets the platter within reach of full speed, so the correction never switches on and it stays at 52–72%.

**What works: know the cost, then trim.** The bench's coast test already measures what it costs to keep the platter spinning: bearing drag and friction. The turntable now pushes that amount up front. A small slow correction trims the rest, and it only learns within 20% of speed, so a hand holding it back teaches it nothing. Result: 100% idle with every brake guess. After the drag it peaks at 113% and is back within 1% in 27–55 ms, which reads as a quick catch rather than a yelp. If the bench misreads the motor by 30% in either direction, it still idles at 100%. Without the trim it would sit at 86% or 114%.

**A finding about the encoder.** At 33 rpm the encoder moves less than one count per 10 kHz tick, so the turntable was steering by a speed reading that was mostly noise. It now smooths its speed over 5 ms, the same as SimpleFOC's default. The rms wobble at idle drops from 0.13% to 0.02%. That's unweighted, so it isn't directly comparable to a record player's wow-and-flutter spec.

**Each feel keeps its own settings.** Before, every feel shared one set of numbers. If you switched from the soft centring spring (stiffness 0.03) to the struck spring, it kept the 0.03 instead of its own 0.085. Now each feel starts from its own defaults, with the brake the feel map chose for it. The brake is on for frets, string, centring spring and haptic filter. It's cancelled for the struck spring, the pendulum and the turntable. So the struck spring rings and the frets stay calm without you sending anything. `set` from Max changes only the selected feel, and the knob says `f <name> brake <x>` on each switch. The feel lab mirrors this: picking a feel sets its brake, and the menu can still override it. After the coast test, the bench analyzer now prints the exact lines to paste into Max (`set kt …`, then `set ffB …` and `set ffC …` with the turntable selected).

**Hear it:** turntable_hold.wav plays the riff on the platter through the same scene four times, with one to four ticks marking each version: the push alone, the ordinary correction (listen for the yelp after the drag), learning only near speed, and the final design. The chart shows the same thing as speed over time. The blue line is hidden under the yellow one because with the brake cancelled they behave the same.

payload.headline: Étude No. 2, fifth draft: a 4:27 hero's journey in twelve chapters, with a cast of surfaces, atlas-click gestures, canons, and phrases that end as questions.
payload.ground: shipped · 4:27, nobody has listened yet · steward leans listen to the whole thing once
payload.catchup: This project is a synthesizer whose wavetable is a surface on a torus. Two scan rates read it, and their ratio decides whether it sounds harmonic or shimmers. Its test piece, Étude No. 2, is played entirely by the Hopf codebox, the version steered from a point on a sphere, and the score is only knob moves. Over three rounds of notes you asked for a story with real grooves, then a looser groove with sung melodies, then (on the fourth draft) phrases that stay open, the weird sounds of the first version back, the voicing atlas clicked in rhythm, counterpoint, and the whole song built as the hero's journey. This cycle wrote that: a fifth draft, 4:27, in twelve chapters. Nobody has heard it yet.
payload.content:
**The cast is the surfaces.** The hero is Penrose, born at the pole where it is the plain 1D synth. The ordinary world is the one-dimensional wavetable, and the journey is the climb up the sphere. The mentor is Knot Shadow's 3:2 whistle. The guardian is a stirred Chladni growl. The shadow is Fisher Ridge, off every ratio. Two new characters come straight out of the voicing atlas:

- **The trickster** is Matérn Field clicked from lock to lock. On almost every lock it sounds the same A4 (measured 439.5 Hz after every click), but with a different set of undertones, so each click changes its colour and never its pitch. In the tests it fills the gaps in the bell pattern. In the reward it clicks on every group of the 7/8 limp.
- **The stair** is Stiff String. On every lock it sounds its x scan rate, so its nineteen locks form a scale of fractions, the Farey scale, part tonal and part not. The hero's motif A C E D is already inside it (1:1, 2:3, 1:3, 1:2, with the C 15 cents sharp). The stair clicks down that scale one lock a beat into the cave, runs an ostinato up it on the road back, and at the resurrection plays the motif as a bass from inside the strange scale.

**The weird sounds return** in the refusal (the hero slides back to the pole through every ratio in between, the smear from No. 1), at the threshold, and in the ordeal. In the ordeal the reed is torn through the atlas in leaps from 55 to 1145 Hz, the hero's dead line slows toward stillness, and then comes 1.6 s of true silence before a coupling snap starts the reward.

**Counterpoint:** a free-time canon with the mentor (the motif inverted, the hero imitating below), a stretto chase on the road back that tightens from a beat to an eighth, and a three-voice motif at the resurrection.

**Questions:** the phrases end on E, on E over G♯, on B, or climbing without landing. Only the very end arrives on A, and that ending is kept in the shape you liked.

Listen: [the fifth draft](open:Projects/2D Torus Wavetable Synthesizer/Etude/etude_two_e_heros_journey.m4a). Chapter times are in the score.

payload.content:
[torus-ab.maxpat](open:Projects/2D Torus Wavetable Synthesizer/RNBO/torus-ab.maxpat) is the README's whole harness, built for you. Penrose loads on open, and nine surface buttons swap it. The four tests are buttons: static row, static column, closed 3:2 orbit, shimmer. Two shared phasors drive 2d.wave~. A listen menu switches between codebox, 2d.wave~ and the error magnified ×1000.

**One change from the old recipe.** The written codebox counts its own phase, so comparing it with 2d.wave~ mixes two questions: does it read the surface right, and do two phase counters agree? So the patch carries two codebox paths. A1 is the codebox as written, the one you'll play. A2 is a new twin, `torus_2d_lookup_extphase.codebox`: the same lookup, copied word for word (a script checks the two copies match), but fed the same two phasors as 2d.wave~. A2 − B tests the lookup and nothing else. Each path has its own meter showing the peak difference in dB, and the pass bar is below −100.

**What a failing number would mean.** I can't run Max, so I modelled the ways 2d.wave~ might read the surface differently and ran the codebox against each on Penrose (table). Each one leaves a different pattern across the four tests. Swapped axes are loud on every test. A one-row offset sits near −30 dB everywhere except the static row. A seam that doesn't wrap shows only as a whisper at −60. So whatever four numbers you read off, they point at a cause. One gap: 'y over 1023 rows' and 'no interpolation between rows' give nearly the same numbers. Your scope tells them apart, because no interpolation draws stair steps.

The picture is the patch drawn from its own file, so you can see the wiring before opening it. The README's file list now points at the patch.

It can be plucked, struck and bowed, it sits on a soundboard, and you can watch it in slow motion. payload.content:
**What's new in [study v1.9](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Waveguide%20Synthesizer/study-v1.9-the-bow-grips/index.html):**

- **A dot where hair meets string.** It's amber and full while the hair holds the string. The instant the hair lets go, it shrinks to a dark bead with a white spark. It runs on the same slowed clock as the string, so you see it let go exactly when the sharp corner arrives at the bow.
- **The bow's grip chart,** in the empty space under the nut, joined to the bow by a dotted thread. It shows one string cycle, with a cursor at the moment the screen is showing. The top strip is the hair: amber where it holds, dark where it slips. The middle is the string's real speed at the bow point against a dashed line for the bow's own speed. While the hair holds, the string rides that line; when it lets go, the string flies back. The bottom is the friction curve: how hard the hair grips against how far the string's speed has strayed from the bow's.
- **Each bow slider now changes one thing on the chart.** Bow speed raises the dashed line. Bow force widens the amber grip window on the friction curve. Bow position moves where the slip lands. Touch or hover a slider and its mark lights up, the same way the nut and bridge do.
- **The chart puts the result in words:** *singing* (lets go once a cycle), *breaking up* (two or three times), *skating* (never catches), or *pinned* (never lets go).
- **The walk has twelve steps now.** The bow steps point at the chart, and a new last step slows one catch and one release right down.

**What it shows (table).** At the default setting the hair holds 90% of the cycle and lets go once. That is the Helmholtz motion every bowed string makes when it sings. At light force it holds only 67% and slips back at a steady speed: the clean square wave from the textbooks. At full force the string under the bow stops moving. The page says so instead of pretending the string sings.

**Fixed along the way:** moving from a pinned step to the next one used to crack at full scale. Now the walk quiets the string between bow steps, and lifting a pinned bow quiets it too. Every step of the recorded walk now peaks between −17.5 and −4.4 dBFS.

**How I checked it:** I ran the page's own engine headless in Node for the numbers and the grip tour. I recorded the whole walk in Chrome, picture and sound, with no page errors. One honest wrinkle: this Mac's audio device wouldn't render for any Chrome tonight (even a bare test tone's clock sat at zero). So the browser recordings ran the page's own engine on the main thread, kept in real time by a stand-in clock, and took the sound straight from the engine's output. The DSP is the page's. Only the path to the speakers was faked.

payload.catchup: Waveguide Synthesizer is the browser string whose on-screen wave is the sound: two delay lines carry a right-going and a left-going wave, and their sum is the string you see and hear. It can be plucked, struck and bowed, and it sits on a soundboard. You set the order: first make every slider visibly change the picture, then the body, then the bow, then even stiffness, then a guided teaching walk. The picture, the body and the bow are done. This cycle is stiffness. Stiffness already sounded right and meant the same at every pitch, but all you could see was the string getting thicker. payload.content:
**What's new in [study v1.10](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Waveguide%20Synthesizer/study-v1.10-the-overtones-run-sharp/index.html):**

- **The overtone ladder, top right, titled 'what the ring hears'.** Each dashed rung marks where a perfectly flexible string would put an overtone: 2, 3, 4… times the note. Each amber bar marks where *this* string puts it, as tall as it is ringing at the pickup right now. When the string is stiff, a slanted line runs from the top of each rung to its bar's foot, so you can see how far each overtone has moved. Under the bars is how sharp overtones 2, 4, 8 and 16 run, in cents.
- **The stiffness slider now lights the ladder** as well as the string's thickness. Drag it and the bars fan out to the right, the high ones furthest. At 0 they sit on their rungs. At 0.4 overtone 16 is 35 ¢ sharp. At 0.7 it is 245 ¢ sharp. At 1.0 it is more than an octave out.
- **One line of words says what you're hearing:** *harmonic, like gut or nylon* · *a little stiff, like a piano's middle* · *stiff, like a piano's outer octaves* · *very stiff: no longer a series, a struck metal bar, toward a bell*.
- **The bars are measured, not drawn from a formula.** The engine works out where its loop really rings each overtone: the frequency at which one trip round the loop takes exactly that many periods. Then it listens at each of those frequencies, at the pickup, in short six-cycle windows. So the ladder shows what the filter actually achieved. That differs from the textbook rule at stiffness 1.0, and also at stiffness 0, where every overtone sits 1 to 2 ¢ sharp because of the loop's own small stretch.
- **The walk has thirteen steps now.** The stiffness step points at the ladder. A new step holds stiffness at 0.70 while the note climbs two octaves, from C3 to C5. The ladder keeps its shape, because one wire of one thickness bends its overtones by the same cents at every pitch. That is v1.5's even stiffness, finally visible.

**How I checked it:** I ran the page's own engine headless in Node at four notes and four stiffnesses. For each, I took the audio and found every overtone's real peak with a fine FFT. Every bar loud enough to measure is within 0.26 ¢ of the peak in the sound, and at most notes within 0.05 ¢ (ladder-vs-sound.json). Then I photographed the ladder at five settings and recorded the whole walk in Chrome, picture and sound. There were no page errors, and every step peaked between −17.5 and −6.2 dBFS. The recording caught one bug, which is fixed: during the pitch sweep the ladder went dark. That turned out to be true to the string rather than a ladder fault. Between replucks the string's own sound dies within about a second at higher notes, and the soundboard rings on after it. So the bars now fall at 30 dB a second instead of 60, slow enough to read after a pluck.

**Passed over:** drawing the stretch on the string itself (a stiff string's strobe picture already can't stand still, and the replay view shows the high ripples running ahead). A cents-against-overtone curve was the other option, but it's more abstract. Rungs against bars can be read without knowing what a cent is.

payload.content:
**What was wrong (study v1.10):** the hair had no limit on how hard it could hold. So a heavy bow held the string for ever ('pinned'), and the share of each cycle the hair held hardly moved with bow position: 85% at 0.60, where the physics of a bowed string (Helmholtz motion) says 60%. The held string also didn't ride the bow: at the default it moved at 0.69 of the bow's speed.

**What [study v1.11](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Waveguide%20Synthesizer/study-v1.11-the-bow-lets-go/index.html) does:** the hair now holds the string only up to a limit set by bow force. While the string rides with the bow, the hair pulls as hard as it must. Each lap, the corner running round the string comes back and pulls harder. The instant the pull passes the limit, the hair lets go and slides, and sliding friction is weaker than holding friction. It catches again when the string comes back to the bow's speed. This is the hyperbolic friction law of McIntyre and Woodhouse.

- **The slip follows bow position** (table). The hair lets go while the corner runs from the bow to the nearer end and back, so a bow near the bridge slips briefly and one toward the middle slips longer.
- **The string rides the bow exactly:** 0.98 to 1.03 of the bow's speed while held, at every pitch from E2 to E5.
- **Force now covers the whole range:** under about 0.2 it skates (no sound), 0.3 to 0.5 it breaks up (lets go twice a cycle), 0.55 to 0.9 it sings, and above about 0.95 it **crunches**: it holds too long, lets go late, and is never the same twice. That is the rough sound a pressed-too-hard bow really makes. The new default force is 0.6.
- **The chart's bottom panel is now 'pull'.** A dotted line shows the limit, and bow force raises it. While the hair holds, the dot sits on the left-hand post. When the pull reaches the limit, the dot runs out along the sliding curve. The chart's words learned 'crunching', detected by how much the hold-and-let-go pattern changes from one look to the next (0.15 to 0.21 when crunching, under 0.03 when singing).
- **The walk's three bow steps** now say what is true: the dark gap shrinks as the bow nears the bridge; too much force crunches; the dot lets go when it hits the limit.

**One design call to know about:** the force slider presses a little harder the nearer the bow is to an end, the way a player does. That cancels one of Schelleng's two limits (the most force a bow can use falls as it nears the bridge), so a single force sings all along the string. The other limit still bites: near the bridge a light bow breaks up, which is the real lesson.

**How I checked it:** I ran the page's own engine headless. The checks were bow position against force on an 8 × 6 grid, five pitches, lift-off clicks (none; the level after lifting matches the level while bowing), and v1.10 side by side (bow-probe.json). In Chrome I photographed the chart at five settings plus a slowed run of frames, then recorded the whole 13-step walk, picture and sound. There were no page errors, and the bow-force step ends on 'crunching' where v1.10 said 'pinned'.

**Passed over:** v1.4's grip curve with a separate breakaway rule bolted on. It would have fixed pinning but not the slip length, because the slip length comes from the hair having a ceiling at all.

payload.subject: Frequency-Time Duality
payload.passage: The threshold itself is *perceptual*, not physical — the same waveform produces different worlds depending on which side of ~20 Hz it sits.
payload.reading: The passage: 'The threshold itself is perceptual, not physical — the same waveform produces different worlds depending on which side of ~20 Hz it sits.' Through Deleuze's passive synthesis (Difference and Repetition, ch. II): 'Repetition changes nothing in the object repeated, but does change something in the mind which contemplates it' (p. 70, Patton), and the imagination 'contracts the successive independent instants into one another thereby constituting the lived, or living, present.' Pitch is that contraction: the repeats fold into one quality. Rhythm is what is left when they come too slowly to fold. So ~20 Hz is not a line in the signal but the width of one act of contraction, the span of a living present. And the page's Recursion section ('a structural feature of how the auditory system parses periodicity at every level of nesting') is Deleuze's contractions nesting inside contractions. That gives the page's open question ('does the threshold sit at the same place on every dimension?') a hypothesis it does not state: each level is its own contraction with its own span, so the nested thresholds need not coincide.
payload.fidelity_note: Passed, with one flag. The check ran against the Deleuze lens's own named fake ('virtual', 'intensity' sprinkled on): reading the dial as 'a virtual field, each zone an actualization' would fit any continuum, and the Deleuze page already says it of the wavetable, so I threw that out. Contraction is specific: moved to the Slapback bullet or the Origin table, it says nothing; it bites only on the claim that the threshold is perceptual and on the Recursion. The flag: the palace's Deleuze page has no passive synthesis or contraction in it today. The apparatus is Deleuze's own, not borrowed from FTD, but the glass reached past what its palace page carries. Quote wording checked on the web (Patton, p. 70). Spark 4, not 5: the claim is a reframing plus a testable hypothesis, not a new mechanism, and it runs mostly one way (Deleuze into FTD).

payload.headline: The Faust crowd compiles at last. In the 30 s sweep, 32 neurons snap into a clean tone and let go. The June Python audition never locked.
payload.ground: shipped · first step of the plan done · steward leans the crowd goes to the H90 first
payload.catchup: Action Potential Oscillator builds a synth from a neuron's biology. The single neuron, four playable Gen~ stages built in March, is done. What comes next is the crowd: many slightly different neurons coupled so that how tightly they agree becomes the sound. In June you picked the Faust route. The Faust engine was drafted but had never compiled, and the only sound we had was a Python stand-in. This cycle the Faust version compiles. I rendered a coupling sweep and put it beside the Python render. That finishes the first step of the agreed plan. The next step is getting the instrument onto the Eventide H90 through RNBO.
payload.content:
**Why it never compiled.** Faust 2.88 is on the Mac now, and the June file died with 'stack overflow in eval'. Each neuron's voltage, phase, timer and recovery velocity were four separate feedback loops that referred to each other in a circle. The three fixes the June handoff note describes never landed in the file. Its spread formula was also wrong, so the neurons weren't really varied.

**What changed (v0.2).** Each neuron is now one feedback loop over its whole state: charge, then spike rise, then spike fall, then a damped recovery from the undershoot. The crowd adds up its voltages and its spike signals in a single step, so the splitting stage is gone. Only the crowd's average spike signal goes back into each neuron's drive, scaled by coupling K. It compiles in 0.1 s. A small offline renderer is in `faust-render/`.

**What the sweep shows.** 32 neurons, coupling rising from 0 to 0.016 and back to 0 over 30 s, chosen to match the June render's shape. Listen to [neuropulse-faust-sweep.wav](open:Projects/Action Potential Oscillator/neuropulse-faust-sweep.wav). For the first 4.7 s you hear a buzzy smear. Then the crowd snaps into a clean harmonic tone, holds, and lets go at about 25.7 s. It locks and unlocks at nearly the same coupling (about 0.005 going up, 0.0046 coming down), so there's barely any memory in the switch. The locked tone sits near 116 Hz, not the 110 Hz you dial in. My guess is that the faster neurons pull the crowd up to their pace. I haven't tested that.

**The comparison is the real news.** In [faust-vs-python.png](open:Projects/Action Potential Oscillator/faust-vs-python.png), the Faust spectrogram turns into clean harmonic lines while it's locked. The June Python audition is broadband noise from start to finish. Its coupling was probably too weak to ever pull the crowd together. So the two don't agree. The Faust render is the first time this project has made the locking you can hear.

**A bonus step toward the H90.** `faust2rnbo` turned the crowd into an RNBO codebox (`rnbo/neuropulse.codebox`, 928 lines). Its Max patch wrapper failed because the Python package py2max is missing. Nobody has opened it in Max yet.

payload.headline: I wrote the crowd's RNBO version by hand, with every control a signal inlet. It matches the Faust crowd sample for sample, and a Max patch holds it.
payload.ground: shipped · the crowd's code is ready for RNBO, not yet opened in Max · steward leans crowd first
payload.catchup: Action Potential Oscillator builds a synth from a neuron's biology. The single neuron has been playable in Gen~ since March. Earlier today the crowd, 32 slightly different neurons whose coupling turns into the sound, finally compiled in Faust and locked into a clean tone. That finished the first step of the plan. The next step is getting the instrument onto the Eventide H90 through RNBO. I asked whether the crowd or the single neuron should go first. While that's open I kept going on the crowd. Faust's automatic RNBO export ran only 16 neurons and froze every control, so I wrote a readable RNBO version by hand. It runs all 32 neurons, takes every control as a signal inlet, and produces exactly the same sound as Faust. It sits in a Max patch nobody has opened yet.
payload.content:
**Why I wrote it by hand.** Faust's automatic export (`rnbo/neuropulse.codebox`) is 928 lines of generated code. It has only 16 neurons, and every control is a fixed setting, not a signal jack. This project's rule is that every knob is a signal inlet you can patch an LFO or envelope into. The new file, [neuropulse-crowd.codebox](open:Projects/Action Potential Oscillator/rnbo/neuropulse-crowd.codebox), is about 150 lines. It uses the same maths as the Faust version, with one array slot per neuron. It has 8 inlets: frequency, coupling, spread, leak time, spike length, undershoot depth, recovery damping and refractory time. It has two outputs: the crowd's voice, and a new one, **synchrony**, which is the share of the crowd spiking right now. You can use it as a modulation signal (0 to 1).

**How I checked it without Max.** I can't open Max, so I wrote a small Node harness (`rnbo/codebox-harness.mjs`). It runs the codebox text itself, line for line, with stand-ins for RNBO's built-in functions. I rendered the same 30-second coupling sweep as last cycle's Faust render, with Faust built in double precision as RNBO runs. The audio differs by at most 6e-8 over 1.44 million samples, and the synchrony output is identical. Against last cycle's single-precision Faust build, the two drift apart after 9 ms because the system is chaotic, but the lock and release come out the same.

**What the signal inlets buy you.** [neuropulse-codebox-phrase.wav](open:Projects/Action Potential Oscillator/neuropulse-codebox-phrase.wav) is 24 s of a four-note phrase, A2 C3 E3 D3. Coupling breathes on a 0.2 Hz sine while the spread between neurons slowly widens. Early breaths lock fully. By the last ones, the crowd only reaches about a third of the way to a lock, because a wider spread needs more coupling. You can see it in [codebox-vs-faust.png](open:Projects/Action Potential Oscillator/codebox-vs-faust.png): harmonic lines appear on the breaths and smear between them. The synchrony curve trails the coupling a little on the way up.

**The Max patch.** [neuropulse-crowd.maxpat](open:Projects/Action Potential Oscillator/rnbo/neuropulse-crowd.maxpat) is written by hand (`make_maxpat.py`), with no py2max. Inside is an rnbo~ with in~ 1 to 8, the codebox, and out~ 1 and 2. Outside, each inlet has a number box feeding a sig~ with its default value, then a gain stage, a DAC, and a synchrony meter. A 0.2 Hz cycle~ sits beside the coupling inlet, unwired, ready to make the coupling breathe. To try it: open the patch, turn on audio, and raise coupling past about 0.005.

payload.headline: I tested four spike shapes in the crowd. The spike's tail barely changes when the crowd locks, but every shape keeps its own colour in the sound.
payload.ground: shipped · spike-shape question answered · steward leans crowd first, then put the locked pitch back on the dialed note
payload.catchup: Action Potential Oscillator builds a synth from a neuron's biology. The single neuron has been playable in Gen~ since March. Today the crowd of 32 coupled neurons compiled in Faust and locked into a tone, and I wrote a hand-made RNBO version that matches it sample for sample. The plan's next step is carrying the instrument to the Eventide H90 through RNBO, and I'm still waiting on whether the crowd or the single neuron goes first. Meanwhile I ran the experiment the project has always pointed at: where does the neuron's biological detail stop mattering to the sound? I tried four spike shapes in the same crowd. The detail stops mattering to how the crowd behaves, but not to how it sounds.
payload.content:
**The four shapes.** (1) The full Stage-4 spike: 1 ms, with a ringing undershoot. (2) The same spike with no undershoot. (3) A bare click, 0.06 ms, which is just integrate-and-fire with a reset. (4) A slow 3 ms spike. For each one I swept the coupling over 19 values. Each run starts with the crowd free for 1 s, then turns coupling on. Synchrony is the true Kuramoto order parameter, worked out from each neuron's own spike times, so it isn't fooled by how wide the pulse is.

**What the crowd does.** The undershoot hardly matters: the full spike reaches half-lock at K≈0.0039, the flat one at 0.0033. Width matters only through the charge a spike hands its neighbours. The click needs about 9 times the coupling (0.035). Per unit of charge, short pulses lock most easily: the click needs 0.035, the 1 ms spike 0.059 and the 3 ms spike 0.139. So the spike's tail does stop mattering here, which is what the entry guessed.

**What you hear.** This is where the entry's guess was wrong. Each shape's spectral shape is almost the same when the crowd is scattered as when it's locked (correlation 0.99). The four shapes stay about 9.5 dB apart when scattered and 14 dB apart when locked. The crowd doesn't average the spike away. The spike sets the colour the crowd plays in. And the coupling has its own sound: locking darkens every shape. The spectral centroid falls from 874 to 496 Hz for the full spike and from 4256 to 2808 Hz for the click, because the low harmonics add up in step while the highs stay slightly smeared. **The tighter the lock, the darker the tone, so coupling acts as a lowpass.** That's 'coupling becomes timbre' as a measurement.

**Listen.** In [neuropulse-spike-shapes.wav](open:Projects/Action Potential Oscillator/neuropulse-spike-shapes.wav), each shape plays 2.5 s scattered, then 3 s locked (coupling set to 3 times its half-lock value), all at matched loudness. Full spike 0–5.5 s (locks at 2.5), no undershoot 5.9–11.4 (locks at 8.4), click 11.8–17.3 (locks at 14.3), slow spike 17.7–23.2 (locks at 20.2). The figure is [spike-shape-findings.png](open:Projects/Action Potential Oscillator/spike-shape-findings.png).

**The pitch pull, confirmed.** Last cycle I guessed that the 116 Hz lock comes from the fastest neuron. It does, exactly: at 5%, 10% and 20% rate spread, the locked crowd plays its fastest member's own solo pitch to within 0.01 Hz (116.2, 121.8, 132.6 Hz, against 110 dialed). Before the lock, coupling only adds drive, so the pitch also creeps up slowly.

**A bug fixed on the way.** A spike whose length isn't a whole number of samples overshot its peak and its floor. The click fell so far below its floor that it spent about 170 extra samples recovering, and its pitch dropped from 110 to 78 Hz. Both `neuropulse.dsp` (now v0.2.1) and the RNBO codebox (v0.1.1) now clamp the spike. I re-checked them against each other: the largest difference is 4e-8 per sample, and the synchrony outputs are identical.

payload.claim: The Population Dynamics section of [Action Potential Oscillator](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Action%20Potential%20Oscillator) guesses that a spike's shape matters for one neuron but averages out in a population. Today's experiment (four spike shapes, 32 neurons, 19 coupling values) splits that guess in two. When the crowd locks barely depends on the spike's tail: half-lock at coupling 0.0039 with the undershoot and 0.0033 without. Spike width matters only through the charge each spike hands its neighbours. How the crowd sounds keeps the shape: each shape's spectral shape is the same scattered or locked (correlation 0.99), and the four shapes stay 9.5–14 dB apart. Locking also darkens every shape, with the spectral centroid falling 35–58%, so coupling works like a lowpass. Proposed replacement for the hypothesis sentence: 'Spike shape stops mattering to the crowd's behaviour, but not to its sound. When the population locks is set by coupling, heterogeneity and the charge each spike delivers. The spike's shape survives as the colour the crowd plays in, and the tightness of the lock darkens that colour.' Evidence: [neuropulse-spike-shapes.wav](open:Projects/Action Potential Oscillator/neuropulse-spike-shapes.wav), [spike-shape-findings.png](open:Projects/Action Potential Oscillator/spike-shape-findings.png).

payload.content:
WHAT I MADE. bayes_engine.js holds the whole instrument in one class. The render, render_chord_belief.js, and the page, belief-instrument.html (built by build_instrument.js), run that same code, so what you play is what I measured. It follows the entry's spec: one Hann cycle in and out, 4 to 128 sustain cycles, amplitude ∝ √(f/cycles), and Poisson onsets at 160 grains/s. Each grain picks its pitch by first choosing the prior or a held note in proportion to their weight, then drawing inside that choice. Grain length rises with closeness to the nearest note, and that closeness only counts in proportion to how strongly the note is believed. That gate is the entry's fix for the click at chord-press. A re-pressed note keeps the conviction it had built up, so the common tones of a chord change stay sharp while a new note has to earn its place.

THE TAKE. chord-belief.wav runs 0–4 s with the flat prior and nothing held. C E G is held from 4–14 s. At 14 s G lets go and A arrives, making A minor (14–22 s). Everything releases from 22–28 s. From 28–34 s the prior is painted into A-minor-pentatonic hills with nothing held, and from 34–42 s low A and E are held over that prior. chord-belief.png shows the belief over time: the bumps pinch to a thread, G blurs out while C and E stay sharp, and the prior's hills appear once it is painted.

WHAT I MEASURED. The level stays between 0.138 and 0.182 RMS across the whole take (about 2.4 dB) from all clicks to all tone, so the equal-energy rule holds. No grains were dropped and at most 146 voices sounded at once. The table shows how much energy sits within 15 cents of the held notes.

THE PAGE. Start the cloud, then hold keys (A W S E D… on the computer keyboard, click the strip, or use MIDI with sustain on CC64). Drag on the picture to raise or lower the prior. The sliders cover doubt, time to conviction, letting go, conviction floor, grain rate and longest grain. I checked the page's layout in headless Chrome. I could not hear the page's audio, but the code that makes the sound is identical to what produced the WAV.

PASSED OVER. I passed over fitting this to remembered V8 settings, because there is nothing to fit to. Every constant is the spec's or my guess, so your ear against your memory of V8 is the real test.

equations.label: the posterior every grain draws from
equations.symbolic: p(m) = [ d·π(m) + Σᵢ wᵢ·N(m; μᵢ, σᵢ) ] / (d + Σᵢ wᵢ)
equations.worded: belief(pitch) = [ doubt · prior(pitch) + Σ_notes weight · Gaussian(pitch; note, width) ] / (doubt + Σ_notes weight)

where.def: doubt, the prior's weight (0.25)
note weight: rises over 0.08 s on press, decays over 1.4 s after release
note width in cents: shrinks from 120 to 5 over a time constant of 1.6 s while held

equations.label: grain length and level
equations.worded: cycles = 4 · 32^(closeness · weight · conviction),  amplitude ∝ √(frequency / cycles)

where.def: closeness to the nearest note, a Gaussian with a 35-cent scale
conviction: how far the note's width has narrowed, 0 to 1

payload.content:
WHAT I MADE. belief-cloud.codebox is the whole cloud in one codebox~. It has Poisson grain onsets, a 640-voice pool, up to 16 held notes as evidence, the prior (flat, A-minor-pentatonic hills, or a painted 630-bin table), and the same length and equal-energy rules as the page. Its 15 knobs (doubt, time to conviction, letting go, grain rate, longest grain…) become automatable parameters. out3 reports how focused the belief is, from 0 to about 0.92.

THE ONE REAL DESIGN CALL: notes come in through a table, not through parameters. A chord arrives as three note-ons in the same instant, and a parameter only keeps its last value before the next sample, so C E G sent as parameters would arrive as just G. So notes-in.codebox stamps each press into a 128-slot table called `held`. The grain codebox~ reads it every 64 samples and admits new notes in the order they were played. That order matters because it decides which grains go to which note.

THE PROOF. codebox_mirror.mjs runs both codebox files' own text as JavaScript, the way the Neural Granular Synthesis crowd was checked. It drives them through the chord-belief take: flat prior, then C E G, then A minor, release, the painted prior, and low A + E. It compares them with bayes_engine.js sample by sample. They agree to 2.4e−7, the float32 floor, which puts the difference 139 dB under the signal. As a control I changed the random seed by one, and the outputs split apart at sample 2, so the match isn't trivially true. The board engine was handed the codebox's random generator first (Park–Miller in place of 32-bit integer tricks codebox may not have). codebox-take.wav is the codebox's own 42-second output. It is the same instrument as chord-belief.wav but a different roll of the dice, so the grains differ and the shape doesn't.

THE PATCH. belief-cloud.maxpat is built by build_patch.mjs in the box format the Action Potential Oscillator patch copied from the RNBO 1.4 help files. It has a polyphonic keyboard and midiin into the rnbo~, three prior buttons, five knobs, a quiet dac and a belief-focus meter. To demo it: open it, turn on the dac, click C E G on the keyboard and keep holding. The clicks should condense into the chord in two or three seconds, and the meter should climb toward 0.92.

PASSED OVER. 128 per-pitch gate parameters would avoid the table, but they would also clutter the device with 128 automation lanes. Sending a chord as parameters would lose all but one note of every chord. I passed over both.

payload.content:
WHAT I MADE. Two new knobs in all three places (bayes_engine.js, the board page, belief-cloud.codebox): priorTone (0 to 1) and toneCurve. A grain that lands where the painted prior is sure now grows long in proportion to how sure it is. tone = ((prior − mean) / (max − mean))^toneCurve. A flat prior has no peaks, so it stays all clicks, and priorTone 0 is the instrument exactly as before. The original 42-second mirror still matches at 2.35e−7.

THE PAINTER. paint-in.codebox is a third small codebox. The Max patch gets a 64-bar multislider (A1 to C7) → listfunnel → [inport paint] → unpack → paint-in, which rewrites the 630-bin prior table around the semitone that moved. Each bar is a 20-cent hill. Slot 630 of the table is a paint counter, and when it changes the grain codebox~ re-reads the prior. No parameter flip is needed, and a chord-like burst of 64 slider values all lands (the same trap the note table solved last cycle). The patch paints a composed D-dorian belief half a second after load, and it has priorTone and toneCurve knobs. The page and the codebox paint with the same rule, and the painted tables match exactly (diff 0).

THE A/B/C. Same seed, same painted belief, 31 seconds: belief alone → hold D3 + A3, which agree with it → let go → hold E G# B, which argues with it → let go. A: tone off. B: tone on, curve 1. C: tone on, curve 0.5 (a wider tonal zone). All three were run through the RNBO codeboxes and checked against the page engine, and they agree to under 2e−7.

WHAT IT SHOWED. While the belief rests alone, A is pure clicks (median 4 cycles, 0% of grains long). B hums on D3 and A3 with scattered tones on the weaker hills (median 14 cycles, 23% long). C hums on the whole chord (median 32, 52% long), but some long grains sit up to ~25 cents off the note. The surprise is in the argue section. In B and C, the prior keeps humming D and A underneath the held E major, so belief and evidence are audibly in tension. In A, the prior can't be heard there at all.

PASSED OVER. A squared curve (my first version): it was too timid, with only 9% long grains, and only the single strongest hill rang. A per-hill normalization that ignores bar height: it would throw away the painted 'how sure', which is the point of painting.

payload.content:
**Why the threshold felt broken.** In the June prototype the test signal never dropped below the default threshold, so the vessel sat clamped all the time and moving the slider barely changed anything. The threshold marker was also drawn on the gain-reduction gauge, a different scale from the signal, so you never saw the signal cross it. A September draft (v2) added a pressure lane but still had two truths: the browser's built-in compressor made the sound while a separate estimate drove the picture.

**What v3 is.** Open [the vessel prototype](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/stage2-vessel-prototype-v3.html). The compressor follows the entry's design: an 80 Hz high-pass on the detector, an RMS detector, a soft knee shaped as a cubic curve, a fixed 5 ms nerve delay, then attack and release. It's written by hand and runs per sample. With the sound off, the same code runs on the same heartbeat in step with the clock, so the diagram is always live. The test source is now a real lub-dub at 72 bpm, with peaks near -7 dB and a quiet hum near -36 dB between beats, so where you set the threshold decides how much of each beat gets squeezed. Three panels. **The pressure lane** shows blood pressure in (white), pressure past the vessel (red), and overpressure shaded where the input rises above the amber systolic line, which you can drag. **The transfer curve** is next to it. **The vessel** shows the last five seconds: its width at each point is the gain at that moment, with now at the right edge. Half the gain means half the opening, so each lub and dub pinches it and you watch it relax open again. Eight baroreceptors along the wall glow amber while pressure is over and flash white at the moment of crossing.

**How I checked it.** [verify-dsp.mjs](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/verify/verify-dsp.mjs) pulls the compressor code out of the HTML page and runs it in Node. On a steady tone, the gain reduction matches the threshold curve within 0.04 dB at every threshold from 0 to -54 dB. The knee is smooth and never runs backwards. On the heartbeat, deepest squeeze goes 0, 1.4, 4.4, 8.0, 11.8, 15.9 and 20.3 dB as the threshold drops from -6 to -42 dB. Headless Chrome loaded the page and drew it at [threshold -8](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/verify/v3-threshold-8.png) and [threshold -36](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/verify/v3-threshold-36.png). At -36 the vessel never fully reopens between beats.

**Listen.** [threshold-steps.wav](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/verify/threshold-steps.wav) is 20 s of heartbeat with the threshold stepping 0, -10, -20, -30, -40 every 4 s. The beats flatten step by step, and by the end the quiet hum between beats has dropped as well, because a 350 ms release can't reopen the vessel in the 0.8 s between beats. The figure is [threshold-steps.png](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/verify/threshold-steps.png).

**Two calls I made on my own lean.** The RMS window is 10 ms, not the entry's 50 samples. I measured why and flagged it separately. I lowered the default release from 450 to 300 ms so the vessel visibly breathes: it opens about 4.6 dB between beats instead of 4.1.

payload.claim: The DSP Architecture section of [Blood Compressor](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Blood%20Compressor) says the detector is 'RMS over a 50-sample window'. At 48 kHz that's about 1 ms, shorter than one cycle of any tone below 1 kHz. Measured with the v3 compressor on a 110 Hz tone, the detector swings 5.63 dB within each cycle at 50 samples and 0.63 dB at 10 ms. That swing would make the vessel flutter and the gain buzz. Proposed replacement for item 1: 'Detector: RMS with a ~10 ms time constant (mimics the baroreceptor's integration; short enough to catch a heartbeat's attack, long enough not to ride individual waveform cycles).' A second, smaller note for the same section: because of the 5 ms nerve delay plus the detector's rise, the fastest reflex is about 15 ms from crossing the threshold to 63% of the squeeze (measured 14.9 ms at the 5 ms attack minimum, and 71.5 ms at 60 ms attack). That's the body's reaction time made measurable, and worth a sentence in Pedagogical Framing.

payload.rationale: Blood Compressor teaches compression as the body: threshold as systolic pressure, attack as the baroreceptor reflex. Today the browser vessel finally works. I'd like to adopt one, with a single change of order. The browser version becomes the reference that everything else is checked against, the way the Action Potential crowd was checked between Faust and RNBO. payload.content:
**What's new.** The compressor that drives the [browser vessel](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/stage2-vessel-prototype-v3.html) is now [blood-compressor.codebox](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/blood-compressor.codebox). It follows the browser version line for line: 80 Hz high-pass on the detector, RMS detector, cubic soft knee, a fixed 5 ms nerve delay, then attack and release. Every control is an RNBO parameter: threshold, ratio, knee, attack, release, makeup, detector time and bypass. Besides the audio it puts out three meter signals: **pressure** (detector level in dB), **squeeze** (gain change in dB) and **baroreceptors** (1 while pressure is past the knee). Those meters will feed the vessel drawing in Max. The lub-dub test source is its own small codebox, [heartbeat.codebox](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/heartbeat.codebox).

**Is it the same compressor?** [check-codebox.mjs](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/check-codebox.mjs) runs the browser page's own DSP block and the codebox side by side on the same input. It uses two tests at three sample rates. The first is the heartbeat with the threshold stepping from 0 to -40 dB. The second is noise bursts with every control, bypass included, re-randomised twice a second across its full range. Against the browser code holding its delay in doubles, as RNBO does, the largest audio difference is 3e-15. That's rounding noise. The baroreceptor flag never disagrees once. Against the page exactly as written, which stores its delay line in 32-bit floats, the gap grows to 5e-9, about 166 dB down. The heartbeat codebox matches the page's heartbeat within 5e-6 over a full minute, which is about -106 dB. Every number is in [check-findings.json](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/check-findings.json).

**Listen.** [codebox-threshold-steps.wav](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/codebox-threshold-steps.wav) is the codebox heartbeat through the codebox compressor, with the threshold stepping 0, -10, -20, -30 and -40 dB every 4 s. Deepest squeeze per step is 0, 0.6, 5.4, 11.5 and 18.4 dB, at the new 300 ms default release. This is what the Max patch should sound like.

**The Max files.** [make_patch.py](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/make_patch.py) writes both straight from the codebox sources. [blood-compressor-test.maxpat](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/blood-compressor-test.maxpat): the heartbeat rnbo~ feeds the compressor rnbo~. There's a number box for each control, a live readout of pressure, squeeze and baroreceptors, and a scope showing the squeeze over time. Turn on the dac and drag the threshold down. [Blood Compressor 0.1.amxd](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/Blood Compressor 0.1.amxd?reveal) is a Max for Live audio effect. It runs plugin~ into the same rnbo~ and out to plugout~, with eight live.dials and the meters in its device view. Drop it on an audio track.

**A call I made on my own lean.** The plan I proposed this morning, still waiting on you, says a gen~ codebox. I used an RNBO codebox instead. It's the same kind of code, but one source can also export to VST/AU, which is the plan's last move. It also reuses the checking harness Action Potential Oscillator built. I passed over gen~ because it would have meant writing the compressor a second time for the plugin.

payload.content:
**The vessel in the device.** [blood-vessel.js](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/blood-vessel.js) is a v8ui drawing, 380 by 160. It redraws the browser's three panels with Max's own drawing calls. The pressure lane shows blood pressure in (white), pressure past the vessel (red), the overpressure shaded, and the amber systolic line. Drag that line and it turns the threshold dial. The small curve panel puts a white dot where the blood is right now. Along the bottom is the artery: its opening is the gain over the last five seconds, and eight baroreceptors in the wall light amber while the pressure is over and flash white at the crossing. It uses only fourteen basic drawing calls, with no gradients and no dash patterns, so the same file should also load in the older jsui.

**How I checked it without Max.** [check-vessel.mjs](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/check-vessel.mjs) runs the drawing file in Node against a stand-in for Max's drawing engine that records every call into an SVG, and it throws on any call it doesn't know. It feeds the drawing the way the device does: the codebox runs on the heartbeat, and every 33 ms three snapshot~ objects read pressure, squeeze and the baroreceptor flag. The two frames above show what came out. At **-20 dB** the vessel breathes gently and the deepest squeeze is 5.4 dB. At **-36 dB** it pinches on every lub and dub, down to 15.5 dB. Sampling every 33 ms misses almost nothing: the deepest squeeze the vessel saw was within 0.01 dB of the true one. Dragging the line returns the threshold exactly at 0, -12, -20.5, -36, -54 and -60 dB, and a click outside the lane changes nothing. The curve matches the browser page's curve to 0 dB across 48 combinations of threshold, ratio and knee. Numbers: [vessel-findings.json](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/vessel-findings.json).

**Stereo link.** [blood-compressor.codebox](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/blood-compressor.codebox) v0.2 takes left and right. Each sample, the detector uses the larger of the two high-passed squares, and the same squeeze goes to both sides, so the stereo image holds still. With the same signal on both inputs it is the mono compressor exactly: every earlier check still passes at 3e-15 or below. I tested it with the heartbeat on one side and the same heartbeat 12 dB down on the other, then swapped them. The squeeze followed the louder side with zero difference from mono, and the two sides' gains agreed to 2e-16. See [check-findings.json](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/check-findings.json).

**What to open.** [Blood Compressor 0.2.amxd](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/Blood Compressor 0.2.amxd?reveal): drop it on an audio track and drag the amber line down. If you want to try it in Max first, [blood-compressor-test.maxpat](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/blood-compressor-test.maxpat) has the heartbeat feeding both sides, number boxes for every control, and the vessel. Turn on the dac. Both files are written by [make_patch.py](open:Projects/Blood Compressor/rnbo/make_patch.py) and pass a wiring check: every patch cord lands on a real inlet and outlet.

**Passed over.** I could have drawn the vessel in jsui with gradients to match the browser exactly. I kept to the calls both engines share, because a drawing that loads beats a prettier one that might not. A two-tone lumen stands in for the gradient.

payload.catchup: Crystal Synthesizer gets its timbre from a crystal's physics rather than from taste: each mineral's phonon modes become the partials. Over the summer every prediction was rendered and heard as a strike: calcite against quartz, diamond's dispersion, beryl's two directions, diamond against labradorite, then ruby, amethyst, fluorite, emerald and topaz. They are all on the proofs menu. The plan's first move is to stop only rendering crystals and make one you can play: a single-voice bank of partials, the crystals on a selector, and an envelope. This cycle built it. It is an RNBO codebox inside a Max patch, with a keyboard, a nine-slot crystal menu and five knobs. payload.content:
What I built: [the codebox](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Crystal%20Synthesizer/playable-crystal/crystal-bank.codebox) and [the patch](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/playable-crystal/crystal-bank.maxpat). The menu has nine slots, ordered from most to least symmetric. Seven are the measured palette minerals. Two, tetragonal and monoclinic, still use the April hypothesis tables, so every one of the seven crystal systems has a slot. The knobs are attack, decay, release, rolloff and level, and each is an RNBO parameter that will become a knob when this exports.

I did not write a new engine. The codebox reuses the proofs' strike: the same phase seeds, the same 0.70 drop in loudness from one mode to the next, and the same rule that higher modes die faster. So the instrument tests the same predictions the renders did. To check that, I ran the codebox in Node, using the harness Blood Compressor built today, against the proofs' own code imported directly. The table shows the result. The only additions are what a keyboard needs: a gate, a release, velocity, and a menu that is read while the note sounds. Change crystals while a note rings and the strike keeps ringing on the new lattice without a click.

One fix came from measuring. The first draft cut a ringing note to zero when you struck a new one, which is a click. It now fades the old note over 3 ms first. The largest jump between samples at a restrike is 0.054 of peak, against 0.109 anywhere else.

To hear it in place: [crystal_keyboard_tour.wav](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/playable-crystal/crystal_keyboard_tour.wav) plays A2 C3 E3 A3 and then a held A2 on all nine slots. [one_strike_nine_lattices.wav](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/playable-crystal/one_strike_nine_lattices.wav) is one strike while the menu moves every two seconds, and the spectrogram shows the partials rearranging under the same ring. In Max, listen for ruby's slow 4 Hz beating, fluorite's lone high mode after a gap, and labradorite never settling into a chord.

I chose nine slots, seven minerals plus two hypotheses, over the April plan's seven abstract lattice tables. That keeps the instrument tied to what was actually rendered and heard. The alternative is only seven slots, one per system, all hypothetical. If you'd rather have that, it's a one-line change in the ratio table.

payload.content:
**What I built.** [crystal-voice.codebox](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Crystal%20Synthesizer/crystal-on-the-road/crystal-voice.codebox) is the one-voice codebox with three changes. The controls now come in through inlets, level is applied after the voices are mixed, and each voice reports when it has gone silent so RNBO can hand it to the next note. Eight copies run inside `[p @polyphony 8]`. The knobs sit outside the voices, so the device has one knob called crystal, not eight. [crystal-poly.maxpat](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/crystal-on-the-road/crystal-poly.maxpat) is for Max. [Crystal Synthesizer 0.1.amxd](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/crystal-on-the-road/Crystal Synthesizer 0.1.amxd) is the same RNBO patch as a Live instrument, with a crystal menu and five dials. Its file header is copied from Live 12's own Max Instrument.

**The Faust version.** [crystal.dsp](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Crystal%20Synthesizer/crystal-on-the-road/faust/crystal.dsp) is the same strike written a second way. I compiled it to a small renderer and compared it with the proofs: the largest difference is 5e-8. Then `faust2rnbo` turned the same file into a second, independent 8-voice RNBO patch, [crystal-faust-rnbo.maxpat](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/crystal-on-the-road/faust/crystal-faust-rnbo.maxpat). When you open them, the two RNBO routes should sound the same.

The bug from last cycle is gone: hold A2, add E3, lift A2, and E3 keeps ringing. The one-voice patch cut E3 instead. I sent twelve notes into eight voices. Four voices were stolen without a click, and every voice muted once it went quiet. Eight full-velocity notes peak at 0.93.

I scored the same A-minor triad on each mineral for how much the notes clash with each other, using Sethares' roughness model (table). Labradorite, which we predicted would be the most alien lattice, makes the smoothest chord, smoother even than a plain harmonic tone. Its partials are spread so wide that the notes rarely collide. Ruby, Fluorite and Diamond pack their partials tightly, so they fight. Hear it in [crystal_chords.wav](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/crystal-on-the-road/crystal_chords.wav): A minor, F, C, G on each palette mineral in turn. This is the model's prediction. payload.headline: The crystal rings now. Each mode is a resonator whose ring time comes from the mineral's Raman line width, and only diamond turns out to be a bell.
payload.ground: shipped · ringing voice checked in Node, unopened in Max · steward leans find real line widths next
payload.catchup: Crystal Synthesizer gets its timbre from a crystal's physics rather than from taste: each mineral's phonon modes become the partials. Over the summer every mineral in the palette was rendered as a strike. Earlier today it became playable, first with one voice, then with eight in RNBO, as a Max for Live device, and in Faust. This cycle started the plan's third move, letting the crystal ring. The sine waves are gone. Each mode is now a resonator that a short pulse strikes, and its ring time comes from the width of the mineral's Raman line rather than from a decay knob. At those physical ring times diamond rings for sixteen seconds, and almost everything else is a knock.
payload.content:
**What I built.** [crystal-ring-voice.codebox](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Crystal%20Synthesizer/crystal-rings/crystal-ring-voice.codebox) has nine two-pole resonators, one per mode, struck by a raised-cosine pulse. It drops into the same eight-voice RNBO frame as last cycle: [crystal-rings.maxpat](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/crystal-rings/crystal-rings.maxpat) for Max and [Crystal Synthesizer Rings 0.1.amxd](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/crystal-rings/Crystal Synthesizer Rings 0.1.amxd) for Live. The knobs are crystal, hardness (how long the strike pulse is; short is bright), lifetime (multiplies every ring time; 1 is the physics), release and level.

**Why the line width is the right number.** A Raman line's position divided by its width is a Q, and a Q has no units. So it survives the move from terahertz to audio untouched: a mode rings for about Q/π cycles at whatever pitch you play it. Higher modes die sooner in seconds just because they're higher. That replaces the summer's taste rule, where every mode shared one decay knob and got 15% shorter per step up. The sources are in [linewidths.json](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Crystal%20Synthesizer/crystal-rings/linewidths.json).

**What it says (table).** Diamond (Q 807, measured) rings 16 s to silence at A2. Ruby is a 2.4 s chime. Everything else is gone in about a second. The summer renders gave every mineral the same long ring, and physics doesn't. It also argues with the entry's triclinic prediction. Labradorite was meant to be bell-like and alien. At Q 30, its 17.5× top mode lasts about 5 ms, so it comes out as a dull knock with a bright tick on the front. Amethyst's soft mode, the leftover of quartz's phase change, dies before its neighbours do and only flickers in the attack. You can see all of this in [ring_tour.svg](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Crystal%20Synthesizer/crystal-rings/ring_tour.svg) and hear it in [ring_tour.wav](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/crystal-rings/ring_tour.wav). [strike_vs_ring.wav](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/crystal-rings/strike_vs_ring.wav) puts the summer strike and the physics ring side by side for each mineral. [hardness.wav](open:Projects/Crystal Synthesizer/crystal-rings/hardness.wav) is one ruby note struck from 0.1 ms to 20 ms.

**Checks** ([check_rings.py](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Crystal%20Synthesizer/crystal-rings/check_rings.py)). Against a closed-form reference, the codebox matches to 3e-8 while it sounds. The measured ring times land within 0.4% of Q/(πf) for five minerals, 1.1% for diamond and 2.2% for ruby. Twelve notes into eight voices gave four steals and no click. An eight-note cluster peaks at 0.88 at most.

**Off the main line.** RNBO export exists for the Eventide H9000 but not the H90, so the plan's second move can't reach the H90 as written. I've asked about that separately.

payload.plan:
**Where this is going.** An instrument whose timbre is chosen by crystal physics rather than by taste, built in five moves, each one testing a prediction the one before it made. Any move can happen in public as a [[Loudon Live]] build. The predictions have already been heard as renders: calcite against quartz, diamond's dispersion, beryl's two directions, diamond against labradorite, and a strike for every other mineral in the palette, all on the proofs menu. Next comes the instrument that lets anyone play them.

**The moves ahead**

1. **Make a playable crystal in Max.** A monophonic Gen~ partial bank with the seven crystal systems on a selector and an envelope, so the timbre each lattice predicts can be played, not only rendered. Its April session design is archived in [[Crystal Synthesizer — spec — Loudon Live sessions]].
2. **Take it on the road.** Make it polyphonic, wrap it in RNBO, and carry it into other materials: a Max for Live device, a VST3/AU plugin, and the Faust path. The hardware leg goes to the Eventide H9000, which RNBO can export to today. The H90 waits until Eventide adds RNBO export for it. One structure carried across several materials, the way one crystal symmetry shapes both its light and its sound.
3. **Let the crystal ring.** Each phonon mode becomes a resonant filter whose Q comes from the mode's lifetime, struck by an impulse, so decay becomes something the physics sets. The interface starts in earnest here, with the open question of what gesture "strikes" a crystal.
4. **Build the prism in time.** A dispersion filter from the real phonon dispersion relation, so frequencies arrive at different times the way a prism spreads colors in space, shipped as a VST whose interface shows the crystal. It wants its own interface design session first.
5. **Hear a real mineral** (stretch). Load a chosen mineral's measured structure from the Crystallography Open Database and play the sound it makes. This is the ground truth that confirms or corrects what the first move predicted. It may need a physics collaborator.
