payload.headline: I built the sitting itself: 78 Wavetable presets in eight ladders, a slot-decoder preset, and an ear sheet that turns your picks into the profile.
payload.ground: shipped · ear-pass kit ready, not yet loaded in Live · steward leans sit solo with the sheet
payload.catchup: Generative Preset Development teaches an AI to make, describe and reshape presets for synths with a fixed layout, starting with Ableton Wavetable. Settled so far: the preset format is cracked, a modified preset loads in Live and sounds as intended (you confirmed this on 2026-06-05), and an analyzer describes any preset in plain synth language. What it still lacks is feel-words grounded by ear, like where a cutoff stops being dark, so every word it uses is borrowed from how Ableton's factory presets happen to set the knob. The next step on the plan is one sitting in Live to fix that. This cycle built that sitting so it needs no knob-sweeping and no numbers. You arrow through ready-made presets and note where the sound changes.
payload.content: The kit lives in [audition-kit](open:Projects/Generative Preset Development/ableton-wavetable/audition-kit?reveal) and is also zipped as one file. There are eight ladders: A cutoff (12 rungs, 40 Hz to 20 kHz), B resonance (10), C amp attack (13, 0 ms to 10 s), D attack curve (6), E release (11), F free LFO rate (12, 0.05 to 30 Hz), G tempo-synced LFO rate (7), and H LFO fade-in (6). Each rung is the factory init Wavetable with Osc 1 alone on a bright wave, so a rung changes only the one setting it tests. Each preset's name shows in the device title, e.g. 'A05 cutoff 549 Hz'. Rungs marked 'corpus split' sit where Ableton's 270 factory presets divide into fifths. Those are the provisional fences the analyzer uses today, so the sitting is moving fences, not building them from nothing. How to sit: load the first rung, press hot-swap, hold a note, and arrow down. Then pick in the [ear sheet](open:Projects/Generative Preset Development/ableton-wavetable/audition-kit/ear-sheet.html) the rung where each band begins. It builds the answers file as you go. Then `python3 apply_bands.py` writes the ear's split points into profile v0.2 and re-runs the analyzer, which now says 'split set by ear' wherever your ear replaced a factory guess. I tested that path end to end on a throwaway copy with made-up answers. The Z00 decoder routes all 13 hidden modulation slots to Filter 1 Freq at 1%, 2% ... 13%. One look at the Matrix, MIDI and MPE tabs tells us which slot is which source, which the corpus census could only guess. The sheet has boxes for that too. Two things I found while building. First, the init Wavetable ships three controller routings onto the oscillator (slot 9 to wave position at 100%), and I zeroed them in the kit. Since the default patch plays a steady tone, slot 9 can't be per-note Random as the census guessed. It's more likely Press or Aftertouch, and the decoder will settle it. Second, the factory LFO-rate bands are the weakest of the five: 157 of the 270 presets have LFO 1 tempo-synced, so their free Hz rate is ignored but still counted, and 54 sit on the untouched 1 Hz default. So the F ladder matters most. I also fixed the analyzer to stop putting a feel-word on the free rate of a synced LFO, and let it read real .adv files directly.

payload.headline: Three Wavetable pads from one prompt, 'light through deep water', plus a reshaper that made Aqueous Pad darker and more menacing, and breathing.
payload.ground: shipped · not yet loaded in Live · steward leans: hear LTDW 1–3 first
payload.catchup: Generative Preset Development teaches an AI to make, describe and reshape presets for synths with a fixed layout, starting with Ableton Wavetable. Settled so far: the preset format is cracked, a modified preset loads in Live and sounds as intended (you confirmed this in June), and an analyzer describes any preset in plain synth language. The step on the plan is still one sitting in Live where your ears set the feel-words, and the kit for it shipped earlier today. Until then, every 'dark' or 'swell' is borrowed from how Ableton's factory presets happen to set the knob. This cycle built the step after that one, making presets from a prompt and reshaping them, so it works now on the borrowed words and gets sharper on its own once your sitting lands. The plan's own test is the first thing it made: 'a pad that sounds like light through deep water', realized three different ways.
payload.content:
How it works: the model reads the prompt and writes a short recipe in the profile's own words, like cutoff 'warm', attack 'swell', LFO 'drifting', plus which wavetables to use and which few routings carry the motion ([the recipe](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Generative%20Preset%20Development/ableton-wavetable/recipes/light-through-deep-water.json)). generate_preset.py starts from the blank init Wavetable, not a factory sound. It fills in the knobs the recipe leaves out by sampling between the 25th and 75th percentile of Ableton's 31 factory pads, picks a value inside each named band (on a log scale for Hz and seconds), and writes the .adv along with a sidecar that says what it chose and why. Then it reads the file back and checks the values.

The three readings of the prompt:
- **LTDW 1 Caustics** is a slow wavetable morph. Crystal Shifter at a warm 906 Hz, with a drifting LFO moving the wave position and a second LFO at a different rate nudging the filter, so the two never lock. Position-spread unison smears it, like ripples of light on a pool floor.
- **LTDW 2 Shaft** is a single oscillator under a swept filter. Voice Harmonics sits dark at 232 Hz with a singing resonance, and a 3.5-second envelope opens the filter, like finding a shaft of light by looking up.
- **LTDW 3 Refraction** is a detuned pair. Amber, plus Sines 3 an octave up, panned apart, with six-voice shimmer unison and smooth-random drift on the pan, like white light splitting into colours.

Run back through the analyzer, all three describe themselves in the words they were asked for ([readback](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Generative%20Preset%20Development/ableton-wavetable/generated/light-through-deep-water/analyzer-readback.txt)). That closes the loop from prompt to recipe to preset to description.

Reshaping (reshape_preset.py) moves a preset by bands, not by numbers. 'Darker' means the cutoff drops one band from wherever it sits, so the word covers the same distance in feel on any preset. Filter 2 follows by the same ratio, so the designer's offset between the two filters survives. 'Darker and more menacing' on Aqueous Pad: cutoff warm 714 Hz to dark 289 Hz, Filter 2 follows to 558 Hz, resonance singing to screaming, +6 dB drive, more sub, a little wider unison. 'Breathe': the attack is already a swell, so it stays put; LFO 1 goes from imperceptible to drifting (0.38 Hz) and gently drives the amp and filter. I also stripped and darkened Refraction to show the reshaper works on generated presets as well as factory ones.

One finding for your sitting: by factory usage, the 'soft' attack band only runs from 1.5 to 40 ms, because factory presets are mostly clicks and plucks. A pad that asks for 'soft' would come out nearly percussive, so all three recipes had to ask for 'swell'. Rungs C04 to C08 of the attack ladder are where your ear will move that fence furthest.

payload.content:
Here's how [describe_preset.py](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Generative%20Preset%20Development/ableton-wavetable/describe_preset.py) works. It reads the preset into plain facts and then writes about them. Aqueous Pad comes out as: 'A slow-swelling pad built on Rust and Ruby (Modern), through a warm† filter, whose life is LFO 2 folding Osc 1.' Then: two tables warped and folded in Modern mode and panned apart, a split pair of warm† low-passes with singing† resonance, a 634 ms swell that settles to 53% over 15 seconds, and, under Motion, the four routings that carry the sound. The other 28 are summed up in one clause. That ranking is the main writing decision. Huston Singletary's pad has 56 live routings. The writer ranks them by depth, weighted by how much the destination changes the sound: wave position, fold and cutoff count fully, pan less, an LFO modulating another LFO less again. It also drops anything identical to what the blank init patch already carries, so the sentence names what makes this preset different. The dagger (†) marks a feel-word borrowed from factory usage. When your ear sitting lands, the daggers disappear with no code change.

Two things got settled from the presets themselves along the way. First, the oscillator effect-mode setting, which the profile still listed as unmapped: 0 is none, 1 is FM, 2 is Classic (pulse width and sync), 3 is Modern (warp and fold). Each oscillator's live modulation targets name its mode's two controls, and all 16 oscillators that have such targets agree, with no contradictions ([evidence](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Generative%20Preset%20Development/ableton-wavetable/profile-draft/osc_effect_mode_evidence.json)). Second, the hidden modulation slot 9, which the earlier survey guessed was 'random per note', looks like a performance controller instead. The init patch routes it to wave position at 100% yet plays a steady tone, and 11 factory routings put it at exactly 100% on an LFO's depth, which is the classic 'controller fades the vibrato in' move. The writer now calls it 'an unnamed controller (slot 9)' and lists it under Playing. The slot decoder in your ear kit will name it.

One click: the [descriptions page](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Generative%20Preset%20Development/ableton-wavetable/descriptions/preset-descriptions.html) has six factory presets and the three 'light through deep water' pads. The text file covers all 17 presets on disk.

payload.content: Same 122 cycles in every table; only the order of the frames changes. CENTROID, the old default (dull to bright by one brightness number): 50 big jumps, brightness follows Position perfectly (1.0). Four of its five worst steps join cycles whose brightness differs by 1 to 32 Hz but whose spectra are far apart. One number can't tell 122 FM spectra apart. WALK, the shortest smooth path through all 122: 13 big jumps, but brightness only loosely follows Position (0.36), so the knob loses its meaning. FAMILY CHAIN: k-means picked five soft families (54 round, 36 bright, 10 nasal, 10 hollow, 12 glassy). They are chained darkest first, and each family is walked smoothly inside. Result: 14 big jumps and 0.90 brightness, nearly as smooth as the walk and nearly as meaningful as centroid. Each family also comes out as its own small table. Phase: rotating each frame to line up with its neighbour halves the worst mid-morph dip (−4.5 to −2.2 dB). No table dips below −6 dB, though, so ordering was the real problem, not phase. Two changes for the interview: past about 30 cycles, the default becomes 'chain the families', and the skill's 'cut to 64 cycles' default should go, since Serum and Ableton read 256 frames. BUILD.md says exactly what to open and what to listen for.

payload.catchup: This project turns a conversation into a wavetable for Serum, Vital, Ableton and Surge. Behind it are the crystal-lattice sweep and the Shepard dark-to-bright, both of which you heard work, plus a Floquet table. Earlier today I ran the chat interview on two big folders of AKWF cycles (122 FM, 142 organ). Both times a 'family chain' glided where the old dull-to-bright order lurched. Which order becomes the default is still your open question. This cycle starts the next part of the plan, widening the sources, with an audio AI's output. I didn't render anything new. payload.content: Cutting cycles from AI notes needed steps AKWF never did. For each of the 599 notes the grader called steady, I averaged 8 periods at the measured pitch and refined it per note. That kept the overtones: median fidelity 0.99, and the refinement moved pitch only 1 cent. 578 notes passed. The grader had tracked 78 notes too low: an octave (64), a twelfth (10), two octaves (3), even more (1). Those 'cycles' held several real periods and would sound high in a synth, so the extractor folds them back to one. 70 were exact duplicates (the probe re-graded some renders under several run names), which leaves 508. That's past Serum's 256 frames, so the main tables keep 256, each pick the cycle least like any already picked. Results: the old dull-to-bright order jumps on 210 of 255 steps by this source's own yardstick, the family chain on 24, the shortest walk on 26. Two things differ from AKWF. First, phase is mandatory. Cut cycles start anywhere, so the unaligned default dips to −20 dB mid-morph; with the same order lined up it dips only −2.6 dB. Second, brightness is the wrong axis. The AI's cycles are dark (median 90% of energy in the fundamental), so no order keeps 'turn it up, it gets brighter' (chain 0.34). The tilt that helped organs makes it worse (0.21). What the three families do separate is how much fundamental there is: pure (84%) to round (66%) to reedy (27%). That's the chain's honest sweep. The AI's instrument labels barely predict the sound (adjusted Rand 0.10). Marimba and flute collapse to near-sines once the attack and breath are gone, and violin carries the overtones. I also drafted the interview-skill changes from all three runs (cut-a-cycle steps, an AI-reuse path, answer the sweep question from the source, drop cut-to-64, family chain past about 24, always align phase). They're a file in my folder for an elder to land after you listen. BUILD.md says which file to drag where and what to listen for.

payload.catchup: Inharmonic Wavetable Synthesis is the synth where two wavetables do two different jobs. Wavetable A decides how loud each partial is. Wavetable B decides how far each partial sits from its harmonic place, in cents, so a flat line is pure harmony and every bend is a material. One knob, B depth, scales the bend. Back in May and June I built a Faust sketch, five auditions, and a scanner that moves through a piano's settling frames. In June I asked whether the scanner or the FFT-driven Wavetable A should come next. That question went unanswered, and it no longer matters, because both are now built. This cycle feeds a real wavetable into Wavetable A: the electric-organ table Generative Wavetable Libraries built this morning. Its 142 frames are FFT'd into 64 partial levels each. They play against two Wavetable B trajectories, a piano string settling and a bell whose partials ease back onto the flat line, each running on its own clock.
payload.content:
Until now Wavetable A was four hand-typed profiles. The entry makes a bigger claim: any wavetable becomes an amplitude template once you FFT it. So I took the sibling project's AKWF organ chain (142 frames x 2048 samples), took bins 1 to 64 of every frame, and ran them through the additive engine. Wavetable B gets two trajectories. The piano one is the June B-coefficient schedule, extended to 64 partials. The bell one puts partial n on the nth zero of the Bessel J0 function, the modes of a circular membrane: partial 2 sits 239 cents sharp and partial 64 sits 456 cents sharp, and over 16 frames they ease back to flat.

What to open, in order:
1. **01-amplitude-wall-alone.wav**: B depth 0, so there is no bend, and the position in the organ table sweeps 0 to 1 over 10 s. This proves the amplitude wall comes from a real table. The spectral centroid climbs from 184 Hz to 990 Hz, round organ to nasal organ.
2. **02-organ-struck-piano-settling.wav**: three strikes at three organ positions, with the piano trajectory at B depth 0.3.
3. **03-organ-bell-dissolving.wav**: the entry's 'crystal morph', heard for the first time. I measured partial 2 at 252.5 Hz at the attack (the bell position) and at 220.0 Hz after 5 s (the harmonic position).
4. **04-two-clocks-chord.wav**: an A major chord for 18 s. The organ position creeps forward while the bell bend and B depth each ride a slow LFO, so the chord should pass from clear to rough and back.
5. **dual-wavetable-instrument.html**: the playable study, made in the board. It draws the glowing line from the entry: the bend is cents, the glow and thickness are the organ's level for each partial, and the faint lines are every stored frame. Strike or Hold, four notes plus the chord (keys a s d f g), and drift, LFO and breathe toggles. Each section has a ◇ review pin.

payload.headline: First real trajectory: I tracked a recorded low piano A into Wavetable B. Its bend doesn't settle. What fades is the upper partials.
payload.ground: shipped · one recording tracked, four renders, the study gains it · steward leans high piano + bowl next
payload.catchup: Inharmonic Wavetable Synthesis is the synth where two wavetables do two jobs. Wavetable A sets how loud each partial is. Wavetable B sets how far each partial sits from its harmonic place, in cents, so a flat line is pure harmony and every bend is a material. Earlier today both walls started playing together: a real organ table against a piano and a bell trajectory, both hand-made. I proposed a plan that starts by building a small library of trajectories measured from real sounds, one recording first and then the rest. That plan still waits on your yes, and this cycle builds its first step. I wrote a small partial tracker and ran it on one real recording, the low A (55 Hz, forte) from the Grand Piano in Live's Core Library. It produced 16 frames of Wavetable B and a matching Wavetable A, both from the same note. The result corrects us. The piano's bend doesn't relax over time. It holds at one shape for the whole note. The 'settling' you hear comes from the upper partials, the most bent ones, going quiet.
payload.content:
**What I built.** [track_partials.py](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Inharmonic%20Wavetable%20Synthesis/trajectory-library/track_partials.py) reads a recording in place and finds partials 1 to 8. It fits the string-stiffness law to them, uses the fit to predict where the next partials will be, and climbs to 64 that way. Then it measures every partial in 16 frames, log-spaced from 0.03 s to 8 s. A partial counts only if it stands 12 dB above the noise and the analysis window can pin it to better than about 5 cents. At 55 Hz that throws out partial 1, so partial 1 takes the fit's value.

**What it found.** The fit gives f0 = 55.14 Hz and B = 4.67e-5. The measured partials sit on that curve to within about half a cent: partial 16 is 10 cents sharp, partial 32 is 40, partial 64 is 152. B frame by frame is 4.73 to 4.88e-5 from the strike to 3.8 s. That's flat within ±2%, so the bend doesn't settle. The whole pitch drifts down about 1 cent over 8 s, and that's all the settling the frequencies do. Our June 'settling piano' started at B = 9e-4, 19 times stiffer, and relaxed toward 7e-5. The heard bend (each partial's bend weighted by its loudness) does halve, from 4.5 cents to about 2. That happens because the high partials go dark first, not because they move. So the settling lives in the cube's interior: the loudness wall dims exactly where the bend is largest. The entry predicted this when it said a piano's amplitudes and bends are two projections of one struck string. The loudness wall also has dark bands near partials 25, 33 and 41. They're probably the hammer's strike point cancelling every 8th mode or so. I haven't confirmed that.

**What to open, in order:**
1. **01-real-piano-two-walls.wav**: the piano rebuilt from its own two walls, measured levels and measured bend.
2. **02-real-piano-two-walls-bend-off.wav**: the same with B depth 0. A/B it against 01. Partial 40 sits at 2285.9 Hz in 01 and at the harmonic 2205.7 Hz in 02, 62 cents apart.
3. **03-organ-flat-real-june.wav**: the organ wall struck three times, with the flat line, then the real piano bend, then the June guess (at the 0.3 depth cycle 7 used). The real bend should sound much subtler than the guess.
4. **04-chord-real-bend-pushed.wav**: an A major chord on the organ wall wearing the real bend. B depth rises from 0 to 3 over 14 s, past what this string really does.
5. **piano-low-A1-trajectory.png**: the measured bend against the flat line and the June curve, B over time, and the loudness wall with the heard bend drawn over it.
6. **dual-wavetable-instrument.html**: the playable study now has 'real piano, low A (measured)' in its trajectory menu.

payload.content:
**The piano across the keyboard.** The same tracker as last cycle now ran on A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, C6 and F#6. I taught it to stop below the top of the audible range, because a stiff treble string runs out of room after 10 to 30 partials. String stiffness (B) climbs about 3x per octave from A2 upward: 4.7e-5 at 55 Hz, 7.4e-4 at A4, 5.0e-3 at F#6. D7 gave only six partials, so it gets a fit but no trajectory. In every register the bend still holds through the note. B moves less than ±5% from frame to frame (±11% at F#6, where few partials are left). So last cycle's finding wasn't a quirk of one bass string. The entry's guess for a bass piano (B 0.001 to 0.002) is where this piano sits around A5 and C6, more than an octave above middle C.

**Things with no ladder.** A bell has modes, not harmonics. [track_modes.py](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Inharmonic%20Wavetable%20Synthesis/trajectory-library/track_modes.py) counts a peak as a mode only if it stands 40 dB proud just after the strike and is still ringing in the same place 0.4 s later. Then it files the k-th mode into slot k and measures its bend against k times the lowest mode. Slots above the last mode are kept silent rather than invented. What it found: the bell (1042 Hz) has 24 modes packed tight, mostly 1000 to 1700 cents flat of the harmonic slots. The vibraphone is the bar's 1 : 4 : 9.9 plus near-harmonic resonator partials. The marimba is 1 : 3 : 4 : 10.5. The singing bowl has a pure octave, then modes at 5.35, 5.74 and 8.34/8.37 times the lowest. That last pair is a split mode 10 Hz apart, and it's the bowl's wobble.

**What to open, in order:**
1. **05-organ-wears-the-keyboard.wav**: one organ note (A2) struck seven times, wearing each string's measured bend from bass to treble. Same timbre and pitch, seven stiffnesses. The treble strings' bends are carried on by the fit past where they were measured, so the last three get bell-like.
2. **06-library-rebuilt.wav**: bell, vibraphone, marimba, bowl, each rebuilt from its own two measured walls. This checks the tracker against the originals in Live.
3. **07-library-on-the-organ.wav**: the organ (A3) struck four times, wearing each object's bend.
4. **08-vibraphone-two-filings.wav**: the open question below. The vibraphone filed in rank order, then filed by nearest harmonic.
5. **09-bell-choir-measured.wav**: A major on the organ wearing the real bell. It's the entry's 'alien bell choir', built from a measured bell instead of Bessel zeros.
6. **keyboard-stiffness.png** and **library-sheet.png**: the numbers behind all of it.
7. **dual-wavetable-instrument.html**: six new materials in the Wavetable B menu.

payload.decision_topic: how a bell or bar is filed into Wavetable B
payload.headline: When a bell or bar becomes Wavetable B, does its k-th mode go in slot k, or in the harmonic slot it's nearest?
payload.ground: still working · library shelf shipped · steward leans RANK
payload.rationale: Catch-up: this synth bends each partial off its harmonic place by a measured amount. A piano has a harmonic ladder, so its bend files itself. A bell, a bar or a bowl has modes, so I had to pick a filing rule. I used rank: the k-th mode goes in slot k. That makes a bell's bend travel. On the organ, every organ partial lands on a bell mode, and that's what 09-bell-choir-measured.wav plays. The cost is huge bends (a tight bell sits 1000 to 1700 cents flat), and a tuned marimba looks bent when it's really sparse. The other rule puts each mode in its nearest harmonic slot. The bends stay small (the vibraphone's are 0 to 19 cents) and the gaps go silent. It reads more honestly on the flat-line display, but it travels less. Play 08-vibraphone-two-filings.wav (rank first, then nearest). The project keeps moving either way. I'll keep using rank until you say otherwise.

options.label: RANK: the k-th mode lives in slot k. Bends travel onto any loudness wall, and they get big.
NEAREST: each mode goes in its nearest harmonic slot. Small bends, honest on the flat line, travels less.
BOTH: store both and make filing a switch on the instrument. More to build and explain, and the lesson gets a moment out of it.

payload.headline: The flock's order really does snap, but under the first mapping it never reached the sound. A new mapping lets you hear it, and the page now uses it.
payload.ground: shipped · page ≡ engine exactly, unheard in a browser · steward leans flock-as-distribution next
payload.catchup: Murmuration is a synth where a flock of 60 boids wanders across a 2D wavetable and every boid is a grain, so the flock's shape is the grain cloud. Its signature knob, Disorder, adds steering noise and should push the flock through a real order→chaos transition, from a pitched tone to a broadband cloud. The page was built in June and checked only by numbers, never by ear. This cycle I built a headless copy of the page and measured it. The transition is real and sharp, but it sits in the bottom sixth of the old slider. Under the first mapping the sound barely changes when the flock orders: grains are about one waveform cycle long and pitch comes from height, and neither depends on order. I added an 'order' mapping that makes the transition audible and remapped the slider so the snap sits mid-travel. Both are now in the page. I also rendered the project's main bet as a blind A/B.
payload.content:
WHAT I BUILT. engine/murmur_engine.js is the page's own flock, grain mapping and AudioWorklet grain voice, copied line for line and made repeatable with seeded randomness. check_page_mapping.js pulls the code out of Murmuration.html, runs it with stubbed audio, and compares it with the engine over 1200 frames for both mappings. The largest difference is 0.

FINDING 1, the transition is real. sweep_eta.js lets 8 seeded flocks settle at each Disorder level. φ (how much the flock agrees on a heading) falls from 0.96 to 0.25 between η 0 and 0.10, then sits at the random floor of about 0.12. Its fluctuations peak at η ≈ 0.07, which is what a true critical point looks like. Raising and lowering η slowly gives the same curve, so there's no hysteresis, and it behaves like a continuous transition. The page's default η 0.06 happens to sit right on the knee. But on the old 0–1 slider everything happens in the first 15% of the travel.

FINDING 2, the sound didn't follow. I ran a scripted 40-second performance through the page's mapping: melted, crystallise, ordered, a predator at 21 s, melt again. In it, pitch-class entropy stays between 3.38 and 3.46 bits whatever the flock does (3.58 would mean all twelve pitch classes equally loud). Two reasons. Grains run at 18–108 Hz, about one cycle of the 110 Hz tone, with a random phase each time, so every boid is a click. And pitch comes from height, which an ordered flock doesn't concentrate. The flock lines up its headings but stays spread across the whole field, with one or two neighbours per boid.

THE FIX, the 'order' mapping. The heading circle becomes the pitch circle, one octave around, so a flock that agrees on its heading also agrees on its pitch. Grain length follows how steadily each boid has held its course over the last quarter second. A boid kept on line by its neighbours plays 250 ms tonal grains, and a tumbling one plays 10 ms clicks. Now the sound tracks φ: 3.40 bits melted, 2.67 ordered, 2.49 re-cohered, back to 3.39 melted again. The page gets a 'Listen by' menu (order is the default, 'place' keeps the first build) and a Disorder slider remapped to η = 0.25·x², so the knee is at mid-slider and the default sits there too.

THE BLIND PAIR. blind-X.wav and blind-Y.wav play the same 40-second performance through the order mapping. In one, the grains are the flock. In the other, each grain wanders on its own random jitter, while the cloud's centre, spread, speed, heading agreement and grain-length mix are copied from the flock frame by frame. Only the coordination between grains differs. They're level-matched. The key is in engine/blind-key.json; please don't open it before listening. The question is on TRICKSTER.

PASSED OVER. Making the flock clump so 'clustered = one tone' comes true: it would mean changing the flocking itself, and alignment, not clumping, is what the transition is. Mapping η straight to grain length: that would be a crossfade dressed as emergence, the softening my own forward vector says to avoid.

payload.headline: My entry says the ordered flock clusters into a pitched tone. Measured, it lines up but stays spread out, and the old mapping stayed broadband.
payload.ground: high confidence · measured headlessly · needs an elder to reword the entry
payload.rationale: Two sentences in [[Murmuration]] promise more than the June model delivers. 'Cohesion morphs a unified pitched tone (boids clustered…)' and 'at η = 0 the flock coheres (φ climbs 0.10 → 0.93, pitched)'. The φ numbers hold. 'Pitched' and 'clustered' don't. The ordered flock agrees on a heading, but it stays spread over the whole field with one or two neighbours each. Under the first mapping, the sound's pitch-class entropy stays between 3.38 and 3.46 bits whether the flock is melted or ordered. payload.content:
WHAT I BUILT. engine/field_reading.js is the distribution reading. Each frame the flock gets smoothed onto the wavetable field: an 80-pixel blur around each boid, wrapped at the edges. Each of 40 cells takes that density as its level, and the levels are power-normalised so the pad never gets louder as it gathers. Each cell's pitch is the average heading of the boids around it, on the same heading→pitch circle as the grains' 'order' mapping. That circle is now a real circle: each cell is a Shepard pair (a tone and its octave below, crossfading), so when a heading passes ±180° the pitch keeps turning instead of jumping an octave. The page has a third 'Listen by' choice, density. check_page_mapping.js now also runs the page's own field code and its own worklet code. Over 1200 frames the largest difference from the engine is 0, for both the weights and the audio samples.

WHAT IT DOES. Same 40-second performance as the blind pair (melted, crystallising, ordered, a predator at 21 s, melting again). When the flock orders, the cells agree on pitch: 0.97–0.99 ordered against 0.32–0.40 melted. The sound focuses harder than the grains do. Pitch-class entropy drops to 2.02 bits when ordered, against 2.67 for the order-mapped grains and 3.42 for the first build. That's the phase transition heard as a chord collapsing to one pitch class. The pad has no Disorder crossfade anywhere. The second finding matches yesterday's: order alone hardly gathers the flock in space, about 31–37 of 40 cells sound either way. So the attractor is this reading's own gesture. In reading-distribution-attractor.wav, dragging the ordered flock on a loop squeezes the pad from about 35 sounding cells to about 9, and its timbre travels with the flock across the terrain. No zipper noise: the jump at control-frame edges is 1.08× the average jump (the blind grains measure about 1.5).

PASSED OVER. Fixed pitches per cell, letting only the density move. Order would never reach the sound that way, the same trap as the first build. A covariance-ellipse formula driving detune directly. With the cells' own headings, the spread already becomes the chord's spread, so a second formula would just be a hand-dialed copy of it.

payload.content:
WHAT I BUILT. Each boid now carries an alarm level from 0 to 1. A boid's alarm rises when it sees the predator (within 150 px), or when it catches the alarm from the most alarmed of its 7 nearest flockmates. That's topological, not by distance, which is what Ballerini et al. (2008) measured in real starlings. The alarm passes on one step weaker each hop, takes a few frames to react at each hop, and fades over about a second. An alarmed boid dashes, pushes apart harder, holds the group less, and dodges away from wherever the alarm is coming from. So the startle runs through the flock as a wave of about 350 px/s, roughly 2.5× faster than any single boid. Real starling waves run a few times faster than the birds; I'm working from memory there and didn't check the source this cycle. The regathering afterwards is plain flocking, with no recovery curve written anywhere. Alarm also swells each grain's gain (up to 2.5×) and each pad cell's level, so the sound has something to hear. A click no longer drops an attractor in this mode, though dragging still does. Alarmed boids flash white with a ring, and the HUD counts them. The whole thing is opt-in in the engine: with it off, the blind pair and every earlier render reproduce exactly. check_page_mapping.js now also runs the page's own startle code with four predator strikes through all three readings. The largest difference from the engine is 0 every time.

FIRST TRY FAILED. Passing the alarm by distance only reached about 10 boids, because this flock is sparse (one or two neighbours inside 56 px). Nearest-7 fixed that. Then the wave ran 15× faster than the boids, and the flock barely dipped. Slowing how fast each boid reacts and strengthening the dodge brought it into range.

THE ÉTUDE. It's one 30-second script with four clicks, each landing in a different flock. A hits a settled flock dead centre. B hits a settled flock upper left. C hits B's spot again while the flock is still recovering. D lands after Disorder has been eased up to just short of the transition. The flock answers each one differently. A catches 22 boids, order dips 0.94 → 0.54, and it's back in 4.2 s. B catches all 60 and shatters the flock to 0.13; it hasn't regathered by the time C lands, and it takes about 8 s to really heal. C, landing in an already broken flock, alarms only 5 boids. D, near the transition, catches 26. One identical click gets four responses, because the response comes from the flock's state at that moment. An authored envelope would give four copies.

HONEST READING OF THE SOUND. The pad breathes on its own: with no click at all, its level rises up to 4.5–6 dB within 0.8 s (90th percentile). So the pad's startle swell (+6.2 and +6.8 dB, peaking 0.3–0.4 s after A and B) sits right at the edge of its own breathing. In the pad the startle comes through more as pitch blooming than as loudness: the chord spreads by about 1 bit of pitch-class entropy on A and B. The place grains are much steadier (no-click floor 1.9 dB), and there the swell stands well clear: +3.3 dB on A and +5.6 dB on B. The old flinch's biggest moves in the pad arrive 2–3 s after the click, which is just the breathing again. Only strike A compares like for like, since the two takes are different flocks after that.

PASSED OVER. A moving hawk that dives across the field: it's richer, but it would make the gesture a path to draw instead of a click to play. Save it for later. Rendering the startle through the 'order' grains: that's the blind pair's mapping, and a labelled take could tip your ear before you answer, so I used 'place' grains instead. A fixed ADSR triggered by the click as a control take: the strike-by-strike table already shows what an envelope can't do, and a second blind test before the first one is answered would just be noise.

payload.headline: A bowed string's ring-back is a timbre event too: on the overshoot one partial slips out of lock and catches again. A critically damped arrival never slips.
payload.ground: shipped · multi-mode pass 2 with a listening pair · steward leans fold the pair into the ear-training reel next
payload.catchup: Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling treats pitch as a damped spring settling on a note. The three ways it can settle are overdamped (eases in), critically damped (arrives clean) and underdamped (overshoots and rings back). The ear-training set and a six-clip single-session reel shipped in June. In August you picked MULTI-MODE: take the model from one gliding pitch to a whole family of partials, and render how the timbre moves during a glide. A first pass from September sat unposted in the workshop. Its slide-versus-bend contrast holds up, but its coupling did nothing: the 'locked' and 'uncoupled' glides have the same partials to within 0.3 cents, because the pull was about 1 rad/s against 15 to 280 rad/s of detuning. This cycle rebuilds the coupling on real physics and ships five clips, a figure and a listening page with one by-ear pair.
payload.content:
**The physics.** A stiff string's own resonances are stretched: partial n sits at n·f1·√(1+B·n²). A plucked string rings right there, slightly sharp of the harmonic series. A bowed string, a voice or a reed is self-sustained. Its excitation keeps pulling every partial back onto an exact multiple of the fundamental, as long as that pull beats the stretch (Fletcher 1978, mode locking in inharmonic instruments). For each partial that is two-oscillator Kuramoto, the Adler equation below. A glide changes the stretch, so a glide moves partials in and out of lock.

**What the five clips show.** (1) Plucked, sliding up an octave: nothing locks, and the top partial ends 82 cents sharp. (2) The same slide bowed: it starts with 4 partials locked, then partial 4 lets go at 0.60 s and partial 3 at 0.75 s, from the top down. Sliding shortens the string, and the stretch grows as pitch cubed. (3) The same octave by tension, like a peg turn while bowing: the stretch now falls as pitch rises, so a beating 4th partial is pulled into lock at 0.76 s and the tone clears. Slide and peg cover the same interval with opposite timbre journeys. (4) and (5) are the pair. Both are bowed and both land on E4 (330 Hz). The underdamped one (ζ 0.2) overshoots to 400 Hz, so partial 3 lets go from 0.82 to 1.31 s and again from 1.93 to 2.31 s on the second ring. The critically damped one never passes the note, and partial 3 never comes loose.

**Why it matters for the teaching.** Until now the regimes were told apart by pitch alone. This gives the underdamped regime a second cue, texture right after the arrival, and that is how a real bowed or sung overshoot sounds. Take the pair on [the listening page](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/mode-locking-listening.html), or play [B, underdamped](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/locking-04-bow-overshoot.wav) against [A, critically damped](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/locking-05-bow-critical.wav). The whole picture is [mode-locking.png](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/figures/mode-locking.png).

equations.label: Partial locking (Adler / two-oscillator Kuramoto)
equations.worded: d(phase_offsetₙ)/dt = 2π·detuningₙ − 2π·locking_range·sin(phase_offsetₙ),   detuningₙ = n·fundamental·(√(1 + stiffness·n²) − 1)

where.def: partial n's phase offset from n times the fundamental
locking range in Hz (0 = plucked, free)
stiffness: grows as f₁² on a slide, falls as 1/f₁² on a tension raise

table.caption: Five clips · 10 partials · 'locked' = detuning inside the locking range
rows: partial 4 lets go 0.60 s, partial 3 at 0.75 s

payload.claim: The Kuramoto Coupling Perspective section of [Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Portamento%20and%20Physical%20Pitch%20Modeling) says a sliding string's modes 'chase each other' as weakly coupled Kuramoto oscillators. Today's build says the coupling lives somewhere else. A free, plucked string's modes don't lock: they ring at their own stretched frequencies. Locking is what a self-sustained instrument does (bow, voice, reed). Its excitation pulls each partial onto an exact harmonic while the pull beats the stiffness detuning (Fletcher 1978). That is the Adler, two-oscillator Kuramoto equation, and a glide moves partials across its threshold. Sliding unlocks them from the top down. Raising tension pulls them back in. An underdamped overshoot makes one slip and catch. The September model, which put Kuramoto coupling on a plain glide, produced no measurable effect (0.3 cents). A bowed or sung tone locks them: the excitation pulls each partial onto an exact multiple of the fundamental for as long as that pull beats the stiffness detuning. A glide moves the detuning, so it moves partials into and out of lock. Sliding unlocks them from the top down, raising tension pulls them back in, and an underdamped overshoot makes one slip and catch, so the ring-back is heard in the timbre as well as the pitch.' payload.headline: A harder bow holds more partials in tune, so a crescendo fuses the tone. A louder overshoot still slips, just higher in the tone and more briefly.
payload.ground: shipped · multi-mode pass 3, five clips + listening page · steward leans fold the soft-bow pair into the ear-training reel next
payload.catchup: Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling treats pitch as a damped spring settling on a note. It can settle in three ways: overdamped (eases in), critically damped (arrives clean) or underdamped (overshoots and rings back). The ear-training set and a six-clip single-session reel shipped in June. In August you picked MULTI-MODE, which takes the model from one gliding pitch to a whole family of partials. Earlier today I showed the model at work on a bowed string. The bow holds the partials onto exact multiples of the fundamental, a glide moves them into and out of that hold, and an underdamped overshoot makes one partial slip and catch again. So the ring-back can be heard in the tone colour as well as the pitch. This cycle takes the next step: the strength of that hold now comes from the bow, so loudness changes how the tone holds together.
payload.content:
**The change.** Last pass, every bowed clip had one fixed pull holding its partials in line. That pull comes from the bow, and a harder bow pulls harder, so now it follows bow force. It rises from 0.5 Hz at pianissimo to 30 Hz at fortissimo, along a curve I chose myself (Fletcher 1978 doesn't give one). The string and pitch model are the same as last time.

**The crescendo pair.** Both clips are a held E4 with the identical crescendo, −24 dB up to full, matched level for level. In [B](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/loudness-01-crescendo-bow.wav) the hold follows the bow. Partials 2 through 6 lock one at a time from the bottom up (1.36, 2.13, 2.63, 3.06, 3.56 s), and by the top the waveform almost repeats itself: 0.96 match a hundred cycles later. In [A, the control](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/loudness-02-crescendo-control.wav) the hold stays frozen at its pianissimo value. Nothing new locks, and the match at full volume is only 0.79. Loudness is the same in both, so the difference you hear is the tone fusing.

**The overshoot at three bow strengths** (G3 to E4, ζ 0.2, level-matched). Soft bow: [partial 2 slips](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/loudness-03-overshoot-soft.wav) on both rings, at −6 dB. Medium: [partial 3 slips](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/loudness-04-overshoot-medium.wav). It matches last cycle's clip to within a hundredth of a second, which checks the new script. Loud: [only partial 6 slips](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/loudness-05-overshoot-loud.wav), at −15.6 dB, once, from 0.84 to 1.27 s. payload.catchup: Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling treats pitch as a damped spring settling on a note. It can settle in three ways: overdamped (eases in), critically damped (arrives clean) or underdamped (overshoots and rings back). In June the project shipped an ear-training set and a 15-minute single-session reel that teaches the three by pitch. In August you picked MULTI-MODE, which takes the model from one gliding pitch to a whole family of partials. Earlier today I showed that on a bowed string an overshoot makes one overtone slip out of tune and catch again, and that the bow's strength decides which one. This cycle turns that into teaching. The reel now has a third round of three listening pairs, built on a bow strength I picked by measuring how audible the slip is, not by guessing.
payload.content:
**What changed in the reel.** [The single-session reel](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/curated-ear-set/single-session-reel.html) keeps its six clips and gains *Round three — hear the arrival in the tone colour*. All three pairs use the same bowed string and the same bow, G3 up to E4.

- **Pair 07:** critically damped against underdamped. You can answer this by pitch, and then the reveal sends you back for the second cue: as the underdamped pitch crests, the top of the tone flutters.
- **Pair 08:** this is the one that matters. Both clips follow the [identical underdamped pitch path](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/timbre-01-firm-underdamped.wav), sample for sample. In the [control](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/timbre-04-underdamped-held.wav) the slipping overtone is held in tune by force. The slip is the only difference, so a student who hears the fray is hearing the overshoot in the timbre alone.
- **Pair 09:** [overdamped](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/timbre-03-firm-overdamped.wav) against [critically damped](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/audio/timbre-02-firm-critical.wav). Neither one slips, and the reveal says so. The tone colour picks out the underdamped arrival and can't help beyond that, so this pair teaches where the cue stops working. To tell these two apart you go back to the approach: critical gets within a semitone 0.6 s after it starts moving, overdamped takes 1.3 s.

**Why a firm bow, not the soft one I leaned toward last cycle.** I measured what the ear would actually hear, which is the slipping overtone going out of tune and beating, and swept bow strength (table). With a soft bow, partial 2 drifts 0.3% at most and makes about one beat in total. That is very likely too small to hear, so last cycle's lean was wrong. With a firm bow (15 Hz locking range), partial 5 goes 2% out of tune and beats about 12 times across three crests: eight on the first, three on the second, one on the third. The [figure](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/figures/timbre-round.png) shows the beats as spikes. I read them straight from the rendered audio with a heterodyne, so the measurement is of the files, not the model. The control's overtone drifts 0.01 Hz, and the critically damped and overdamped clips stay under 0.3 Hz.

The renderer is [timbre_round.py](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/timbre_round.py), with every number in [timbre-manifest.json](open:Projects/Portamento and Physical Pitch Modeling/multi-mode/timbre-manifest.json).

It says the i 'forces oscillation' and that the equation is 'exactly' an RLC resonant circuit. Instead of deleting the i, I turned it by an angle. payload.content: I rotated the time axis, dψ/dt = −i·e^(−iθ)·Hψ, in the same box as the walls proof: hard walls, ground level at 220 Hz, the same pluck and the same pickup. [wick.wav](open:Projects/Quantum Synthesizer/proofs/wick.wav) plays nine strikes from 0° to 90°, each through two ears as in the ladder proof. The clock is the phase turning, which nothing physical can hear. The detector is what a measurement registers. [wick.mp4](open:Projects/Quantum Synthesizer/proofs/wick.mp4) is the same audio with the poles, the wave in the box and the spectrogram. [wick-poster.png](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Quantum%20Synthesizer/proofs/wick-poster.png) shows it all in one still, and you can watch the high partials drop out first. What it does to the entry: each level is one lossless pole sitting on the axis, not a damped conjugate pair. Schrödinger is an RLC bank with every resistor set to zero, and the angle of i is the one knob that puts the resistance back, the same amount in every resonator. Removing the i doesn't send the particle to infinity. Everything fades toward the ground state's shape. A side finding: the detector's beats sit at differences of levels but die at their sums, so to a real measurement the damping is about 5/3 stronger. The replacement paragraphs are in [the opening draft](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Quantum%20Synthesizer/proofs/opening-paragraphs%20%E2%80%94%20draft) for an elder to land.

payload.headline: The witness is built: two Max patches plus a model that renders audio. As written, it's exactly a half-note echo. The second version isn't.
payload.ground: shipped · patches written, not yet opened in Max · steward leans SILENCE-KEEPS
payload.catchup: Retrospective Delay is a one-measure delay that is always listening. A circular buffer holds the last measure of everything you play, and one gain knob decides whether that past comes back. The plan builds it in five moves, each one a Loudon Live session. The first is 'the witness': a write head and a read head sweeping one buffer, in vanilla Max, as a Max for Live audio effect. The fourth move's face, the Gorey-ink séance cat, was drawn and wired to the knob back in June. This cycle went back to the first move and built it as real Max patches, with a model that renders audio. The model turned up something the session hangs on: the witness as written is exactly a half-note echo.
payload.content:
I made two patchers and a reference model that runs the patch sample by sample (48 kHz, 120 BPM, read head half a measure behind). The input is two measures of a phrase, three of silence, one more phrase, then silence.

**A, as specified.** Its output is identical to a plain half-note echo, with zero difference at every sample. It can't be anything else: the read head trails by half a measure, and that slot isn't overwritten until a full measure has passed, so the buffer's length never matters. In silence the ghost plays once and is gone. The Reveal block says a student who tries to rebuild this in Ableton's Echo will find they can't. For A, they can: one tap at a half note with feedback at zero.

**B, silence keeps.** The buffer still writes on every sample. When you aren't playing, though, it writes down what it already holds, so the last measure stays and keeps coming back until you play again. That is the home entry's line, 'when you play silence, the last phrase repeats', and Echo can't do it. The cost is a quiet level threshold, which bends the 'no gate' wording of the always-recording rule a little.

Along the way I fixed four bugs in the April build notes. The `[!- 0.5]` read offset computes 0.5 minus the phase, which runs the read head backwards and gives you a reverse delay; it's also control-rate on a signal. `[* 176400]` should be `*~`. With the 4-second buffer, `wave~` reads the whole thing unless its end point is set to the measure length. And the note's 'the ghost will continue' is only true of B. The patches use `phasor~ 1n @lock 1` for the measure clock and `translate notevalues ms @listen 1` for the measure length, so both follow Live's tempo.

To try one: drop a Max Audio Effect on a track in Live, open the editor, paste in the patcher, start the transport, and turn the gain up.

payload.ground: shipped · built on the silence-keeps witness, patch not yet opened in Max · steward leans SILENCE-KEEPS
payload.catchup: Retrospective Delay is a one-measure delay that is always listening. A buffer holds the last measure of everything you play, and one gain knob decides whether that past comes back. The plan builds it in five moves, each a Loudon Live session. Last cycle built the first move, the witness, and found that as written it's just a half-note echo. Version B fixes that: when you go quiet it keeps the last measure, so silence brings the phrase back. I asked you to pick between the two; that question is still open, and I kept going on B. This cycle built the second move, the séance, which makes the witness playable. You get a gain knob that summons or hides the ghost, a choice of quarter, half or whole-note lag, and no clicks. payload.content:
The séance adds three things to the silence-keeps witness.

**The knob, ramped, on the way out of the buffer.** Turning it down hides the past but doesn't erase it. In the performance render the ghost is turned fully away for a measure, then brought back, and it's still there. The April session notes put the gain on the write side instead. That would make turning it down slowly erase the ghost, which is a different instrument and breaks the witness idea. I went with the read side and said so in the draft.

**A lag choice of 1/4, 1/2 or 1/1, switched with no click.** Moving one read head is a splice. So there are two read heads: the idle one jumps to the new lag, then a 30 ms fade hands over to it. The whole note is sent as 0.999, not 1.0. At exactly 1.0 the read head sits on the write head, and vanilla Max doesn't promise whether poke~ or wave~ runs first. That's a ready-made question to carry into the Gen~ move.

**The seam, which turned out to be somewhere else.** The plan says to crossfade at the loop boundary. The model shows there is no click at the measure line, because the read head never jumps there. The click is where you stopped playing: once the witness switches from listening to holding, the newest sound it heard ends up right next to the oldest. Smoothing that switch over about 10 ms (`slide~ 480 480` after the gate) removes it. Smoothing the gate is the crossfade. That makes a better reveal for the session than the one planned.

To try it: drop a Max Audio Effect on a track in Live, paste in seance.maxpat, start the transport, play a phrase, stop, and raise the knob. Start with the performance render: phrase, summon, re-lag in silence, a new phrase over the ghost, dismiss, a silent measure, then summon again.

payload.headline: The séance now runs as one gen~ codebox, the whole note is exactly 1, and the compressor's 11 ms window turns out to be the same two lines.
payload.ground: shipped · gen~ port matches the vanilla model exactly · not opened in Max · steward leans SILENCE-KEEPS
payload.catchup: Retrospective Delay is a one-measure delay that is always listening. A buffer holds the last measure of everything you play, and one gain knob decides whether that past comes back. The plan builds it in five moves, each a Loudon Live session. The first two are built in vanilla Max: the witness (the always-listening buffer, in the version where silence keeps your last measure) and the séance (the knob, a choice of lag, no clicks). This cycle built the third move, the first of the two deliberate migrations. The séance's core moves into Gen~, and the same buffer is set beside the compressor's 11 ms window. The witness question from earlier today is still open, and I built on silence-keeps.
payload.content:
**One sample's worth of thought.** [seance.genexpr](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Retrospective%20Delay/stage-3-grammar/seance.genexpr) is the whole séance in about thirty lines: the tape, two read heads with the 30 ms handover, the witness's listen-or-hold write, the ~10 ms seam smoothing, and the slewed knob. [grammar.maxpat](open:Projects/Retrospective Delay/stage-3-grammar/grammar.maxpat) puts it in a gen~ object with only the transport clock, the measure length and the two controls outside. The controls now send `gain`, `lag` and `measure` messages instead of driving signal chains. A line-for-line Python copy of the codebox matches the vanilla séance model: the largest difference between the two ghosts is 1.4e-16.

**Why 0.999 can become 1.** In vanilla Max you can't choose whether poke~ or wave~ runs first. In gen~, lines run in the order you write them, so the read can go before the write. The two order renders show what's at stake. With read-first, the ghost while you play is the measure before (correlation 1.000). With write-first, the 'ghost' is just you, louder (correlation 1.000 with the input right now). In silence they sound the same, which is why nobody would catch it by ear in the vanilla patch.

**The same buffer at 11 ms.** [compressor-window.genexpr](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Retrospective%20Delay/stage-3-grammar/compressor-window.genexpr) is Compressor Design's 500-sample RMS window. Its middle two lines, `oldest = peek(win, w); poke(win, sq, w);`, are the séance's read-then-write at a whole-note lag. The model checks its running sum against a plain windowed RMS (difference 7.8e-16). Then the shrinking-measure render freezes one phrase into four tape lengths. You hear a phrase, then a stutter, then a flutter, and at the compressor's 500 samples a 96 Hz tone. Time turns into pitch somewhere between 50 ms and 11 ms. That gives the session its closing reveal.

The [session draft](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Retrospective%20Delay/stage-3-grammar/stage-3-the-grammar.md) runs about half framing and half making, as the standing orders set for the migrations. It opens on last session's 0.999 question, builds the codebox in five listened-to steps, and ends on the shrinking measure. To try the patch, paste grammar.maxpat into a Max Audio Effect, start the transport, play, stop, and raise the knob. Start with [order-read-first.wav](open:Projects/Retrospective Delay/stage-3-grammar/order-read-first.wav) against [order-write-first.wav](open:Projects/Retrospective Delay/stage-3-grammar/order-write-first.wav).

payload.headline: The first echo that really changes voice: one sung phrase, re-sung by another singer three times, with the melody knob at locked, half and free.
payload.ground: shipped · real model ran on your Mac · steward leans wire it into the helper next
payload.catchup: Semantic Delay is a delay effect for a DAW. Instead of repeating your phrase, each echo comes back sung by a different voice. A voice-conversion model called SoulX-Singer-SVC does the swap. It's too slow for live monitoring (about 1.65 seconds of compute per second of audio on the M1 Max), so the delay is long by design, in seconds. The plan has two pieces: a small plugin, and a separate Python helper that holds the model. We built the helper's message format, a playable Python version of the instrument and multi-voice echoes, but always against a placeholder that handed audio back unchanged, so until today no echo had actually changed voice. In June you chose the next step: give every echo the original phrase's melody, with one knob running from 'sing the melody exactly' to 'wander onto a scale'. This cycle ran that on the real model on your Mac. It works. The echoes come back in the reference singer's voice and follow whatever pitch line the knob hands them.
payload.content:
I took one 6.4-second sung phrase (the SoulX example vocal), tracked its pitch with the model's own pitch tracker, and asked the model to re-sing it in the voice of the example reference singer three times. Each time the knob was in a different place. **Locked**: the echo sings your melody. **Half**: it holds the shape but rounds off the leaps. **Free**: it keeps your words and rhythm but sings its own line on a pentatonic scale. Listen to the [delay timeline](open:Projects/Semantic Delay/standalone/demo/stage4-real/stage4-real-coupling-delay.wav): the dry phrase first, then the three echoes in that order. The plot shows each one: grey is your melody, blue is what the knob asked for, red is what the model actually sang.

What I measured: the model sings the line it's given to within about a tenth of a semitone, so it obeys the knob rather than ignoring it. The echo moves 0.33, 0.83, then 1.5 semitones away from your melody as the knob relaxes, a clean ladder. A rough timbre check puts every echo about five times nearer the reference singer than the original, so the voice really did change. Speed held at 1.65 seconds of compute per second of audio once the model was warm, the same figure we measured in April.

Hearing it on the real model caught two faults, and I fixed both. First, at 'locked' the echo slurred every note change by about 40 ms. The follower now speeds up as the knob tightens, so locked really is locked. Second, the pitch tracker read one note more than an octave low, and the echo was asked to dive there. The model refused, wisely. A new step now folds those octave slips back into place before the knob acts.

payload.catchup: Semantic Delay is a delay effect where each echo comes back sung by a different voice instead of repeating you. It has two parts: a small plugin, and a separate Python helper that holds the voice-conversion model (SoulX-Singer-SVC), because the model is far too heavy to run inside a DAW's audio thread. Until now the helper held a placeholder that handed audio back unchanged. Last cycle the real model sang in a standalone script. This cycle I finished the first move of the plan, putting the real model behind the helper. payload.content: What I built: a new `soulx_backend.py` holds the model and its pitch tracker. You start the helper with `--backend soulx`. The old placeholder is still the default, so the existing tests run anywhere. The helper now does the whole job the placeholder only pretended to do. It resamples whatever rate the host sends, tracks the phrase's pitch, re-sings it in the chosen singer's voice, and returns it at the host's rate. Registering a singer now saves a real 24 kHz recording with its pitch beside it, and that singer is still listed after a restart. payload.content:
**The cat used to say only what the dial said.** Turn the knob and it woke, reached, triumphed. That's charming, and it's redundant. Now [face.genexpr](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Retrospective%20Delay/stage-4-character/face/face.genexpr) is the grammar's codebox, unchanged, plus three outlets: the slewed gain (the knob as heard), an envelope on the raw ghost before the knob (is anything on the tape?), and `1 - listen` (is the tape holding?). The model checks that the sound is untouched: the face's output matches the grammar's exactly, difference zero.

**Two frames the knob could never show.** In [face-moments.png](open:Projects/Retrospective Delay/stage-4-character/face/face-moments.png), bottom-left: the cat asleep, pale strands still around it, candle lit. You dismissed the ghost, but the past is still on the tape. Bottom-right: knob all the way up, cat reaching, no strands. The room is empty. Those two frames are the session's whole argument: a face should show what the instrument is doing, not what its controls are set to.

**One thing I caught by looking.** In the first render the ectoplasm was dark ink, the old JSUI's colour, and it disappeared against the plates. 'Summoned' and 'empty room' looked identical. I moved it to pale bone, drawn after the lights-down darkening, so it reads even while the cat sleeps. I also stretched the presence envelope's release to 1 second, so the rests inside a phrase don't flicker as 'empty'.

**The film.** [face-film.mp4](open:Projects/Retrospective Delay/stage-4-character/face/face-film.mp4) is the séance's 15-measure performance with sound, the cat reacting at 30 fps, and a caption and three small meters under it. Watch measures 9 to 12: dismissed, asleep with the past kept, then summoned again, and the same phrase comes back.

**In Max.** [face.maxpat](open:Projects/Retrospective Delay/stage-4-character/face/face.maxpat) is the grammar device with `snapshot~ 33` on the three new outlets feeding a jsui running the rewritten [seance-cat.js](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Retrospective%20Delay/stage-4-character/jsui/seance-cat.js). The cat never sees the dial. The [session draft](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Retrospective%20Delay/stage-4-character/stage-4-the-face.md) runs about 70% making, as the standing orders set for non-migration moves. The room finds the three facts themselves, each one from an earlier session. Then they build the outlets, wire the cat, and watch the film calling out moments before the captions do. It ends on the bridge to the portal: RNBO has no JSUI, so what happens to the face when the instrument leaves Max?

The first four are drafted with working models and unopened patches: the witness (the bare buffer), the séance (silence keeps the past, with your 5 ms input crossfade), the grammar (the same thing as one gen~ codebox), and the face (the Gorey cat reading three facts from the device). payload.content:
The plan asks one question of this move: once it lives outside Max, is it still the same instrument? I can now answer it in two halves.

Yes, the arithmetic is the same. [portal.codebox](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Retrospective%20Delay/stage-5-portal/portal.codebox) is about 70 lines of rnboscript. [portal_mirror.mjs](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Retrospective%20Delay/stage-5-portal/portal_mirror.mjs) runs that file's own text against the face's gen~ model over the whole fifteen-measure performance. All five outlets match: four exactly, and the ghost to 5.6e-17. portal-performance.wav is the codebox's own render.

No, the world around it is different. Leaving Max showed me two things Max for Live had been quietly giving the device:

1. A running transport. The gen~ write head followed a phasor~ locked to Live's transport. When the transport stops, that phasor stops, and the tape writes one slot forever. A plugin host or a hardware box doesn't promise a transport. But the ghost only ever needed the distance between the two heads, not where the bar line is. So the portal's write head counts its own samples, and tempo comes in as a bpm knob.
2. A sample rate the tape was sized for. gen~'s tape held 4 seconds at 48 kHz. At 96 kHz a slow measure doesn't fit, the tape quietly shrinks, and the ghost comes back early. The table shows where. Listen to slow-tempo-gen-tape.wav, then slow-tempo-portal.wav: both run at 96 kHz and 60 BPM with a half-note lag, and the first one lands on beat two instead of beat three. The portal's tape doubles to 384000 slots. This bug is also in the grammar and face codeboxes.

The tape also lives inside the codebox rather than in a buffer~, which matters because the H9000's RNBO target doesn't support buffer~ yet.

Three more pieces shipped. [portal.maxpat](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Retrospective%20Delay/stage-5-portal/portal.maxpat) is an rnbo~ holding the codebox, with in~/out~ and the face's three facts sent through outports. portal-web.html runs the codebox's own text in your browser, with a tape ring showing both heads, the knob, the lag and the tempo, and a review layer on it. [The session draft](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Retrospective%20Delay/stage-5-portal/stage-5-the-portal.md) shapes all of this into the last Loudon Live session. It runs about half framing, half making, per your standing order for the migrations.

payload.headline: The H90 can't run RNBO yet. Should the portal aim at VST/AU, Max for Live and the browser instead, with hardware only if it opens up?
payload.ground: still working · all five moves drafted · steward leans adopt
payload.rationale: Retrospective Delay is the one-measure delay that is always listening, built in five Loudon Live moves. All five are now drafted. The last move, the portal, ports the device to RNBO so it can leave Max. The plan says it goes out as a VST/AU and onto the Eventide H90. As far as I can find, the H90 has no RNBO route. Eventide supports RNBO on the H9000 rack processor, and for the H90 has said only that it's considering it. Crystal Synthesizer's portal hit the same wall. I built the codebox so it would run on an H9000 unchanged: no buffer~, no transport needed. I also added a browser page as a third way out. My knowledge could be stale, so if the H90 has opened up, KEEP and I'll check it. The proposed plan only changes where the portal goes.
payload.plan:
**Where this is going.** A one-measure delay that is always listening: a circular buffer holds the last measure of everything you play, and one gain knob decides whether that past comes back. It is built in five moves, and two of them are deliberate migrations (vanilla Max to Gen~, then Gen~ to RNBO) where the friction is the lesson. Any move can happen in public as a [[Loudon Live]] build. All five moves are now drafted as session plans with working models and patches. None has been opened in Max yet, so the next work is opening them, starting with the portal's export.

**The moves ahead**

1. **The witness.** In vanilla Max, a write head and a read head sweep one buffer, one measure apart, wrapped as a Max for Live audio effect. You play and hear your whole phrase come back as a single ghost, not as echoes.
2. **The séance.** Make it performable: the gain knob as the one gesture that summons or silences the past, a choice of lag length, and a crossfade at the loop seam. Silence becomes the most expressive thing the player can do.
3. **The grammar behind the spell.** Port the core to Gen~ and see that the patch was always running at signal rate. Then set it beside the compressor's 11 ms buffer: the same mechanism holding a hundred times less time.
4. **The face.** An animated character in JSUI whose three states (dormant, awakening, triumphant) are the gain knob's meaning made visible. The cat reads three facts from the device, not the knob; it hasn't yet been played in Max.
5. **The portal.** Port to RNBO and export as a VST/AU, back into Live as a Max for Live device, and as a web page, so the instrument lives outside Max. Hardware is a stretch goal: the Eventide H9000 if one is in the room, the H90 if Eventide opens it to RNBO. Then ask whether it is still the same instrument.

The April session designs for these moves are archived: [[Retrospective Delay — spec — Loudon Live sessions]].

keep — the H90 stays in the plan as written (say so if you know of a route, or have an H9000 to use).

payload.catchup: Semantic Webcam is a live camera that draws you in typeset language: brightness picks the character in each cell, and whole words fill the mid-tones. It has grown one facet at a time, and the seven facets are collected in one deck. In June you picked EYES-AND-FINGERS: bring back the parked word-flock cam (card 02), but find the real face and hands instead of guessing from motion. payload.content:
Card 06 (True Features Cam) is card 02 rebuilt on MediaPipe's face and hand mesh, which finds the irises, the lip centre and ten fingertips. Each feature pulls its own vocabulary of single words. I fixed one bug before shipping. The landmarks were placed on the raw camera frame, but the picture is cropped and mirrored, so the words would have circled the wrong side of your face. They now go through the same mapping as the picture.

Card 07 (Anatomy Cam) is the bigger move. It starts from card 05, the cam that picks each word by how much ink it carries so it matches the light. Then it marks every cell with the body part it sits on: the nearest tracked feature within a set radius. A run of words now breaks wherever the body part under it changes. Each run walks the word-pair grammar of its own text (seeing, speaking or touching, three short texts I wrote), and the tonal fit still steers it. In the proof frame the eyes read 'I SEE YOU READ… THE IRIS OPENS IN THE DARK', the mouth reads 'CONSONANT… CANNOT SAY… AN OPEN DOOR', and the hand reads 'POINT AT… FEEL THE CUP'. Each region is tinted: cyan for the eyes, rose for the mouth, green for the hand. Keys: a turns the anatomy on and off (for an A/B against card 05), k toggles the tint, m shows the region rings.

The deck now holds seven facets, with 02 relabelled 'guesses' and 06 and 07 added. Its footer points to Enrichment now that the Oblique Enrichment deck has been retired.

How I checked it: I served the folder over http and drove both cams in headless Chrome with a fake camera. Both report 'true features', which means the face and hand models really load and run, and there were no page errors. The fake camera has no face in it, so for the proof frame I froze the picture and placed four features by hand to show the regions rendering.

payload.headline: Card 08, the Tonal Bench, measures it: picking words by ink makes each line's ink follow your brightness, though cell by cell the effect is faint.
payload.ground: shipped · the page's question now has numbers · steward leans raise tone bias to 0.85
payload.catchup: Semantic Webcam is a live camera that draws you in typeset words. Brightness picks the character in each cell, and whole words fill your mid-tones. It has grown one facet at a time, and the cards are collected in one deck. Card 05 picks each word by how much ink it carries. Card 07 gives your eyes, mouth and hands their own texts. The page has always carried one question: is language a tonal medium, or did it only feel that way? Last cycle I proposed a short plan. Its first step was to measure that instead of trusting a feeling, and this cycle did it. Card 08 runs card 05's own word-choosing code on a still photo, three ways, and scores how closely the words' weight follows the light. Short answer: yes, words carry brightness, but only at the size of a whole line.
payload.content:
What I built: [08-tonal-bench.html](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Semantic%20Webcam/08-tonal-bench.html) runs without a camera. It takes card 05's word-choosing code unchanged and feeds it a still: the public-domain Grace Hopper portrait, plus a synthetic pattern of soft waves. Each still goes through three versions. Grammar uses the word-pair walk alone. Tonal is the same walk, but among the candidate words it picks the one whose ink best matches the brightness. The control is the tonal walk aimed at a random brightness. It keeps everything tonal does except the link to the actual light, so it rules out the gain coming from word length or some side effect of choosing among candidates. I ran four texts and twelve seeds, so each number is a mean over 48 renders.

What I measured: line match is the correlation between each run of words' mean ink and that run's brightness. Patch match is the same correlation cell by cell after a small blur, which is closer to what the eye sees.

The answer: on the portrait, line match goes from +0.02 (grammar) to +0.49 (tonal), and the control sits at +0.00. The waves give the same pattern (−0.07 / +0.43 / −0.00). So the effect is real, and the light is what causes it. But patch match only rises from +0.04 to +0.17. A word is a wide brush. It can hold the brightness of a line, but not of a few letters. You can see this in the proof image: the grammar and tonal frames look almost the same, because the glyph tiers (dot, dash, word, shade, white tile) do most of the drawing. Words only nudge the mid-tones.

A useful side result: sweeping the tone bias (how hard tonal fit overrides grammar) gives 0 → +0.10, 0.3 → +0.30, 0.6 (cards 05 and 07 today) → +0.49, 0.85 → +0.57, and 1.0 → +0.58. Moving the default from 0.6 to 0.85 gets most of the remaining effect while still leaving grammar a little say.

I also added card 08 to the deck.

table.caption: Grace Hopper portrait · mean of 48 renders (4 texts × 12 seeds) · mid-tones only

equations.label: line match
equations.worded: line_match = weighted_correlation( run_brightness , run_ink ), where run_brightness = (mean_brightness − mid_low)/(mid_high − mid_low) and run_ink = (1/run_length)·Σ glyph_coverage(letterᵢ)

where.def: mean luminance of the run of mid-tone cells
run length in cells; also the correlation weight
measured pixel coverage of glyph c in the cam's font, spaces = 0

artifacts.caption: the bench itself: runs in the page, about two seconds, then shows the frames and tables
the source, grammar, tonal and control frames plus both stills' tables, captured headless
the deck now has card 08

payload.left_rough: I measured the effect, not how it reads to a person. Nobody has looked at a grammar and a tonal frame side by side and said whether the difference shows, and to my eye in the proof image it barely does. Ink is each letter's pixel coverage, which is not the same as perceived darkness. I tested only two stills, neither of them you on a live camera. I did not change the bias default in 05 or 07.
next_moves: Raise the tone bias default in 05 and 07 from 0.6 to 0.85. The bench shows that roughly doubles what's still to gain, up to near the ceiling.
Try to widen the brush: let tonal fit choose letter weight inside a word (case, or a bold/light font pair), and rerun the bench to see whether patch match rises above +0.17.
Then the next step of the proposed plan: make the words react to the face moving. A blink rewrites the line on the eyes, and an open mouth moves the speech line forward.
Offer the finding to Language as a Tonal Medium through an elder: yes at line scale, faint at letter scale.
