payload.content:
**Why re-render instead of fix.** The finishing pass can only change a take's level. A take MusicGen played thin or breathy stays that way at any level, so the only real fix for a bad key is a better take.

**What it does** ([redo_keys.py](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Generative%20Sample%20Libraries/ai-source-probe/redo_keys.py)). For each key you name, it renders six fresh takes on seeds never used before and grades them. It throws out the take that held the key, and fresh takes may only fill the keys you named, so nothing else moves. Then it reruns the same chain as the shipped build (pitch check, bow attacks, loops, one level, velocity, DecentSampler) and plays each named key old then new. A redo file keeps each round's rejections, so a second round doesn't undo the first.

**Round one.** I picked the three keys the measurements liked least. A#3 swelled 4.3 dB into its loop. C4's take sat so quiet it needed an 18.8 dB lift. C5 needed a 12.6 dB cut. Eighteen renders took about four minutes. Exactly those three keys changed, and the other 39 play the same samples as before. All 42 keys are on pitch in SFZ and DecentSampler, and all 24 seams are clean on a 12-second hold.

**Hear it in place.** [ab.wav](open:Projects/Generative Sample Libraries/ai-source-probe/instruments/finished/violin_r1/ab.wav) holds each key 4 s, the shipped build first and then the redo. For the whole instrument, play the shipped [phrase.wav](open:Projects/Generative Sample Libraries/ai-source-probe/instruments/finished/violin/phrase.wav) and then the redo's [phrase.wav](open:Projects/Generative Sample Libraries/ai-source-probe/instruments/finished/violin_r1/phrase.wav). The tune is in C, so C4 and C5 come round often. To play it, drag [MusicGen Violin.dslibrary](open:Projects/Generative Sample Libraries/ai-source-probe/instruments/finished/violin_r1/MusicGen Violin.dslibrary) onto DecentSampler.

**How this answers your open violin ask.** If you name keys, they go straight into this loop as the next round. I also drafted where the loop would sit in the interview skill: [interview-redo-step-proposal.md](obsidian://open?vault=The%20Palace&file=Projects/Generative%20Sample%20Libraries/interview-redo-step-proposal.md). It needs an elder to land it.

payload.headline: The glide is built and measured. With one shared glide the octaves agree to 0.0 cents; give each voice its own and they split by 32 to 1006 cents.
payload.ground: shipped · six measured clips, playable browser glide, theory section, Gen~ notes · steward leans the timbre move next
payload.catchup: The Shepard Tone Synthesizer is a teaching instrument that reveals the endless-staircase illusion one layer at a time, after Escher's impossible staircase. The first two layers are done: a still drone that the ear hears as one note across seven octaves, and a stepping climb with the seam deliberately shown. In June you chose the glide as the next layer: every octave slides together, so the pitch moves smoothly instead of in steps. The question is why the octaves must move as one. Six glide renders from September were never posted. This cycle measured that question directly, built a version you can play in the browser, wrote the matching theory section on my page, and wrote down what the Gen~ patch will need, since Max is paused. Next on the plan is the timbre move: each octave gets its own filter, and we hear what that does to the illusion.
payload.content:
**Start here:** [the playable glide](open:Projects/Shepard Tone Synthesizer/session-3-interactive.html). Press start, then play C, E, G, C on the keys (or A, D, G, A on your keyboard) and keep climbing. The circle shows every octave as a dot on one spoke. Raise 'drift' and the spoke fans out, and the readout gives the split in cents. Try 'Hz slew' for the common patching mistake, and 'endless up' with drift for the surprise below. The review layer is on, so you can leave notes against each section.

**What I measured.** I rendered one climbing phrase (C E G C′ E′ G′ C″, 0.8 s a note) six ways and tracked, sample by sample, how far the audible octaves disagree about which note they're playing. A, one shared glide on pitch: 0.0 cents. B to D, each voice with its own glide time, ±15 %, ±40 % and ±80 % across the stack: up to 32, 93 and 217 cents. E, each oscillator ramping at 150 Hz per second: up to 1006 cents, because the low voices land almost at once and the high ones crawl. F, one shared glide run on Hz instead of pitch: 0.0 cents. The glide's curve changes, but a single smoother keeps every ratio. So the curve is a free choice, but sharing one glide is not. That answers my page's old Design Challenge 4.

**The surprise.** I expected mismatched glide times to smear only the moves between notes. On an endless climb they never heal. Each voice trails the moving target by its own glide time, so the octaves stay mistuned for as long as the climb lasts. The formula predicts 16.2 cents at 2 st/s with ±30 % drift, and the engine measures 16.2.

**Checks.** The browser engine and the Python renderer are separate code. On the lockstep phrase their outputs correlate at 0.9999999992, and on clip C they agree to 0.1 cent.

**The September renders**, posted at last: the glide at 0, 120, 450 and 1200 ms, a broken out-of-sync glide, and a long endless glissando. They're in the artifacts below.

equations.label: One glide, on pitch
equations.worded: (pitch now) = (smoothing) × (pitch a sample ago) + (1 − smoothing) × (target pitch),   smoothing = e^(−1/(glide time × sample rate))

where.def: target pitch in semitones
glide time

equations.label: Every voice rides the same path
equations.worded: (frequency of voice k) = 261.63 Hz × 2^((pitch now) ÷ 12 + (voice k's octave number))

where.def: whole octaves, −5 … +5

equations.label: Why drift never heals on an endless climb
equations.worded: (voice k's distance from its octave, in cents) ≈ (climb speed in semitones per second) × (voice k's glide time − the shared glide time) × 100

where.def: semitones per second

table.caption: The same climbing phrase, six ways to glide · worst disagreement among audible octaves (louder than −20 dB)

artifacts.caption: The playable glide: keys, glide time, drift, Hz slew, endless up and down, the pitch-class circle. Review layer on.
The stack climbing two octaves; each voice's error under drift and under Hz slew; the disagreement for all six clips.
A · one shared glide: one note sliding up forever.
B · ±15 % drift: up to 32 cents apart.
C · ±40 % drift: up to 93 cents apart.
D · ±80 % drift: up to 217 cents apart.
E · the patching mistake: every oscillator ramps at 150 Hz/s.
F · one shared glide on Hz: a different curve, still one note.
Renders and measures all six; writes the figure and manifest.
Every parameter and every number quoted here.
September · no glide: the steps, for reference.
September · 120 ms glide.
September · 450 ms glide.
September · 1200 ms glide.
September · voices out of sync: where the illusion breaks.
September · the endless glissando.

payload.left_rough: Nobody has heard any of it, me included. payload.headline: The timbre layer is built and measured. Overtones keep the illusion if each filter follows its voice and the window sits on the voice, not the sum.
payload.ground: shipped · timbre layer proven in Python and browser · steward leans tuning next, in Python
payload.catchup: The Shepard Tone Synthesizer is a teaching instrument that shows Escher's endless staircase in sound, one layer at a time. Three layers are done and measured: a still drone the ear hears as one note across seven octaves, a stepping climb that shows its seam, and the glide, where every octave slides together because they all share one pitch path. The plan's next layer was the timbre: give each voice overtones and its own tone filter that follows its octave, and hear what that does to the illusion. Max work is paused, so this cycle built that layer in Python and in the browser. Six renders, a figure, and an instrument you can play in the browser are in the bundle. There's a matching theory section on my page, and build notes for the Max patch once the pause lifts. The result: the illusion survives overtones, but two wirings break it, and one of them is the architecture my own page drew.
payload.content: Each voice is now a sawtooth through its own tone filter. Every clip is the same endless climb at 2 semitones a second, and only the wiring changes. A filter set four times above each voice's pitch keeps 92 % of the energy on the played note. At sixteen times it is 84 %, plus 9 % on the fifth, which the ear takes as color because every voice adds the same fifth. There are two ways to break it. If the filter follows the played note instead of each voice ([D](open:Projects/Shepard Tone Synthesizer/proofs/2026-10-18-stage4-D-tracks-note.wav)), the pitch stays seamless but the brightness drops about 0.2 octave once per octave: the seam comes back in the tone. If the loudness window sits on the summed audio, as my architecture section drew it ([E](open:Projects/Shepard Tone Synthesizer/proofs/2026-10-18-stage4-E-sum-window-11.wav)), voices far below hearing get in through their overtones. The wrapping voice arrives at −30 dB instead of −134, and voices under 20 Hz flutter. Widening the stack to 15 voices ([F](open:Projects/Shepard Tone Synthesizer/proofs/2026-10-18-stage4-F-sum-window-15.wav)) pushes the thump down to −64 dB, but the flutter stays. With sine waves those two wirings were identical, which is why Stages 1 to 3 never caught it. I've corrected the architecture section on my page. Try it in [the browser instrument](open:Projects/Shepard Tone Synthesizer/session-4-interactive.html). Its spectra match the Python renders: 1.0000 on A and D, 0.9975 at worst on E.

payload.headline: Lumpiness is now a knob. It sets how hard the lock hits, from a switch to a slow arrival, and moves the lock point only about 3%.
payload.ground: shipped · third knob measured, spec updated · steward leans give it a gentler curve next
payload.catchup: Neural Granular Synthesis plays a crowd of neurons, and how much they agree is the timbre. Two knobs drive it. Tightness is how hard the neurons pull on each other. Life is the share of pacemakers that ignore the pull. Past the lock point, which theory puts at tightness 1/(1 − life), hiss snaps into a tone. Last cycle showed that the soft, gradual lock I'd been blaming on pacemakers actually comes from how unevenly the crowd is spread out. This cycle I made that unevenness a knob of its own, called lumpiness, and measured it on 512 neurons. It does what I guessed: it sets how hard the lock hits and barely moves where it sits. The crowd's RNBO codebox doesn't have it yet, because Max work is paused.
payload.content:
**WHAT THE KNOB IS.** Each neuron has a place in the crowd's spread of natural rates, and a starting phase. At lumpiness 0 those places are evenly spaced, the way the codebox does it. Lumpiness adds a random nudge to each place, scaled by the knob, and wraps the result back into range. The wrap matters. The crowd's overall spread stays uniform at every setting, so theory's lock point shouldn't move. Only how evenly the crowd covers that spread changes. At lumpiness 1 the crowd is as random as the one on the board.

**WHAT IT DOES.** I swept tightness from 0.8× to 1.2× the lock point. That's 4 lumpiness settings × 2 lives × 3 random crowds, each settled for 4 seconds. In the table, 'width' is how far you have to turn tightness, as a share of the lock point, to go from loose (synchrony 0.3) to locked (0.7). With no pacemakers the width grows from 0.025 to 0.111. With half pacemakers it grows from 0.024 to 0.173. So pacemakers do soften the lock, but only in a lumpy crowd. On their own they don't change the attack at all. The cost: the half-lock point slides from 0.99× to 0.96× of the lock point.

**WHAT IT MEANS FOR PLAYING.** Each knob now has one clear job. Tightness says where you are relative to the lock. Life moves the lock point and makes the tone breathe. Lumpiness sets the attack. One catch: the knob is front-loaded. With no pacemakers, the width more than doubles by lumpiness 0.25 (0.025 to 0.064), and with half pacemakers it gets nearly all the way (0.134 of 0.173). A playable knob should spend more of its travel near zero, probably by squaring it.

**LISTEN.** In [lumpiness-attack.wav](open:Projects/Neural Granular Synthesis/lumpiness-attack.wav), three 9-second passes at half pacemakers and 512 neurons ramp tightness from 0.8× to 1.15× the lock point. The ramp crosses the lock point at 4 seconds. The first pass is even (lumpiness 0), the second half lumpy (0.5), the third fully lumpy (1). The even crowd should stay hiss and then snap to a tone at about 4.2 s. The lumpy ones should start pulling together before 3 s and swim in. The right panel of [lumpiness.png](open:Projects/Neural Granular Synthesis/lumpiness.png) traces their synchrony over time.

**PAGE EDITS.** The spec gets a new section on lumpiness, with the equation written in symbols and in words and the numbers above, plus a row in the table of how the knobs combine. My entry's list of population controls gains lumpiness, and the pacemaker line now says what pacemakers actually do.

payload.headline: The jitter below the lock was never the meter. Just short of locking, the crowd surges toward agreement, and the pacemakers cause it.

payload.catchup: Neural Granular Synthesis plays a crowd of neurons, and how much they agree is the timbre. Tightness is how hard they pull on each other, life is the share of pacemakers that ignore the pull, and lumpiness (added last cycle) is how unevenly the crowd is spread. Past the lock point, hiss snaps into a tone. Since cycle 13 I'd left one question open: the evenly spread crowd's synchrony jumps around below the lock, and I didn't know if the 10 ms meter was causing that or the neurons were. payload.content: I read the crowd's synchrony at every sample (24,000 a second) on 512 neurons, at fixed tightness just under the lock, and compared three readings of the same run: the raw per-sample value, the 10 ms snapshot the meter shows, and a 10 ms average. All three swing by the same amount, and none of the wobble is faster than 50 Hz, so the meter isn't folding fast motion into noise. The swings are slow, one to six surges a second, and they come from the pacemakers. In an even crowd with no pacemakers, synchrony sits near chance with a swing of 0.05. At 20% pacemakers the swing is 0.08, and at half it's 0.16, with spikes up to 0.65–0.8, nearly locked, before it falls back. The free-running pacemakers keep sweeping past the core and briefly drag it into agreement. You can hear it: in the audition, with the level-rider on, the loudness swings more than twice as much with half pacemakers (0.26 against 0.11). This also explains a note I'd carried since cycle 12, that the even crowd at 50% pacemakers locks early at 0.95×: the surges reach the lock before the steady state would. I wrote the first part of an answer into the open question on my page about pacemakers and liveliness.

**Open [the flow dish](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/slime-mold-flow-dish.html) and press THE MUSIC MOVES.** The dish fills with a fine gold lattice, and within a few seconds it thins to a few roads. SPREAD A MESH floods it again whenever you want it to rethink. Two new dropdowns put cycle 10's mold back so you can compare by ear. [The strip](open:Projects/Slime Mold Delay/headless/2026-10-18-mesh-dish-carving.png) shows a browser run at 1.5, 9, 14 and 29 seconds.

**A mesh alone made it worse.** On the clustered dish (listener at the left, four flakes fanned out on the right) a mesh with the old law went from 1.73× to 2.0× the shortest network. Drawing it showed why. The old law lets a tube's thickness level off as its flow rises, so two parallel roads that split a load both stay full and neither has to lose. The mesh carved down to one separate road per flake.

**Two changes made the roads compete.** First, thickness now grows faster than the flow it carries (Tero's power law), so a road carrying twice the flow ends up more than twice as thick, and parallel roads fight until one wins. That alone gave a rake: each flake kept its own road and they met only at the listener. Parallel roads sit at the same pressure, so the cross-links between them carry nothing and die before the roads can merge. Second, the flakes take turns, the trick in Tero's Tokyo model: the flake that just sounded pushes, and the other flakes that are still sounding draw half the flow alongside the listener. That puts pressure between neighbouring roads, so roads can merge into trunks. Two smaller changes go with it. Under the new law a road feeding one flake is thin by design, so a tube is pruned when it carries almost no flow, not when it's thin, and its gain follows its flow so that flake isn't buried. A flake that falls silent stops drawing, so its road can let go when the music moves.

**What changed, on 40 seeded dishes per row** (table). The round dish now feeds all five flakes in 30 dishes instead of 10. In 5 of them the network uses less tube than the shortest straight-road network, which means real shared trunks, the way the mold does it. The cycle-10 mold never did that.
